application: Check whether a shopper can identify the correct size using measurements and relevant conversions without leaving the product page.
do: Put body measurements, size conversions and fit guidance on the product page itself.
dont: Offer only size labels like S, M and L with no measurements.
finding: Uncertainty about sizing can stop shoppers choosing otherwise suitable apparel. Baymard reports that 83% of desktop and 87% of mobile apparel sites lack sufficient sizing information, meaning they miss at least one of the 10 size-guide elements the article lists, even though nearly all offer some sizing details.
limitation: Published benchmark percentages describe the sampled sites and period, not every current retailer.
measurement: Size-related returns; size-guide use; product-to-cart rate
method: Large-scale usability testing of desktop and mobile apparel e-commerce sites, feeding Baymard's Apparel UX benchmark
plain: Shoppers who can't tell which size will fit often don't buy. Nearly all clothing sites give some sizing details, but most miss at least one key part of a good size guide.
sample: Not stated on page (number of sites, participants and test period not given)

stat.text: of mobile apparel sites (83% on desktop) in Baymard's benchmark lack sufficient sizing information.

application: Show available and unavailable sizes clearly; test selection and error recovery on mobile.
do: Show sizes as buttons, with unavailable sizes visibly marked.
dont: Hide sizes and their stock status inside a dropdown menu.
finding: Dropdowns can hide size availability and make the selector easy to overlook; visible buttons expose the choices earlier. Baymard's benchmark found 71% of desktop sites now use size buttons (up from 63% in 2017), while 28% of sites selling many size variants still rely on dropdowns.
limitation: The recommended pattern is not a quantified revenue guarantee; large variant sets need careful layout.
measurement: Selection errors; add-to-cart completion
method: Large-scale desktop and mobile usability testing, including an eye-tracking study, combined with Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: When sizes sit in a dropdown, people can miss the selector and can't see what's in stock until they open it. Size buttons show every option and its availability at once.
sample: Benchmark of the top 93 e-commerce sites; participant counts and testing period not stated

application: Build a product shoot brief that answers fit and appearance questions; assess whether review photos and fit feedback would help.
do: Show on-model photos, browsable customer photos and an overall fit rating from reviews.
dont: Rely only on flat product photos with no fit feedback.
finding: Apparel shoppers need evidence of appearance and fit. Baymard reports that 90% of sites miss at least one key part of the apparel buying process, and recommends complete sizing information, on-model imagery, browsable reviewer photos, per-size buttons and an aggregate fit score in reviews.
limitation: Benchmark percentages describe Baymard's sampled sites; some figures on this page differ from those in Baymard's related articles (e.g. sizing 82% here vs 83% elsewhere) without explanation, and overlapping Baymard entries are not independent studies.
measurement: Product questions; fit returns; product-to-cart rate
method: Usability testing and UX benchmarking of Apparel & Accessories sites across desktop, mobile and European sites
plain: Clothes shoppers need to see how an item looks and fits on a real body. Most sites miss at least one key piece, such as on-model photos, customer photos or a fit score from reviews.

application: Use it as a broad audit entry point, then open the underlying article relevant to each observed issue.
do: Check each product page for size buttons, in-scale images, unit prices and an easy-to-find return policy.
dont: Treat benchmark ratings as proof that a fix will raise sales.
finding: Only 48% of benchmarked desktop sites (38% mobile web, 36% apps) reached a 'decent' or better product-page UX rating, and no site was rated state of the art. Common gaps include missing size-selection buttons, in-scale images, unit pricing and return-policy access on the page.
limitation: Benchmark ratings are researcher judgements against Baymard's own guidelines, not measured sales impact; the free article covers only a subset of the guidelines, and some figures differ slightly between sections of the page.
measurement: Task completion; product-to-cart rate
method: Expert benchmark: Baymard researchers manually reviewed and scored product-page UX against weighted guidelines across 12 topics, supplemented by moderated usability testing and quantitative surveys
plain: Experts scored the product pages of 155+ big shops, and fewer than half reached 'decent' on desktop. Common misses: size buttons, photos that show scale, unit prices and the return policy on the page.
sample: 155+ leading US and European ecommerce sites, scored separately for desktop, mobile web and apps (30,000+ manually assigned scores); surveys of 1,026-1,193 respondents; benchmark period not stated

application: Compare product copy with actual customer-service questions and identify missing decision information.
do: Compare product copy against real customer-service questions and fill the gaps.
dont: Leave key decision details for shoppers to ask customer service about.
finding: Product pages should answer questions, support comparison, show customer experiences, and make purchase actions understandable.
limitation: Qualitative guidance with no participant count or statistics on the page; 2019 research, so specific interfaces and shopper expectations may have shifted.
measurement: Product questions; returns; purchase completion
method: Qualitative usability research on ecommerce sites with think-aloud observation, plus review of hundreds of product-page examples
plain: A product page's job is to answer shoppers' questions, help them compare options, show what other customers experienced, and make the buying steps clear.

application: Inspect recently viewed items, navigation labels, selected states, and product comparisons for unnecessary memory demands.
do: Show recently viewed items and keep chosen options visible on screen.
dont: Make shoppers remember a product name or an earlier choice to find it again.
finding: Recognizing visible options generally requires less memory effort than recalling information without cues.
limitation: A general usability principle, not proof that every extra visible element improves performance.
measurement: Task errors; backtracking; time to find
method: Not stated (conceptual article drawing on cognitive-psychology memory models and one cited CHI 2008 study on web revisitation)
plain: People find it easier to pick from options they can see than to remember things unaided. Show recently viewed items, clear labels and current choices instead of making shoppers recall them.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Recognition instead of recall

application: Segment speed and conversion by device and traffic source; build a business case from your own data.
do: Track real-user page speed alongside sales for each device and traffic source.
dont: Treat a link between speed and sales as proof without a controlled test.
finding: Farfetch tracked real-user performance alongside business KPIs and found, by correlation, conversion falling about 1.3% on average per extra 100ms of LCP; after LCP work cut product-page LCP by over 600ms, an A/B test showed a conversion uplift in the 1–5% range.
limitation: Most figures are observational correlations from one retailer with no reported sample size or period; only the LCP image change was A/B tested, so speed alone is not shown to cause the other differences.
measurement: LCP; conversion by performance cohort
method: Observational case study: lab data plus real-user monitoring of Core Web Vitals and other timing metrics, statistically correlated with business KPIs; one A/B test of LCP image-loading changes
plain: Farfetch found fewer visitors bought when its pages showed their main content more slowly. When it sped up product pages, a test showed a small rise in buying.
sample: Not stated on page (no data volume, period, geography or device split given)
strengthWhy: Single-site case study without a control group.
title: Farfetch: connecting speed with business measures

application: Check whether above-the-fold product and hero images are discovered and prioritized appropriately.
do: Load the first product and hero images straight away with high priority.
dont: Lazy-load or fade in the first image people see.
finding: After removing lazy loading and transitions from first-position images and adding fetchpriority, the share of good LCP rose from 57% to 96%; the matched store cohort saw mobile session-to-paid-order conversion up 8.9% year over year.
limitation: Year-over-year comparison of a matched Brazilian store cohort without a control group; seasonality and other platform changes may confound causality. Not a randomized lift estimate.
measurement: LCP; mobile paid-order conversion
method: Before-and-after case study: PageSpeed Insights and real-user monitoring diagnosed LCP problems (CSS transitions, lazy-loaded hero images, missing priority hints); fixes rolled out and business metrics compared year over year with no control group
plain: The first images shoppers saw were set to load late. Once they loaded first, the share of pages with good main-content speed rose from 57% to 96%.
sample: Platform of over 180,000 stores; conversion cohort = same Brazilian stores active in Jan 2025 and Jan 2026, mobile visitors from Google organic search (store count not stated)

stat.text: good LCP share after Nuvemshop stopped lazy-loading its first images, up from 57% (web.dev case study).

strengthWhy: Single-site case study without a control group.
title: Nuvemshop: prioritizing the right images

application: Use the linked official quick reference to scope keyboard, labels, contrast, focus, and other checks.
do: Scope accessibility audits against WCAG 2.2 Level AA using W3C's quick reference.
dont: Treat an automated scan result as proof the site is accessible.
finding: WCAG sets testable success criteria at levels A, AA and AAA, organised under four principles (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust); WCAG 2.2 (October 2023, updated December 2024) is backward compatible with 2.1 and 2.0, apart from 4.1.1 Parsing now being obsolete, and W3C encourages using the latest version.
limitation: This entry is an orientation, not a conformance audit or legal conclusion; automated testing alone is insufficient, and WCAG 3 is still only an early draft, not a standard.
measurement: Task access; keyboard completion; issue counts
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: WCAG is the international checklist for accessible websites, graded Level A, AA and AAA. Version 2.2 is the latest and builds on the older 2.1 and 2.0 versions.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: WCAG overview and official standards

application: Measure real-user experience and inspect important page templates; separate field observations from lab diagnostics.
do: Track LCP, INP and CLS from real visitors, separately for mobile and desktop.
dont: Judge speed only from one lab test on a fast office computer.
finding: Core Web Vitals cover loading (LCP, good at 2.5 s or less), responsiveness (INP, 200 ms or less) and visual stability (CLS, 0.1 or less); a page passes when all three meet the target at the 75th percentile of real page loads, measured separately for mobile and desktop.
limitation: Passing performance thresholds does not guarantee conversions, rankings, or an otherwise usable page.
measurement: LCP; INP; CLS
method: Not applicable (metric definitions and thresholds)
plain: Google scores how fast the main content appears, how quickly a page reacts to taps, and whether things jump around. A page passes when three quarters of real visits meet all three targets.
sample: Not applicable; thresholds are assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads, split by mobile and desktop
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Core Web Vitals definitions

application: Audit event coverage and item parameters, then reconcile purchases and refunds with commerce records.
finding: Google's GA4 guide defines a standard set of ecommerce events, from list views and item selection through cart, checkout, shipping and payment steps to purchase and refund, plus promotion views and clicks, all sharing a common items array.
limitation: Documentation of how to send events, not evidence about user behaviour; the page does not address consent, attribution or cross-device gaps, so correct tagging still leaves those measurement limits.
measurement: Event completeness; duplicate transactions; reconciliation
method: Not applicable (official developer documentation with code samples)
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GA4 ecommerce measurement

application: Recruit relevant shoppers for a narrow task, observe problems, fix them, and repeat.
finding: Nielsen argues that roughly five participants per round reveal most of the problems a larger qualitative test would, so budget is better spent on repeated small rounds; he notes quantitative studies need at least 20 users, card sorting about 15 per group, and distinct user groups need their own participants.
limitation: Five participants is not a universal sample rule and cannot establish conversion lift or population prevalence.
measurement: Observed task failures; issue recurrence
method: Expert argument based on diminishing returns, supported by a look at 83 NN/g consulting projects (users tested vs findings reported) and a poll of 217 conference attendees
sample: 83 NN/g consulting studies; 217 UX Conference attendees surveyed on their practice
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Choosing a usability-study sample

application: Distinguish cart creation, checkout entry, and payment failure in your own funnel before choosing fixes.
do: Split your funnel into cart, checkout entry and payment steps before choosing fixes.
dont: Treat every abandoned basket as a lost sale you can win back.
finding: Baymard's average of 50 studies puts documented cart abandonment at about 70%, but its own survey shows many abandoners were just browsing; among the remaining reasons, unexpected extra costs led by a wide margin, ahead of slow delivery, distrust of card handling and forced account creation.
limitation: Different studies, years, definitions, and survey samples should not be treated as one clean experiment or recoverable-revenue estimate.
measurement: Cart-to-checkout; checkout-to-purchase; payment failures
method: Average of 50 published third-party cart-abandonment studies, combined with Baymard's own quantitative survey of US online shoppers on why they abandoned
plain: About 70% of online baskets are abandoned, but many of those people were only browsing. Among those who quit for a reason, surprise extra costs led by a wide margin.
sample: 50 studies spanning 2006–2025; reasons survey of US online shoppers, sample size not stated on page

stat.text: average documented cart abandonment across 50 studies compiled by Baymard (2006–2025).

strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.

application: Check if shoppers can combine relevant sizes or colors and remove active filters without losing context.
do: Offer price, rating, colour, size and brand filters where they apply. Let people tick several values, and show chosen filters with an easy remove.
dont: Make filter values either-or, or hide what's been applied so people can't tell why results look thin.
finding: Product finding depends on usable lists, relevant filters, combinable choices and visible applied filters. In Baymard's 2025 benchmark, 58% of desktop and 78% of mobile sites scored mediocre or worse overall for product lists; 51% lacked some essential filter types, 14% blocked multiple selections within a filter type, and 20% had no applied-filters overview.
limitation: Researcher-scored sites do not establish sales gains from your implementation; catalogue needs differ, and the scoring scale is not fully explained on the page.
measurement: Product-finding success; zero-result filters
method: Manual expert review and weighted scoring of sites against Baymard's product list and filtering guidelines (2025 benchmark), informed by Baymard's large-scale usability testing
plain: When experts scored 170+ big US and European shops, most made narrowing down products harder than it should be. The fixes are simple: let people tick several options, and always show what's applied.
sample: 170+ leading ecommerce sites in the US and Europe; 21,000+ UX parameters scored; usability-test participant numbers not stated

stat.text: of mobile shops (58% on desktop) scored mediocre or worse for product lists in Baymard's 2025 review.

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.

application: Write a test plan and monitor data quality and guardrails before interpreting an apparent win.
finding: Recommends computing a full metric set (data quality, overall evaluation criterion, feature and guardrail metrics) early and often, alerting on guardrail moves and sample ratio mismatch, auto-stopping harmful tests, and segmenting results by date. One example: a Microsoft News test's early 28% click lift faded day by day, revealing a novelty effect.
limitation: Large-platform practices may need adaptation for small retailers; the article does not solve limited statistical power.
measurement: Data quality; guardrail metrics; experiment validity
method: Practitioner guidance from Microsoft's Experimentation Platform team, based on its experience running A/B tests plus cited literature (part 2 of a series)
sample: Not stated on page (number of experiments not given)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Trustworthy experimentation while a test runs

application: Replace unclear category or CTA labels with language shoppers can interpret, then test first-click choices.
do: Write menu and link labels that name exactly what is behind them.
dont: Use vague labels like 'Learn more', 'Explore' or in-house brand names on their own.
finding: Raluca Budiu explains that people choose links by information scent, their rough guess at how useful a destination will be for their goal. Scent comes from the link label (the strongest cue), nearby text and images, page context and prior trust in a brand; vague labels such as 'Learn more' and jargon weaken it, and context is less reliable on small screens.
limitation: A framework-based article with examples, not a tested study; it reports no data, and scent depends on audience and task, so it cannot pick the best taxonomy on its own.
measurement: First-click success; backtracking
method: Conceptual article applying information-foraging theory (including social foraging) with illustrative site examples; no study reported
plain: People decide what to tap by guessing where each link leads. Specific labels like 'Laptops' make that guess easy; vague ones like 'Learn more' or 'Solutions' leave them guessing.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Information scent and navigation labels

visual.cap: A shopper looks for a new laptop

application: Keep clear labels visible as users type and revisit fields.
do: Put a visible label above each field that stays there while people type.
dont: Rely on grey placeholder text inside the box as the only label.
finding: Katie Sherwin lists problems with using placeholder text as the only label: it vanishes while typing (straining memory), makes checking and fixing entries harder, can be mistaken for a pre-filled answer, often has poor contrast and is not read by some screen readers. Floating labels fix some but not all of these; labels outside the field are still best.
limitation: Draws on unquantified testing and eyetracking with no sample sizes or effect sizes; short familiar forms like search or login are less affected.
measurement: Correction errors; completion
method: Expert guidance based on the author's user testing and eyetracking studies plus NN/g mobile usability research; no study design reported
plain: If the hint inside a box is the only label, it disappears as soon as someone types. Then they can't check what each box was for, and some screen readers never read it.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Persistent form labels

visual.cap: A shopper checks their details before continuing

application: For complex applications, show a clear summary with specific edit links and an explicit submit action.
do: Show a summary of every answer with a 'Change' link, then return people to it after edits.
dont: Make people click back through every step to fix one answer.
finding: GOV.UK places one check-answers page just before confirmation in small to medium services (one per section for very long ones), listing each question, answer and a 'Change' link, then a declaration and a submit button named for its action. After a change, people return to the summary rather than redoing later steps, and skipped optional questions show as 'Not provided'.
limitation: Government-service pattern with no research results on the page; for a short checkout an extra review screen may add friction rather than help.
measurement: Submission errors; successful corrections
method: Design-system pattern guidance; links to a service team blog post and a research discussion but reports no method
plain: Before someone sends an application, show all their answers on one page with a 'Change' link beside each. Fixing one answer should bring them straight back to that summary.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Review answers before submission

visual.cap: An applicant spots a typo before sending

do.cap: one tap to fix, then back

application: Audit rejected names, addresses, and formatting; make errors specific and actionable.
do: Accept harmless variations like spaces and hyphens, and validate when the form is submitted.
dont: Reject a postcode or card number just because it has spaces or dashes.
finding: GOV.UK says to reject only answers that cannot be correct, are too ambiguous to use, or are missing when required, while ignoring stray spaces, hyphens, brackets and full stops when the meaning stays clear. Validate on submit rather than when a field is left or while typing, then redisplay the page with the entered values, an 'Error: ' prefix in the title, an error summary that takes focus, and inline messages.
limitation: GOV.UK's advice to switch off native HTML5 validation (novalidate, no 'required' attribute) assumes its own accessible error components; do not simply remove validation. The page reports no research data and asks for research on client-side validation and on omitting 'required'.
measurement: Repeated errors; recovery rate
method: Not stated (pattern guidance; says the approach has been used over an extended period on services such as Renew or replace your adult passport)
plain: Only reject answers that cannot be right or are missing, and ignore harmless extras like spaces or dashes. Check when the form is sent, then say what went wrong and keep what people typed.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Validation that helps people recover

application: Check label associations and accessible names in addition to visual layout.
do: Link every visible label to its field with matching for and id values.
dont: Rely on a title tooltip or nearby text alone to name a field.
finding: Each form control needs a label tied to it in code, preferably a label element whose for attribute matches the control's id, or a label wrapping the control; aria-labelledby, aria-label or visually hidden labels suit cases where the purpose is clear from context, and the title attribute is not recommended. The tutorial maps to WCAG 1.3.1, 2.4.6, 3.3.2 and 4.1.2.
limitation: Correct labels address only part of accessibility; verify actual browser and assistive-technology behavior.
measurement: Unlabeled controls; assisted task completion
method: Not applicable (implementation tutorial with code examples)
plain: A label that just sits near a box is not enough; it has to be linked to the box in the code. Then screen readers can say what each box is for.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Programmatically associated labels

application: Test whether users notice submission status and can identify and correct the affected field.
do: Put the result in the page heading and title, and list errors with links to each field.
dont: Signal errors with red colour alone, or with a message screen readers never announce.
finding: After a form is sent, the tutorial advises stating the result in the main heading and page title, listing errors above the form with links to each field, and showing messages beside fields with text and icons as well as colour, moving focus to the first error. Checks while typing or on leaving a field use aria-live regions; it references WCAG 3.3.1 (Level A) and 3.3.3 (Level AA).
limitation: Do not rely on visual appearance alone; interaction and announcement behavior require testing.
measurement: Duplicate submissions; error recovery
method: Not applicable (implementation tutorial with code examples)
plain: After someone sends a form, tell them clearly whether it worked. If it did not, list each problem with a link to the field and explain how to fix it.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Clear success and error feedback

application: Group shipping choices, contact options, and related questions in both layout and markup.
do: Wrap each radio group and repeated address block in a fieldset with a short legend.
dont: Rely on layout alone to show that boxes belong together.
finding: Related controls should be grouped in code as well as visually: a fieldset with a short legend for radio groups and for repeated sets such as shipping and billing addresses, role="group" with aria-labelledby as an alternative, and optgroup for related options in a select. The tutorial maps to WCAG 1.3.1 and 3.3.2 (both Level A).
limitation: Visual proximity alone does not communicate the relationship to every assistive technology; this is tutorial guidance, not user research, and long legends may be repeated by some screen readers on every control.
measurement: Group comprehension; assisted task errors
method: Not applicable (implementation tutorial with code examples)
plain: Related choices, like a set of radio buttons or a billing address, need a group name in the code as well as on screen. Then screen readers can say which group each box belongs to.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Semantic and visual form grouping

application: Review spacing between each label, its field, and the next question.
do: Place labels just above their fields and add extra space between groups such as contact and payment details.
dont: Space labels evenly between fields so it's unclear which box each one describes.
finding: Marieke McCloskey advises placing each label closer to its own field than to neighbouring fields, grouping related fields with extra white space between groups, and putting labels above fields; her example regroups a 15-field form into three groups of 4–6 fields. The article reports no study data.
limitation: No study data or effect sizes are reported, so no universal pixel spacing or guaranteed conversion uplift follows from this article.
measurement: Field confusion; task completion
method: Not stated (expert guidance with illustrative form examples, including a recreated 15-field registration form)
plain: Put each label right next to its own box and leave more space between groups of questions. Then people can see at a glance which label goes with which box.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Whitespace that clarifies relationships

application: Separate essential actions from advanced settings and test whether secondary features remain discoverable.
do: Put the most-used options up front and label the link to advanced settings clearly.
dont: Bury settings three or more levels deep, or hide information people need to decide.
finding: Show only the most important options first and reveal specialised ones on request; Jakob Nielsen argues this improves learnability, efficiency and error rates when the split between initial and secondary features is right and the route to secondary options is clearly labelled. He advises no more than two levels of disclosure.
limitation: Essential decision information should not be hidden simply to achieve a cleaner appearance; the supporting studies are not described, so benefits are argued rather than measured.
measurement: Primary task success; secondary feature discovery
method: Expert commentary citing a usability study of 46 web-based applications and a hotel reservation test, without giving their methods or results
plain: Show the few options most people need first, and tuck rarely used ones behind a clearly labelled link. More than two layers of hidden options gets people lost.
sample: Not stated on page (one cited study covered 46 web-based applications)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Progressive disclosure

do.cap: basics first, extras one tap away

application: Use the framework to structure an expert review, documenting concrete issues and their context.
do: Have several reviewers check a flow against the ten heuristics and log each issue against one of them.
dont: Treat a heuristic review as proof that real users will succeed.
finding: Jakob Nielsen's ten heuristics cover visibility of system status, matching real-world language, user control and freedom, consistency, error prevention, recognition over recall, flexibility, minimalist design, error recovery, and help. The set has stayed the same since 1994, with wording and examples refreshed in 2020.
limitation: Heuristic evaluation is not user testing; general principles do not prove prevalence or severity.
measurement: Observed issue severity; later user validation
method: Heuristics first developed in 1990 by Jakob Nielsen with Rolf Molich; revised in 1994 through a factor analysis of 249 usability problems
plain: Ten broad rules of thumb for judging an interface, such as keeping people informed, using their language, letting them undo mistakes and preventing errors. Experts use them to review designs before testing with users.
sample: 249 usability problems (1994 factor analysis); not described further on page
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Ten usability heuristics

application: Classify image purpose in context before writing alt text; communicate an image link's action when needed.
do: Describe the destination for linked images and give purely decorative images an empty alt.
dont: Use the file name or the same generic description on every image.
finding: The decision tree chooses alt text by an image's purpose: text in images is repeated in alt unless it already appears nearby, images inside links or buttons describe the action or destination, informative images get a short description, complex images such as charts need their information elsewhere on the page, and purely decorative images get an empty alt.
limitation: A generic image description is not always the right alternative, complex information may need text elsewhere, and the tree says it does not cover every case or cite specific WCAG success criteria.
measurement: Image meaning and action comprehension
method: Not stated (decision-tree tutorial from the W3C WAI Education and Outreach Working Group)
plain: The right description for an image depends on what it does. A linked picture should say where it goes, a decorative one should be skipped, and a chart needs its data written out nearby.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Alternative text depends on image purpose

application: Check initial focus, tab containment, closing behavior, and appropriate focus restoration.
do: Move focus into the dialog, keep Tab inside it, and return focus to the opening button on close.
dont: Let Tab wander behind an open pop-up, or drop focus at the top of the page when it closes.
finding: When a modal dialog opens, focus moves inside it; Tab and Shift+Tab wrap within it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the control that opened it. The container needs role dialog, aria-modal set to true and an accessible name (ideally from a visible title), and a visible close button is strongly recommended.
limitation: APG is informative implementation guidance, not a conformance certification; aria-modal should be set only when outside content is both blocked and visually obscured, and production code still needs testing with assistive technology.
measurement: Keyboard task completion; focus failures
method: Not applicable (pattern guidance with two examples)
plain: When a pop-up opens, keyboard focus should jump into it, stay inside while it's open, close with the Escape key, and land back where the person was afterwards.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Accessible modal interaction

application: Define the primary task and check whether the visual emphasis supports it across screen sizes.
do: Make the one main action the most prominent element and keep type to about three sizes.
dont: Give several buttons and headings equal weight, so nothing stands out.
finding: Visual hierarchy orders elements so the eye meets them by importance, using contrast in value and saturation, scale and grouping (proximity, white space, containers). NN/g suggests limits such as about 3 type sizes, at most 2 large elements, and not relying on colour alone.
limitation: Expert guidance with no user study or data; the numeric limits are rules of thumb, and an expert review cannot show how every audience reads a screen.
measurement: First-click success; comprehension
method: Expert article using annotated examples from websites and packaging and a blur 'squint test'; cites two design textbooks; no user study
plain: People notice the biggest, highest-contrast things first. When everything shouts, nothing stands out, so pick what matters most and make only that prominent.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Visual hierarchy

visual.cap: A shopper looks for the next step

application: Provide meaningful status during slow interactions and test perceived responsiveness.
do: Show a progress bar with a Cancel button for any wait likely to pass ten seconds.
dont: Leave the screen frozen with no sign anything is happening for several seconds.
finding: Nielsen sets three response-time limits: about 0.1 second feels instant, about 1 second keeps the user's flow of thought, and about 10 seconds is the limit for keeping attention. Delays over about 1 second should show the system is working, and over about 10 seconds need a percent-done indicator and a way to cancel.
limitation: Broad historical thresholds drawn from older perception research, not modern conversion benchmarks or hard limits; it reports no new data.
measurement: Abandonment during waits; repeated clicks
method: Synthesis of earlier perception research (Miller 1968; Card et al. 1991) from Nielsen's book Usability Engineering; updated 2014; no new study
plain: Under a tenth of a second feels instant; around one second people notice but stay on track; beyond about ten seconds they lose focus. Longer waits need visible progress and a way to cancel.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Response-time expectations

visual.cap: What a person experiences while waiting
visual.note: Illustration. Times are the source's own thresholds.

application: Check that an open, wide search field appears near the top of every template, and review zero-result and first-results outcomes for the most common queries.
do: Show a wide, open search box near the top of every page.
dont: Hide search behind a small magnifying-glass link that opens a separate page.
finding: In the author's ecommerce study, 51% of users found what they wanted on the first query, 32% on the second and 18% on the third, and almost half of users whose first search failed stopped searching. Replacing a search link with an input box on one homepage raised search use by 91%.
limitation: Dates from 2001 with no sample sizes. The 91% figure comes from one site, and query behaviour has likely changed since autocomplete and mobile search became common. Treat as foundational, not current.
measurement: Search usage rate; first-query success rate; search exit or refinement rate
method: Draws on usability tests that are not fully described: an ecommerce shopping study across several sites and intranet tests.
plain: Make search an open box on every page, not a link to a search page. In an older study, putting a box on one homepage nearly doubled how often people searched.
sample: Not stated on page (a 2002 addendum scores 20 sites against an earlier checklist)

stat.text: rise in search use when one homepage swapped a search link for an open box (Nielsen, 2001; single site).

strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Why site search should be an open box on every page

visual.cap: A visitor wants to find a product fast

application: Limit suggestions to about 10 on desktop and 4 to 8 on mobile, style category-scoped suggestions differently from plain queries, and make the highlighted suggestion keyboard-navigable.
do: Show about 10 suggestions on desktop and 4 to 8 on mobile, with arrow-key support.
dont: Dump a long list of 15+ suggestions that fills the whole phone screen.
finding: Baymard's benchmark found autocomplete on 80% of ecommerce sites (up from 72% in 2014), yet only 19% implemented every detail well. In testing, lists longer than about 10 suggestions on desktop or about 8 on mobile overwhelmed users.
limitation: Test sample size is not given, and the 80% and 19% figures describe how common the patterns are, not their effect on conversion.
measurement: Suggestion click-through rate; suggested vs typed searches; search-to-product-view rate
method: Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark combined with desktop and mobile usability testing
plain: Most shops show search suggestions as you type, but few do it well. Too many suggestions overwhelm people, so keep the list short, especially on phones.
sample: Test participant and site counts not stated on page; linked gallery holds 446 autocomplete examples

stat.text: of ecommerce sites implemented every autocomplete detail well, though 80% offered autocomplete (Baymard benchmark).

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Nine patterns for effective search suggestion dropdowns

visual.cap: A shopper types 'sofa' on a phone

application: Before judging your search on looks, test realistic queries of each type: product type, feature, symptom, misspelling and synonym.
do: Test search with real queries: product types, features, problems, misspellings and synonyms.
dont: Sign off site search because the search box looks good.
finding: Testing on 19 sites surfaced more than 700 search-specific usability issues, which Baymard turned into guidelines. It found weak search in every industry and argues search quality can only be judged by testing queries, not by inspecting the interface.
limitation: A landing page for a mostly paid research product; detailed guidelines and scores are behind Baymard Premium. The page contains internal count inconsistencies (guideline and page totals), so cite its figures with care.
measurement: Search success rate by query type; no-results rate; search-to-add-to-cart rate
method: Moderated usability testing of 19 leading ecommerce sites in 8 verticals, plus a benchmark scoring sites against Baymard's search guidelines
plain: Testing on 19 shops found more than 700 search problems. You can only tell if search works by trying real searches, not by looking at the search box.
sample: Participants aged 21 to 56; 19 sites tested; 344 US and European sites benchmarked; testing years not stated
strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Baymard's ecommerce search research programme

application: Audit checkout step by step, prioritising guest checkout, field count and validation, then compare drop-off by step before and after each change.
do: Audit checkout step by step, starting with guest checkout, field count and validation.
dont: Quote Baymard's estimated conversion gain as a promised result.
finding: Baymard puts average cart abandonment at 70.19%, from studies tracked over 14 years. In its benchmark, 65% of sites scored mediocre or worse on checkout UX and 2% scored good. It estimates a typical large site could raise conversion about 35% through better checkout design.
limitation: The 35% figure is an estimate drawn from test sessions, not a measured live-site result. The abandonment rate is an aggregate that includes people who were only browsing. Detailed guidelines are paywalled. Shares its evidence base with BD-018.
measurement: Step-to-step checkout completion; cart abandonment rate; checkout completion time
method: Moderated think-aloud usability testing, a benchmark scoring sites against 110+ checkout guidelines on a weighted 7-point scale, eye-tracking and quantitative studies
plain: Baymard's experts rate most big shops' checkouts mediocre or worse, and only a few as good. Guest checkout, the number of fields and error messages are common places to start.
sample: Across Baymard's programme: 25 test rounds, 4,400+ participant/site sessions, 344 US/EU sites benchmarked, 12 quantitative studies with 20,240 participants over 14+ years; no checkout-only breakdown

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's checkout benchmark scored mediocre or worse on checkout UX.

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Baymard cart and checkout research hub

application: Inventory every validation message; rewrite generic ones to name the problem and fix, place errors beside the field with an icon or text as well as red, and confirm entered data survives a failed submit.
do: Place each error beside its field, flag it with an icon or text as well as red, and say how to fix it.
dont: Show a vague message like 'Invalid input' or wipe what people typed after a failed submit.
finding: Useful error messages sit next to the cause, use more than colour to stand out, describe the problem specifically in plain words without blame, and suggest a fix. They keep what the user already entered and avoid flagging a field before the user has had a chance to complete it.
limitation: Heuristic guidance built on examples, not a measured study, so it does not show the size of any effect on completion.
measurement: Error rate per field; resubmission success after an error; abandonment after an error
method: Not stated
plain: A useful error message sits right next to the problem, says plainly what went wrong and how to fix it, and keeps what the person already typed.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Writing and placing error messages people can act on

visual.cap: A shopper mistypes their email at checkout

application: On a failed submit, show a linked error summary above the heading, prefix the page title with an error label, and check each link moves focus to the right input, including multi-part fields such as dates.
do: Show a linked error summary at the top and move focus to it after a failed submit.
dont: Leave people to scroll and hunt for red fields.
finding: When validation fails, show a summary box at the top of the main content even for a single error. Each item links to the field at fault with the same wording as the inline message, and keyboard focus moves to the summary.
limitation: No effectiveness data on the page. A government-service pattern not validated specifically on ecommerce flows.
measurement: Time to correct after failed submit; second-attempt success rate; screen-reader task completion
method: Not stated
plain: When a form has mistakes, show a box at the top listing each one, with links that jump straight to the field. Keyboard and screen reader users land on it first.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Summarising validation errors at the top of the page

visual.cap: An applicant presses Continue with one answer missing

application: Remove every field you cannot justify, label optional fields explicitly, and test whether your checkout progress indicator helps before keeping it.
do: Make the page heading the question itself and label optional fields '(optional)'.
dont: Add a progress bar or required-field stars without checking they help.
finding: Question pages use a back link, a heading that is the question itself, and a left-aligned continue button. Optional fields are marked optional instead of starring required ones. One government team removed a 12-step progress indicator and saw no change in completion rate or time.
limitation: Written for government transactional services. The progress-indicator example is one service, reported second-hand, and may not transfer to retail checkout.
measurement: Fields per form; completion rate; median time to complete
method: Not stated (refers to user research generally and one team's experiment reported in a GOV.UK blog post)
plain: Each form page asks one clear question as its heading, marks optional fields as optional, and has a back link. One team removed a 12-step progress bar and saw no change in completion or time.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Structuring forms as one question per page

visual.cap: Someone filling in a government form on a phone

application: Check login and registration markup for correct autocomplete values, real labels instead of placeholders, a show-password control, and server-side validation alongside browser checks.
do: Use autocomplete values such as username and current-password, and add a show-password toggle.
dont: Build custom sign-in fields that password managers cannot recognise or fill.
finding: Sign-in forms work better with semantic form elements, correct input types, the right autocomplete tokens (username, current-password, new-password) and stable name/id values so password managers can fill them. It also recommends a show-password toggle and keeping fields clear of the mobile keyboard.
limitation: Implementation advice with no measured conversion effects; last updated in 2020, so it predates passkeys and newer credential APIs.
measurement: Sign-in success rate; password resets per sign-in attempt; sign-in page exit rate
method: Not stated (best-practice guide with demos)
plain: Sign-in forms built with standard fields and the right hints let browsers and password managers fill in details. A 'show password' button helps people check what they typed.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Building sign-in forms that browsers can autofill

visual.cap: A returning customer signs in on a phone

application: Audit checkout fields for correct autocomplete attributes, a single card-number field that accepts spaces, flexible name and address inputs, and a visible guest option.
do: Use plain card and address fields with autofill hints, and accept international formats.
dont: Build custom card widgets or a card-type picker that autofill can't fill.
finding: The guide recommends guest checkout by default, removing navigation and promotions from checkout, and asking only for data that is needed. Name and address fields should allow international formats, and card entry should use plain inputs with autocomplete hints rather than custom widgets or a card-type picker.
limitation: No original data; guidance, not evidence of uplift. Last updated in 2020.
measurement: Autofill usage on checkout fields; payment-step error rate; guest vs account completion
method: Not stated (best-practice guide citing outside sources such as Baymard)
plain: Checkout forms work better when guests can buy without an account, distractions are removed, only needed details are asked for, and card fields let the browser fill them in.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Making checkout address and card fields less painful

visual.cap: A shopper reaches the card details step

application: Measure the rendered physical size of swatches, quantity steppers, close icons and filter chips on real phones; enlarge or space out anything under about 1cm, starting with add-to-cart and checkout actions.
do: Make tappable items at least about 1cm square on the real screen, with gaps between neighbours.
dont: Squeeze tiny close icons or swatches right next to each other.
finding: NN/g recommends interactive elements of at least about 1cm by 1cm as rendered on screen, with larger primary calls to action and space between neighbouring targets. The 1cm figure traces to Parhi et al. (2006); the MIT work cited puts typical fingertip width around 1.6 to 2cm.
limitation: Guidance, not a new controlled study; NN/g reports no participant counts for its own observations.
measurement: Mis-tap rate on small controls; physical target size in mm; variant-selection time
method: Expert guidance from reviewing real apps and sites plus published finger-size research (Parhi, Karlson & Bederson 2006; MIT Touch Lab)
plain: Buttons and links on a phone need to be at least about 1cm across on screen, with space between them, so a fingertip hits the one it means to.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Physical sizing for finger-friendly tap targets

visual.cap: A shopper taps with their thumb

application: Audit icon buttons, pagination dots, rating stars and mini-cart controls; flag anything under 24x24 CSS px that also fails the spacing test.
do: Make icon buttons, rating stars and pagination dots at least 24 by 24 px, or space them apart.
dont: Pack tiny quantity and remove buttons right next to each other.
finding: Success Criterion 2.5.8 (Level AA) requires pointer targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. Smaller targets can pass through exceptions: sufficient spacing (a 24px circle on each target overlaps no other), an equivalent conforming control, inline text links, browser-controlled sizing, or essential presentation.
limitation: A conformance floor, not an optimal size. 24 CSS px is well below what touch-usability research recommends (see BD-045), and the page reports no user-performance data.
measurement: Targets under 24x24 px per template; undersized targets passing the spacing exception; 2.5.8 pass/fail by page type
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Anything people tap or click must be at least 24 by 24 pixels, unless it has enough space around it or another control does the same job. Tiny icons crammed together fail.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: WCAG 2.2 minimum pointer target size

visual.cap: Shown at actual size on your screen

application: Check sale-price labels, placeholder text, grey helper copy and text over hero images against 4.5:1, and give designers a token palette of pre-validated pairs.
do: Check sale prices, helper text and text over images reach 4.5:1 against their background.
dont: Use light grey text on white for prices or form hints.
finding: Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Level AA) requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for regular text and 3:1 for large text (18pt, or 14pt bold). Logos, decorative text, inactive controls and incidental text in images are exempt.
limitation: Passing the ratio does not guarantee readability; thin typefaces and busy backgrounds are not fully captured. Non-text contrast is a separate criterion (1.4.11).
measurement: Text pairs below 4.5:1; share of design tokens passing AA; automated contrast errors per page
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Text needs enough difference from its background to be read: 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. Check pale grey prices and placeholder text first.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Text contrast thresholds under WCAG 2.2

application: Tab through listing, product and checkout pages with sticky headers, promo bars and cookie banners active; add CSS scroll-padding so focused fields never end up hidden.
do: Add scroll padding so focused fields stay clear of sticky headers and banners.
dont: Let a cookie banner or sticky footer cover the field that has keyboard focus.
finding: Success Criterion 2.4.11 (Level AA) says a component receiving keyboard focus must not be entirely hidden by author-created content. Partial overlap is allowed; sticky headers and footers, cookie banners and non-modal dialogs are named as common causes of failure.
limitation: AA forbids only complete hiding, so a mostly covered element still passes. It does not judge how visible the focus indicator itself is.
measurement: Fully hidden focus stops in a keyboard pass; templates with scroll-padding; keyboard-only checkout completion
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: When someone moves through a page with the keyboard, the highlighted item must not end up completely hidden behind sticky headers, cookie banners or pop-ups.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Keeping keyboard focus visible past sticky UI

application: Gate parallax, fly-to-cart effects and animated page transitions behind prefers-reduced-motion and confirm they stop when the OS setting is on.
do: Honour the device's reduce-motion setting for parallax, page transitions and fly-to-cart effects.
dont: Force decorative animation on everyone with no way to switch it off.
finding: Success Criterion 2.3.3 (Level AAA) requires that motion animation triggered by interaction can be disabled unless the motion is essential. Sufficient techniques include honouring the prefers-reduced-motion media query in CSS and JavaScript.
limitation: AAA, so not required by most AA-based legal and procurement targets. No prevalence or harm data on the page.
measurement: Share of animations gated by reduced-motion; non-essential motion with no off switch; QA pass rate with reduced motion on
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Animations that play when you scroll or click, like parallax or items flying into the basket, should stop when someone asks for less motion, unless the motion is essential.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Letting people switch off interaction-triggered motion

application: Audit homepage and product carousels for a visible pause control, keyboard-reachable previous/next buttons, slide-position announcements and logical focus order; default to no auto-rotation.
do: Add a visible pause button and previous and next buttons that work from the keyboard.
dont: Auto-rotate slides with no way to stop them.
finding: Carousels need structure assistive technology can interpret, full keyboard operation with predictable focus, and a way to stop and restart automatic rotation, because moving content can make text hard to read.
limitation: Last updated 2017, before WCAG 2.2. Explains how to make carousels accessible, not whether they perform well.
measurement: Pause control present; keyboard operability pass/fail; click-through on slides after the first
method: Not applicable (tutorial)
plain: Sliding banners must work with a keyboard and a screen reader, and need a way to pause them, because moving content can make text hard to read.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Building accessible carousels

application: Test product-page tabs (description, specs, reviews): arrows move between tabs, Tab reaches the panel, roles and states are exposed. Use manual activation when panels load lazily.
do: Let arrow keys switch tabs and the Tab key move into the open panel.
dont: Build tabs from plain links that screen readers can't recognise as tabs.
finding: The tabs pattern uses tablist, tab and tabpanel roles with aria-selected and aria-controls. Tab moves into the active tab and then the panel; arrow keys move between tabs. Selecting on focus is advised only when the panel appears without perceptible delay.
limitation: A reference pattern with no user-testing data; it does not say whether tabs beat accordions or long-scroll layouts for discoverability.
measurement: Keyboard pattern conformance; screen-reader announcement accuracy; engagement with non-default tabs
method: Not applicable (pattern reference)
plain: Tabs such as Description, Specs and Reviews should work from the keyboard: arrow keys move between tabs and the Tab key jumps into the content. Screen readers also need to know which tab is selected.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Keyboard and ARIA blueprint for tabs

application: Make the most common failure types (contrast, alt text, form labels, empty links, empty buttons, document language) the first sweep of any accessibility audit.
do: Start every audit by sweeping for low contrast, missing alt text and unlabelled form fields.
dont: Treat a clean automated scan as proof that a site is accessible.
finding: In the 2026 report, 95.9% of the million home pages had automatically detected WCAG failures (94.8% in 2025), averaging 56.1 errors per page. Low-contrast text was most common (83.9% of pages), followed by missing alt text (53.1%) and unlabelled form inputs (51%).
limitation: Home pages only, and only what automated tools detect. Zero detected errors does not mean accessible; says nothing about checkout or deep templates.
measurement: Automated errors per page; pages with low-contrast text; unlabelled inputs and empty buttons
method: Automated WAVE testing of the rendered DOM against WCAG 2.2 A/AA; errors are detected issues highly likely to be conformance failures
plain: An automatic scan of the top million home pages found almost all had detectable accessibility failures. The most common were low-contrast text, missing image descriptions and form boxes without labels.
sample: 1,000,000 home pages from the Tranco ranking, collected February 2026

stat.text: of the top million home pages had automatically detected WCAG failures in WebAIM's 2026 scan.

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Annual automated accessibility scan of top home pages

application: Make the mobile menu control large, high-contrast, labelled and visibly separate from the logo; expose four or five top categories directly where space allows.
do: Make the mobile menu button large, high-contrast, labelled 'Menu' and clearly apart from the logo.
dont: Tuck a small, faint menu icon right beside the logo.
finding: On phones, a prominent menu at the top of the page got far more use than a small, low-contrast menu icon beside the logo: 89% of participants used navigation on one site versus 44% on another, and time to first navigation use was shorter (24 vs 33 seconds).
limitation: Six specific 2016 sites with no per-site sample sizes, and results varied by site. Shows that visibility mattered there, not a universal conversion effect.
measurement: Share of sessions using navigation; time to first navigation use; category-finding task success
method: Quantitative remote usability testing (with WhatUsersDo) comparing hidden, visible and combination navigation; this article reports smartphone results
plain: On phones, a menu that stands out at the top of the page got used far more than a small, faint menu icon next to the logo, and people found it sooner.
sample: 179 participants across six websites; per-site samples, geography and period not stated

stat.text: of participants used navigation on the site with a prominent menu, versus 44% on another (NN/g study, 179 participants across six sites).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: What helps mobile users find the menu

visual.cap: A visitor on a phone looks for a category

do.cap: menu and top sections stand out

application: Cap hero carousels at about five slides, show position indicators, turn off auto-advance on mobile, and repeat critical promos elsewhere on the page.
do: Keep to a few slides, show which slide is showing, and repeat key offers elsewhere on the page.
dont: Auto-rotate banners on mobile or put an important offer only on a late slide.
finding: Visitors often scroll past a rotating hero and see only its first slide, so later slides can go unseen. The guidance favours few slides, clear position indicators, large distinct controls, and no auto-rotation on mobile or when slides look like ads.
limitation: Largely qualitative with no described study design. Does not prove carousels convert worse than a static hero.
measurement: Click-through by slide position; sessions that see slide 2+; static vs carousel A/B conversion
method: Not stated (expert guidance with site examples; refers to unspecified eyetracking research)
plain: Many visitors scroll past a rotating banner and only ever see its first slide, so the offers on later slides often go unseen.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Making homepage carousels earn their space

application: Front-load product descriptions and policy pages: lead with the key point, start subheads and bullets with information-carrying words, and replace vague link text with descriptive labels.
do: Start headings and bullet points with the words that carry the meaning.
dont: Publish product or policy text as long, unbroken paragraphs.
finding: When a page offers no formatting cues and readers want to be efficient, gaze concentrates on the top lines and the left edge and much of the right side is skipped. The pattern appeared on mobile and mirrors in right-to-left languages. Headings, bolded keywords and lists redirect scanning.
limitation: Qualitative heatmaps without percentages or statistical tests. Describes default behaviour on unformatted text; does not measure the effect of reformatting on sales.
measurement: Scroll depth and dwell on content blocks; engagement with late-paragraph links; comprehension in user tests
method: Eyetracking heatmaps, gaze plots and gaze replays from NN/g studies
plain: Faced with a plain wall of text, people read the first lines and then skim down the left edge, missing most of the rest. Headings, bold keywords and lists help them find what matters.
sample: Example heatmaps from 45+ and 47 participants; mobile and Arabic examples unsized; geography and period not stated
strengthWhy: Eyetracking study: measures where people look, not sales.
title: Why unformatted text gets scanned in an F shape

application: On listing pages where shoppers compare or refind items, test Load More or pagination against infinite scroll, and restore scroll position when users return from a product page.
do: Use a 'Load more' button on lists where people compare or come back to items.
dont: Use endless scrolling on a product list that also has a footer people need.
finding: Endless scrolling suits aimless browsing of similar items but makes refinding items hard, hides the footer, can suggest the list has ended, and creates accessibility and SEO problems. A Load More button avoids several issues at the cost of a click; no pattern suits every site.
limitation: Drawbacks are expert judgments rather than measured outcomes; the cited studies' samples are not summarised.
measurement: Product views per listing session; return-to-position success; footer link engagement
method: Not stated (expert guidance drawing on three cited academic studies and site examples)
plain: Endless scrolling suits casual browsing, but makes it hard to find an item again, hides the footer, and can make a list seem to end early. A 'Load more' button avoids several of these problems.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Infinite scroll, Load More or pagination

application: Replace full-page spinners on listing and product pages with layout-matched skeletons, and pair this with real performance work rather than using it to mask slowness.
do: Show a layout-shaped placeholder while a full listing or product page loads.
dont: Cover the whole page with a spinner, or use placeholders to hide a slow site.
finding: A placeholder that previews the page layout during a full-page load reassures users the page is working and can make the wait feel shorter. The article suggests it for loads under about 10 seconds, a spinner for a single module, and a progress bar for longer waits.
limitation: Timing thresholds are given without supporting data; no evidence of an effect on conversion or abandonment.
measurement: Perceived wait (survey); bounce during load; Largest Contentful Paint
method: Not stated (explanatory guidance citing one 2018 academic study)
plain: While a whole page loads, a grey outline of the layout reassures people that something is coming and can make the wait feel shorter than a spinning wheel.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: When skeleton placeholders beat spinners

visual.cap: A shopper opens a category page

application: Audit checkout submit, payment processing and uploads: acknowledge the click immediately, loop for short waits, show percent or steps for long ones, and drop 'don't click twice' warnings.
do: Acknowledge every tap at once and show progress for anything over about a second.
dont: Leave the screen frozen during payment, or show a 'don't click twice' warning instead of progress.
finding: In the cited experiment, people shown a moving progress bar were more satisfied and on average willing to wait about three times longer than people shown nothing. It recommends feedback for anything over about 1 second, a looping indicator for 2 to 10 seconds and percent-done for longer waits.
limitation: Rests on one experiment whose sample and setting are not described. Does not show effects on completion or revenue in live commerce.
measurement: Abandonment during processing; duplicate submissions; post-task satisfaction
method: Cites a University of Nebraska-Lincoln experiment comparing a looping progress bar with no indicator, plus Nah (2004) and anecdotes
plain: People wait longer and feel better when they can see something is happening. In the cited test, a moving progress bar beat showing nothing at all.

stat.text: longer, on average, was how long people were willing to wait with a moving progress bar versus no feedback, in one experiment cited by NN/g.

strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Animated progress feedback raises tolerance for delays

visual.cap: A shopper presses Pay now

application: Check that each key template shows its main message and primary action in the first screen, with the most important supporting content in the second.
do: Put the main message and the main button on the first screen, with key details just below.
dont: Hide the main action at the bottom of a long page behind decorative banners.
finding: About 57% of viewing time was above the fold and 74% within the first two screenfuls; attention dropped sharply after the fold. In 2010 the above-fold share had been 80%, so people scroll more now, but the top of the page still gets the most looks.
limitation: Desktop only, data year not given, and it measures where eyes look, not clicks or conversion; it does not show that every primary action must be above the fold.
measurement: Primary CTA click rate; Scroll depth; Share of clicks on below-fold content
method: Eyetracking analysis of where fixations fell on pages viewed on a 1920×1080 screen, compared with a 2010 study on 1024×768 monitors
plain: People do scroll, but most of their looking happens on the first screen, and nearly three-quarters within the first two. Things lower down get far less attention.
sample: 120 participants, 130,000+ fixations, across news, ecommerce, blog, FAQ and encyclopedia pages; collection year not stated

stat.text: of page-viewing time was above the fold (NN/g eyetracking, 120 participants, 130,000+ fixations, desktop).

strengthWhy: Eyetracking study: measures where people look, not sales.
title: Most attention lands in the first two screens
