visual.note: Illustration. The dashed line marks the bottom of the first screen.

application: Audit checkout and subscription flows: include mandatory fees in the first price shown, require affirmative opt-in for recurring charges, make cancelling as easy as signing up, and give accept and decline equal visual weight.
do: Show mandatory fees in the first price and make cancelling as easy as signing up.
dont: Reveal unavoidable fees only at checkout or bury the cancel option.
finding: The report groups deceptive design into interfaces that create false beliefs, hide or delay key terms such as drip-priced fees, lead to unauthorised charges such as hard-to-cancel subscriptions, and undermine privacy choices. A cited third-party study found users not shown fees upfront spent about 20% more and were 14% more likely to buy.
limitation: A non-binding U.S. staff report; the pattern list is not exhaustive, many cited cases are allegations or settlements, and its statistics come from outside studies. Not legal advice.
measurement: Gap between first price shown and final total; cancellation vs sign-up steps; opt-in rate under neutral defaults
method: Qualitative staff report drawing on a 2021 public workshop, public comments, academic research and FTC enforcement cases
plain: A US regulator's review lists tricks that mislead shoppers, such as hiding fees until late, making subscriptions hard to cancel and steering privacy choices. A study it cites found hidden fees made people spend more.
sample: Not stated; cited figures come from third-party studies
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: FTC staff review of manipulative interface tactics

application: Audit input borders, checkbox outlines, custom focus rings, selected-state swatches and chart lines on PDP and checkout against their adjacent colours with a contrast checker and fix anything under 3:1.
do: Check input borders, checkbox outlines and focus rings reach at least 3:1 against neighbouring colours.
dont: Round a near miss like 2.999:1 up to a pass.
finding: SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (Level AA) requires the visual cues needed to identify UI components and their states, plus graphic parts needed for understanding, to reach at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colours; ratios are not rounded, so 2.999:1 fails. Disabled controls, unmodified browser-default styling, and essential graphics such as logos or photos are exempt, while custom focus indicators must meet the 3:1 threshold.
limitation: Normative minimum only; it does not show that 3:1 is sufficient for all low-vision users or measure task impact, and it excludes hover states and disabled controls.
measurement: Share of UI components meeting 3:1 boundary contrast; custom focus indicators passing 3:1; chart/graphic elements below threshold
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Input borders, checkboxes, focus rings and meaningful graphics must stand out from what's next to them with at least 3:1 contrast, so people can see controls and what's selected.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Contrast Rules for Controls, Focus Rings and Meaningful Graphics

application: Zoom key templates (home, PLP, PDP, cart, checkout) to 400% in a 1280px-wide browser and log every element that forces sideways scrolling, clips, or hides functionality.
do: Zoom each key template to 400% in a 1280px-wide window and fix anything that scrolls sideways or disappears.
dont: Use fixed-width layouts that make people scroll left and right to read each line.
finding: SC 1.4.10 Reflow (Level AA) requires content to be usable without losing information or function and without two-way scrolling at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels (vertical-scrolling content) or a height of 256 CSS pixels (horizontal-scrolling content); 320px matches a 1280px viewport zoomed to 400%. Content that genuinely needs a 2D layout, such as maps, video, games or data tables, is exempt for those parts only.
limitation: Defines a pass/fail threshold, not evidence of how many users zoom or how much reflow failures reduce conversion.
measurement: Templates passing reflow at 320 CSS px; count of components causing horizontal scroll; functions lost at 400% zoom
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Someone zoomed in to 400% should still be able to read and use the page by scrolling only up and down, not sideways too. Maps, videos and data tables are exempt.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Single-Direction Scrolling at 400% Zoom

application: Run a text-spacing bookmarklet on buttons, nav menus, product cards and promo banners, and replace fixed heights or overflow:hidden containers that clip or overlap text.
do: Let buttons, menus and product cards grow with their text instead of fixing their height.
dont: Put labels in fixed-height boxes that hide overflowing text.
finding: SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing (Level AA) requires that no content or function is lost when users set line height to 1.5x the font size, paragraph spacing to 2x, letter spacing to 0.12x and word spacing to 0.16x. Clipping, overlap, or ellipsis truncation that cannot be revealed counts as failure (F104).
limitation: Values are a tested baseline rather than a proven optimum; the page does not quantify how many users apply spacing overrides.
measurement: Components clipping text under override; fixed-height containers with text; truncated labels without reveal mechanism
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Some people widen the gaps between lines, letters and words to read more easily. When they do, no text or function should get cut off, overlap or disappear.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Layouts Must Survive User-Overridden Text Spacing

application: Add a 'same as billing' delivery option, keep card and address data after a failed payment, and pre-fill earlier answers in multi-step checkout or account flows.
do: Offer 'Same as delivery address' and keep entered details after a payment error.
dont: Rely on browser autofill and make people retype what they already gave you. (WCAG 3.3.7, Level A.)
finding: SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (Level A, new in WCAG 2.2) requires that information a user already entered or was given within the same process be pre-filled or offered for selection when needed again, with exceptions for essential re-entry, security (such as passwords), and data that is no longer valid. Relying on browser autofill alone does not satisfy it; the site itself must supply the data, though cross-session storage is not required.
limitation: Covers only a single process/session; it gives no data on abandonment or error rates caused by re-entry.
measurement: Fields requiring re-entry within one flow; data retained after validation or payment errors; presence of 'same as billing' option
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Within one process, a site should not make people type the same thing twice, like their address for delivery and billing. It should fill it in or offer it to pick.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Never Make Users Retype What They Already Gave You

visual.cap: A shopper reaches the billing step

application: Test login and 2FA screens with a password manager and pasted one-time codes; remove paste blockers and mark up username/password fields with correct autocomplete attributes.
do: Allow paste and password-manager autofill on every login and one-time-code field.
dont: Block pasting, or split a code into boxes that reject a pasted code.
finding: SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA) bars cognitive function tests, such as recalling a password or solving a puzzle, at any login step unless an alternative method, a helper mechanism (password manager support, copy-paste), object recognition, or recognition of the user's own uploaded non-text content is offered. Scripts blocking paste or autofill, and split one-time-code fields that reject pasted codes, are described as failures.
limitation: Applies to logging into existing accounts, not sign-up; it does not measure security trade-offs or completion-rate gains.
measurement: Login steps blocking paste or autofill; OTP fields accepting full pasted code; availability of non-cognitive login alternative
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Logging in must not depend on remembering or solving something unless an easier option exists. Letting people paste passwords and codes, or use a password manager, meets this.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Login Without Memory Tests: Paste, Autofill and Alternatives

visual.cap: A shopper pastes a code from their messages
visual.note: Illustration. The code is a made-up example.

application: Inspect the accessibility tree for custom dropdowns, swatch pickers, quantity steppers and icon buttons, and confirm each has a role, accessible name and announced state change.
do: Use native HTML controls, or give custom ones a role, a name and announced state changes.
dont: Build clickable divs or icon-only buttons with no accessible name.
finding: SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A) requires every UI component's name and role to be programmatically determinable, its states and values to be programmatically settable, and changes to be announced to assistive technology; native HTML controls used per spec pass. Listed failures include scripted div/span controls lacking a role (F59), controls with no accessible name (F68), and image-only links without a name (F89).
limitation: Defines what must be exposed, not whether a given screen reader handles it well, and gives no prevalence data on failures.
measurement: Interactive elements missing accessible name; custom controls without role; state changes not announced
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Custom buttons, dropdowns and pickers must tell screen readers what they are, what they're called and their state, such as selected or open. Standard HTML controls already do this.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Custom Widgets Must Expose Name, Role and State

application: Prioritise a logical heading outline on PLP/PDP, remove or replace CAPTCHA in checkout, and test custom menus and dialogs with both JAWS and NVDA plus a mobile screen reader.
do: Give every product list and product page a clear, logical set of headings.
dont: Put a CAPTCHA in front of checkout.
finding: On desktop, JAWS (40.5%) and NVDA (37.7%) were the most common primary screen readers, and 71.6% of respondents said headings are their first way to find information on a long page versus 3.7% for landmarks. CAPTCHA ranked as the most problematic item, followed by menus, tabs and dialogs that behave unexpectedly and ambiguous links or buttons; 91.3% reported using a screen reader on mobile.
limitation: Self-selected, uncontrolled sample that the authors say may not represent all screen reader users; results vary by region and self-reported proficiency.
measurement: Heading structure completeness per template; presence of CAPTCHA in key flows; custom widgets passing JAWS/NVDA/VoiceOver tests
method: Online survey of screen reader users
plain: In a survey of screen reader users, most said headings are the first thing they use to find their way around a long page. CAPTCHA was rated the most troublesome problem.
sample: 1,539 valid responses collected December 2023 to January 2024; about 47% North American; uncontrolled sample

stat.text: of screen reader users in WebAIM's survey said headings are their first way to find information on a long page.

strengthWhy: Survey: what people say, not what they do.
title: How Screen Reader Users Navigate and What Frustrates Them (2024)

application: Audit site search autosuggest and filter dropdowns against the pattern's keyboard map and ARIA attributes, checking that the highlighted suggestion is conveyed via aria-activedescendant.
do: Let Down Arrow move into suggestions, Enter accept one and Escape close the list.
dont: Highlight suggestions only visually so screen readers stay silent.
finding: The APG combobox pattern defines select-only and editable comboboxes whose popup may be a listbox, grid, tree or dialog, with Down Arrow moving into the popup, Escape dismissing it, and Enter accepting a suggestion. It specifies role=combobox with aria-expanded, aria-controls (preferred over the legacy aria-owns), aria-activedescendant for virtual focus, and aria-autocomplete matching the suggestion behaviour.
limitation: Authoring guidance, not a usability study; it does not report how real assistive-technology combinations perform with each variant.
measurement: Keyboard interactions supported vs pattern; required ARIA attributes present; suggestions announced by screen readers
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Search suggestions and type-ahead dropdowns need a standard keyboard map: Down Arrow moves into the list, Escape closes it, Enter picks a suggestion. Screen readers must also be told which suggestion is highlighted.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Building Accessible Autocomplete and Select Comboboxes

application: Check PDP spec/shipping/returns accordions and FAQ sections: header must be a real button inside a heading, with aria-expanded updating on toggle.
do: Put each accordion title in a button inside a heading, and update its open or closed state.
dont: Make accordion titles clickable text that screen readers can't tell will expand.
finding: The APG accordion pattern places each section title in a button that is the sole child of a heading, toggled with Enter or Space, with aria-expanded reflecting visibility and aria-controls pointing to the panel. Panels can optionally be regions labelled by their button, but the guide advises against this when many panels may be open at once (roughly more than six) to avoid landmark clutter.
limitation: Prescribes markup and keyboard behaviour only; it does not address whether hiding content in accordions helps or hurts findability.
measurement: Accordion headers implemented as buttons within headings; aria-expanded accuracy on toggle; excess region landmarks
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Each expandable section title, like Shipping or Returns, should be a real button inside a heading that tells screen readers whether the section is open or closed.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Accordion Markup: Buttons in Headings with Expanded State

application: Replace image-based promo banners containing text with live HTML text and verify they stay legible under 200-400% zoom and Windows high contrast mode.
do: Replace promo banners that have words baked into images with live HTML text.
dont: Put sale messages inside images that blur and break when zoomed.
finding: WebAIM describes common low-vision conditions (macular degeneration, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, cataracts) and notes these users rely on magnifiers, browser zoom, larger text and high-contrast or custom colour modes. It recommends real text over images of text, layouts that keep content and function when zoomed, avoiding horizontal scrolling, adequate contrast without relying on colour alone, and softening harsh pure black on white.
limitation: Expert guidance with no stated research method or statistics; it does not quantify the impact of any recommendation.
measurement: Images of text on key pages; content legibility in high contrast mode; horizontal scroll at high zoom
method: Not stated
plain: People with low vision often zoom in, enlarge text or switch to high-contrast colours. Pages work for them when text is real text, layouts survive zooming and colour isn't the only signal.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Designing for Low Vision: Conditions and Practical Tactics

application: Audit the account-selection step: label the option with the word 'Guest', render it as a primary button placed above sign-in, and show it before any email field is requested.
do: Make 'Guest checkout' a full button above sign-in, using the word 'Guest'.
dont: Style the guest option as a small link below the sign-in form.
finding: In Baymard's benchmark, 47% of sites that permit guest checkout fail to make it the most prominent option on the account step; separately, 24% of surveyed US shoppers said forced account creation alone caused them to abandon at least one cart in the prior quarter. Testing showed vague labels, text-link styling, low placement and hiding the guest option behind email entry all slowed or derailed users.
limitation: Test participant counts and benchmark size are not given; the 24% figure is self-reported US survey data, not observed conversion impact.
measurement: Guest vs. sign-in path selection rate; drop-off at account-selection step; time to proceed past account step
method: Qualitative usability testing across multiple desktop and mobile rounds, plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark of live sites and a quantitative abandonment survey
plain: Many shops that allow guest checkout make it hard to spot. Testers slowed down or got lost when it was a small text link, placed low, vaguely labelled or hidden behind an email box.
sample: Abandonment survey: 4,384 US adults (2022); usability test and benchmark sample sizes not stated on page

stat.text: of surveyed US shoppers said forced account creation alone made them abandon a cart in the prior quarter (Baymard survey of 4,384 US adults, 2022).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Guest checkout should be the top, button-styled choice

visual.cap: A first-time shopper starts checkout

application: Move any 'create an account' prompt from mid-checkout to the confirmation page, pre-fill it from order data so only a password is needed, and list 3–5 concrete benefits such as order tracking and faster reorders.
do: Offer account creation on the order confirmation page, pre-filled so only a password is needed.
dont: Interrupt guest checkout with a 'Create an account' prompt.
finding: Baymard's benchmark found 42% of sites prompt guest shoppers to register before or during checkout rather than waiting until confirmation. In testing, early prompts distracted users, were sometimes misread as mandatory, and annoyed people who had already chosen guest; offering registration after purchase, when only a password is needed, worked better.
limitation: No participant or site counts are given, and the page does not quantify the conversion or registration-rate difference between early and post-purchase prompts.
measurement: Post-purchase account creation rate; checkout completion rate for guest users; mid-checkout exit rate on steps containing registration prompts
method: Large-scale checkout usability testing with observed participants, plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark of live retail checkouts
plain: Asking guests to register during checkout distracts them and can look compulsory. Offering it on the confirmation page, where only a password is needed, worked better in testing.

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's benchmark prompt guests to register before or during checkout instead of at confirmation.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Ask guests to create accounts only after the order is placed

visual.cap: A guest shopper is about to pay

application: Use the ten listed pitfalls as an audit checklist: guest prominence, password rules, delivery dates, cutoff countdowns, cart quantity controls, fulfillment options, field marking, optional-input interface type, adaptive errors and phone-number explanations.
do: Use the ten listed pitfalls as a checklist, starting with delivery dates and specific error messages.
dont: Mark only the optional fields and leave required ones unmarked.
finding: On desktop, 64% of benchmarked checkouts rated mediocre or worse and none rated perfect; common failures included showing delivery speed instead of a date (48% of sites), static cutoff times instead of countdowns (83%), and validation errors that do not adapt to the specific problem (94%). In testing, 32% of participants skipped a required field when only optional fields were marked.
limitation: Ratings are expert judgements against Baymard's own guidelines rather than measured conversions, the full rating scale is not defined on the page, and the 35% conversion-uplift figure is an estimate for an average large site.
measurement: Checkout completion rate; form validation error rate per field; share of checklist pitfalls present at audit
method: Manual expert review and scoring of leading US and European ecommerce checkouts against Baymard's Cart & Checkout guidelines, informed by prior large-scale checkout usability testing and Baymard surveys
plain: Expert reviewers rated most big shops' desktop checkouts mediocre or worse. Common slips include showing delivery speed instead of a date and error messages that don't explain the specific problem.
sample: 41,000+ manually reviewed checkout performance scores; 180+ leading ecommerce sites (per page description); one cited survey of 1,026 US adults who had shopped online in the prior three months

stat.text: of benchmarked checkouts showed validation errors that don't adapt to the specific problem (Baymard 2025 checkout benchmark, 180+ sites).

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: 2025 benchmark of the most common checkout UX failures

application: Replace transit-time labels in the shipping selector with an estimated date or narrow date range beside each option's price, update it for holidays and backorders, and fall back to speeds if a carrier API times out.
do: Show an estimated delivery date or narrow date range next to each shipping option's price.
dont: List only transit times in business days and leave shoppers to do the maths.
finding: 41% of benchmarked sites gave no estimated delivery date. When shown only transit durations like a number of business days, test participants calculated arrival dates themselves and reached different answers because of differing assumptions about cutoffs, weekends and holidays; users treated a shown date as a promise.
limitation: No participant or site counts are given, and no conversion data shows how much delivery dates change purchase behavior; the 5–7 day window threshold is a tendency, not a tested rule.
measurement: Shipping option selection distribution; checkout abandonment at shipping step; 'where is my order' contact rate vs. promised date accuracy
method: Multiple rounds of qualitative checkout usability testing with think-aloud observation, plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: Shoppers want the day their order will arrive, not a count of business days. Given only durations, testers worked out the date themselves and reached different answers.

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's benchmark gave no estimated delivery date.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Show a calendar delivery date next to each shipping option

visual.cap: A shopper needs a gift to arrive by the weekend

application: Add postal-database address validation at the shipping step, present mismatches in a prominent overlay showing original vs. suggested address, and ensure the browser Back button closes the overlay.
do: Show a clear overlay comparing the typed address with the postal database's suggestion.
dont: Rely on a small inline hint that people scroll straight past.
finding: In one test round, 9% of more than 150 orders contained shipping address mistakes such as misspelled streets or wrong house numbers, yet 47% of benchmarked sites offer no address validator. Validators presented as an overlay comparing the typed address with suggestions reliably made users check their entry, while subtle inline validators were often ignored.
limitation: The claim that mobile users err more often is not backed by comparison data on the page, and no delivery-failure or cost data is reported.
measurement: Share of orders with corrected addresses; undeliverable or returned-to-sender rate; validator overlay acceptance rate
method: Multiple rounds of large-scale checkout usability testing on desktop web, mobile web and mobile apps, plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: Typos in delivery addresses are common, and autofill doesn't catch them. An overlay comparing the typed address with a suggested one made testers check, while small inline hints were ignored.
sample: One test round of 150+ placed orders analyzed; benchmark site count not stated on page

stat.text: of 150+ orders in one Baymard test round had shipping address mistakes.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Address validators catch typos that autofill misses

visual.cap: A shopper mistypes their street name

application: Use plus/minus buttons with an optional numeric field, auto-update totals after a 200–300 ms typing pause, let minus or 0 remove the item, and provide undo after removal.
do: Use plus and minus buttons that update the total automatically, with undo after removing an item.
dont: Make people type a number and then find a separate 'Update' link.
finding: 61% of benchmarked sites offer only a dropdown or only a text field for cart quantity. In testing, text fields led to accidental values and unsaved changes when an 'Update' link was missed, long dropdowns were slow to use, and plus/minus buttons were understood fastest.
limitation: Findings are qualitative with no participant counts or error rates; no measured effect on order value or completion is reported.
measurement: Cart quantity edit error rate; cart-to-checkout progression rate; item removal undo usage
method: Large-scale checkout usability testing observing participants changing cart quantities on named retail sites, plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: Changing quantities in the basket went wrong with text boxes, through missed 'Update' links and accidental numbers, and was slow with long dropdowns. Plus and minus buttons were understood fastest.

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's benchmark offer only a dropdown or only a text field for cart quantity.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Plus/minus buttons beat dropdowns for cart quantity edits

visual.cap: A shopper wants one more of an item

application: Visually enclose card fields in a distinct styled container, place one or two recognizable trust badges and brief reassurance copy inside it, and regression-test the layout after every checkout release.
date: 2016-10-05 (content updated with 2023 seal study and 2025 survey data)
do: Put card fields in a clearly boxed area with a recognisable security badge and a short reassurance.
dont: Let card fields blend into the rest of the page with no visible security cues.
finding: 19% of surveyed US users said they abandoned a checkout in the prior three months because they did not trust the site with card details. Users judge security from visual cues rather than technical facts, and in the 2023 seal test Norton ranked highest while a homemade badge outperformed most established SSL seals.
limitation: Seal results measure relative preference among eight badges in US general-population samples, not effect on real conversions; Baymard discloses that Norton's parent company has been a client.
measurement: Payment step abandonment rate; A/B conversion with and without seal/encapsulation; survey-rated perceived security
method: Large-scale checkout usability testing observations combined with repeated comparative seal-preference surveys (2013, then six studies 2015–2023) with randomized seal order via Google Consumer Survey and SurveyMonkey Audience
plain: Shoppers judge whether a payment form is safe by how it looks, not by the technology behind it. In a US survey, 19% had abandoned a checkout because they didn't trust the site with their card details.
sample: 2025 checkout survey: 1,026 US adult internet users; seal study sample size not stated on page

stat.text: of surveyed US shoppers abandoned a checkout in the prior three months over card-trust worries (Baymard survey, 1,026 adults, 2025)

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Perceived payment security and which trust seals users believe

visual.cap: A shopper reaches the card form

application: When adding browser-native or wallet payments, call canMakePayment() first and only render the express-pay button when it resolves true, falling back to the standard card form otherwise.
do: Show the express-pay button only after checking the browser supports it, with the card form as a fallback.
dont: Show a fast-pay button on browsers that can't support it.
finding: The API builds a request from supported payment methods and a required total (with optional line items), checks support with canMakePayment(), opens the payment app sheet via show(), and closes it with complete() after the payment provider responds. The basic-card method is deprecated as of Chrome 100, and Chrome 102+ requires show() to be triggered by a user gesture.
limitation: The page is dated 2018, offers no user research on conversion or usability benefits, and does not describe non-Chrome browser behavior.
measurement: Share of checkouts using native/express payment; payment sheet completion vs. cancel rate; time from payment step to order placed
method: Not applicable (technical documentation)
plain: Browsers can open their own pop-up for paying with saved cards and wallets. Check the browser supports it first, then show the fast-pay button; otherwise show the normal card form.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: How the browser Payment Request API flow works

application: For ticketing or lodging flows, show the all-in price on listing and product pages, make it the most prominent price, and show the final payable amount at least as prominently before the pay button.
do: Show the all-in ticket or lodging price as the most prominent price on listing pages.
dont: Show a lower base price first and add mandatory booking fees at checkout.
finding: From 12 May 2025, businesses advertising live-event tickets or short-term lodging must display a total price including all known mandatory fees more prominently than other price figures. Taxes, government charges, shipping and optional add-ons may be excluded from that total but must be disclosed with amount and purpose before payment is requested.
limitation: Applies only to live-event ticketing and short-term lodging in the US; it is legal guidance, not evidence of user behavior, and general retail is outside the rule's scope.
measurement: Price difference between first-displayed and final price; share of pages showing all-in price; checkout abandonment at fee reveal
method: Not applicable (regulatory guidance)
plain: In the US, sellers of event tickets and short-stay lodging must show the total price, including all compulsory fees, more prominently than other prices. Taxes, shipping and optional extras can be shown separately before payment.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: FTC junk fees rule: upfront total pricing obligations

application: Audit every price shown from ads to checkout for UK users: fold booking, service, packaging and fixed delivery fees into the headline price and remove any mandatory fee that first appears at checkout.
do: Fold booking, service and fixed delivery fees into the headline price for UK shoppers.
dont: Let a mandatory fee appear for the first time at checkout.
finding: The CMA treats adding unavoidable charges after an initial headline price as prohibited drip pricing; mandatory fees and taxes must be in the price shown from the first advertisement. Delivery charges count as mandatory when the shopper cannot collect, and where they cannot be calculated in advance the calculation basis must sit next to the headline price with equal prominence; later discounts and optional extras are allowed.
limitation: UK-specific and explicitly not a definitive interpretation of the law; it describes compliance expectations rather than measuring consumer harm or conversion effects.
measurement: Number of mandatory fees first revealed after product page; headline-to-final price variance; checkout abandonment at shipping/fee step
method: Not applicable (regulatory guidance)
plain: In the UK, unavoidable fees and taxes must be in the first price a shopper sees. Delivery counts as unavoidable when there's no collection option; optional extras and later discounts are still allowed.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: UK CMA guidance banning drip pricing under the DMCC Act

application: Audit category, product and help pages so the first sentence of each section states the main point or decision-relevant fact, with specs and caveats moved below.
do: Open each section with the main point or the fact a shopper needs to decide.
dont: Bury the key answer under background, history and caveats.
finding: Because web readers skim and often abandon a page early, NN/g recommends opening with the key takeaway and then ordering supporting detail from broadest to most specific. The article argues this aids comprehension, lowers interaction cost and makes it easy to cut text from the bottom.
limitation: Guidance article with no study of its own; it does not quantify how much front-loading improves comprehension or conversion.
measurement: Scroll depth; time to locate key fact in task tests; first-paragraph comprehension score
method: Not stated (practical guidance drawing on linked NN/g reading-behavior research)
plain: People skim and often leave a page early, so put the main point first and the details after it. That way even a quick reader gets the answer.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Put the Conclusion First: Inverted Pyramid for Web Copy

application: Review every button, label and error string against these rules: remove 'click here' links, 'the green button' instructions, apologetic validation messages and redundant words like 'now'.
do: Write error messages that say exactly what to fix, such as 'Enter your postcode'.
dont: Use 'click here' links, 'the green button' instructions or apologetic error messages.
finding: The Service Manual tells teams to keep action labels short, make link text understandable out of context, avoid instructions based on colour or position, use sentence case, and keep validation errors brief without apologies or jokes. It also advises fixing an interface rather than adding explanatory copy, and testing wording with users.
limitation: Style guidance for public services; it cites no performance data and was last substantively updated in 2018, so it may not reflect newer research or commercial contexts.
measurement: Form error rate; task completion rate; screen-reader link-list comprehension in testing
method: Not stated
plain: Keep button labels short and make every link make sense on its own. Error messages should say what to fix, with no apologies or jokes, and instructions shouldn't rely on colour or position.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GOV.UK Rules for Interface Copy: Buttons, Labels and Errors

visual.cap: Someone leaves the postcode field empty

application: Add COGA Objective 3 patterns to the content audit checklist, e.g. flag idioms, double negatives, multi-instruction paragraphs and long documents lacking a summary.
do: Give each step a single instruction written in common words.
dont: Pack several instructions, idioms or double negatives into one paragraph.
finding: This W3C Working Group Note (supplemental to WCAG, not required for conformance) sets an objective of clear, understandable content, with design patterns such as using common words, simple tense and voice, literal language, succinct text, separate instructions per step, summaries for long documents and generous white space. It stresses involving people with cognitive and learning disabilities in testing.
limitation: Non-normative note, not a testable success criterion; it does not provide measured effect sizes for each pattern.
measurement: Share of pages with summary at top; average sentence length; task success for participants with cognitive disabilities
method: Not applicable (standard); task force note built on cognitive accessibility user research, issue papers and gap analysis
plain: People with memory, attention or learning difficulties can struggle with long, complicated text. Use common words, one instruction per step, a summary for long pages and plenty of space.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: W3C Patterns for Clear Content for Cognitive Accessibility

application: Measure reading level of key mobile content (product descriptions, policies) and cut length and complexity, since hard text costs mobile users more time.
do: Shorten and simplify product descriptions and policies people read on phones.
dont: Assume dense, technical text works on phones because it works on desktop.
finding: Comprehension on phones averaged about 3 percentage points higher than on computers, a statistically significant but practically small difference. For difficult articles, in-person readers took roughly 30 ms more per word on mobile, suggesting they slowed down to keep understanding.
limitation: Measured article reading and quiz comprehension, not task flows or purchase behaviour; speed data came only from the 40-person in-person phase, and the device-by-difficulty comprehension interaction was only marginal.
measurement: Flesch-Kincaid grade; reading time per word on mobile vs desktop; comprehension quiz score
method: Participants read easy (avg 404 words, 8th-grade Flesch-Kincaid) and hard (avg 988 words, 12th-grade) articles on phone and computer, then took multiple-choice comprehension quizzes; reading speed timed in the in-person phase; supplemented by focus groups
plain: People understand text on phones about as well as on computers. But with difficult text they read more slowly on a phone, so hard wording costs mobile readers extra time.
sample: Four phases (10-person pilot, 30 online, 40 in-person, 206 online); intro states 276 participants; 1,629 article-read cases analysed
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Mobile Comprehension Holds Up, but Hard Text Slows Readers

application: Inventory every empty cart, wishlist, search-results and order-history state; ensure each has a status message, a one-line explanation and a primary action (e.g. browse bestsellers).
do: Show a message, a one-line explanation and a button in every empty basket or list.
dont: Show a blank area, or 'No records', before the data has finished loading.
finding: Kaplan argues that blank containers leave users unsure whether data is loading, broken or absent, so empty states should state clearly that nothing exists yet, teach what the area is for, and offer a direct action link or button. Showing a 'no records' message before loading finishes is flagged as harmful to trust.
limitation: Example-driven guidance focused on complex enterprise apps; no user data shows the size of the benefit.
measurement: Click-through from empty states; feature adoption after first empty view; support tickets about 'missing' data
method: Qualitative analysis of screenshots from real applications, grounded in usability heuristics; no formal study described
plain: A blank screen leaves people wondering whether something is loading, broken or just empty. Say clearly that nothing is here yet, what the area is for, and give one button to get started.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Writing Empty States That Explain Status and Next Steps

visual.cap: A shopper opens an empty basket

do.cap: says why, offers a next step
do.title: Your basket is empty

application: Set a max-width of around 70-80 characters on body copy and product descriptions, left-align text, and use at least 1.5 line-height.
do: Keep body text to 80 characters per line or fewer, left-aligned, with 1.5 line spacing.
dont: Fully justify long paragraphs so the gaps between words become uneven.
finding: SC 1.4.8 Visual Presentation (Level AAA) requires that, for text blocks, users can pick foreground and background colours, lines are no wider than 80 characters (40 for CJK), text is not fully justified, line spacing is at least 1.5 within paragraphs with larger paragraph spacing, and text resizes to 200% without horizontal scrolling. The rationale is that long lines and uneven word gaps make it hard to track lines.
limitation: AAA criterion that most sites are not required to meet; the page cites little direct research on optimal line length beyond the CJK width ratio.
measurement: Characters per line at common breakpoints; line-height ratio; horizontal scroll at 200% zoom
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Very long lines, fully justified text and cramped line spacing make it hard to follow from one line to the next. This Level AAA rule sets limits such as 80 characters per line and 1.5 line spacing.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: WCAG 1.4.8: Line Length, Spacing and Justification for Legibility

application: Compare on-site labels and navigation terms against the words customers type into site search, and replace internal jargon with those terms.
do: Rename labels and menu items using the words customers type into site search.
dont: Use internal product codes or team jargon in navigation labels.
finding: Digital.gov defines plain language as communication the target audience grasps on first reading or hearing, and notes people search using everyday terms rather than jargon. It outlines Plain Writing Act of 2010 duties for agencies, such as naming plain language contacts and training staff, and notes the Act excludes regulation text.
limitation: Policy primer with no data; it explains why and who must comply but offers little evidence on outcomes.
measurement: Search query vs page vocabulary match rate; zero-result searches; readability grade of key pages
method: Not stated
plain: Plain language means people understand it the first time they read or hear it. Customers search with everyday words, not your internal terms, so labels should use their words.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: US Federal Primer on Plain Language Obligations

application: Run readability checks on returns, warranty and terms pages and add a short plain summary at the top of any page scoring above a lower-secondary level.
do: Add a short plain-language summary at the top of complex returns, warranty or terms pages.
dont: Publish legal or warranty text with no simpler explanation.
finding: SC 3.1.5 Reading Level (Level AAA) says that when text, after removing proper names and titles, demands reading ability above lower secondary education (about 7-9 years of schooling), a supplement or alternative version must be provided. Sufficient techniques include a simplified summary, illustrations, a spoken version or rewriting the text more simply.
limitation: AAA and not commonly mandated; readability formulas are proxies and do not confirm actual comprehension.
measurement: Readability grade per page; share of complex pages with a summary; comprehension test pass rate
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: If a page needs more than about 7 to 9 years of schooling to understand, this Level AAA rule asks for a simpler version, such as a short plain summary, pictures or a spoken version.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: WCAG 3.1.5: When Text Needs a Simpler Version

application: Crawl for links labelled 'click here', 'read more' or 'learn more' and rewrite them, or add context in the same list item, so each names its destination.
do: Write link text that names the destination, such as 'See delivery costs'.
dont: Use 'click here', 'read more' or 'learn more' as the whole link.
finding: SC 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context), Level A, requires each link's purpose to be clear from its text alone or from its text plus programmatically determined context such as the same sentence, paragraph, list item or associated table header, unless the purpose would be ambiguous to everyone. It helps screen reader, motor-impaired and cognitively impaired users decide which links to follow.
limitation: Defines a minimum accessibility bar; it does not show which link wording maximises clicks or findability.
measurement: Count of generic link labels; screen-reader link-list task success; link click-through rate
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Links should say where they go, like 'Delivery costs' rather than 'Click here'. People using a screen reader often jump from link to link, so vague link words leave them guessing. This is a WCAG Level A rule.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: WCAG 2.4.4: Making Link Text Say Where It Goes

application: Apply a 25-word sentence and 5-sentence paragraph limit to B2B and technical product content too, rather than assuming experts prefer jargon.
do: Split sentences longer than 25 words and keep paragraphs to five sentences or fewer.
dont: Assume specialist or business-to-business readers want jargon and long sentences.
finding: GOV.UK makes plain English mandatory, caps paragraphs at five sentences and asks writers to split sentences over 25 words, citing literacy difficulties in roughly 1 in 6 adults in England. It also cites a legal-language study in which 80% of people preferred clearly worded sentences, with that preference rising for more complex issues and more educated or specialist readers.
limitation: Secondhand evidence: the expert-preference figure comes from a cited study whose sample and method are not given on the page.
measurement: Share of sentences over 25 words; paragraph length; comprehension or preference ratings from expert users
method: Not stated (guidance citing Literacy Trust data, a 2014 GDS blog post and a legal-language study)
plain: Short sentences and plain words help everyone, experts included. GOV.UK asks writers to split sentences over 25 words, and cites a study where 80% of people preferred clear wording, specialists even more so.

stat.text: of people preferred clearly worded sentences in a legal-language study cited by GOV.UK (sample and method not given)

strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GOV.UK Plain English Rules, Including for Expert Readers

application: Audit every third-party urgency, countdown, social-proof and low-stock widget installed on product and cart pages, and remove any whose claims are not backed by real inventory or activity data.
do: Check every urgency, countdown and low-stock widget against real stock or activity data.
dont: Install third-party countdown or social-proof plug-ins without checking what they claim.
finding: The crawl surfaced 1,818 dark-pattern instances spanning 15 types in 7 categories; 183 sites were judged outright deceptive, and 22 third-party vendors were found selling such patterns as ready-made plug-ins.
limitation: Covers shopping sites only and counts instances it could detect automatically; it does not measure how much each pattern changes purchases or harms consumers.
measurement: Count of dark-pattern instances per page template; share of urgency/scarcity messages verifiable against live data; number of third-party persuasion scripts loaded
method: Automated crawling plus expert review techniques to detect dark patterns on product pages
plain: An automated scan of about 11,000 shopping sites found 1,818 manipulative design tricks of 15 kinds, and 183 sites were plainly deceptive. Many tricks came from ready-made plug-ins sold by 22 companies.
publisher: arXiv (Mathur et al., Princeton / U. Chicago; ACM CSCW)
sample: About 53K product pages from about 11K shopping websites

stat.text: dark-pattern instances found across about 11K shopping sites (Mathur et al., ACM CSCW; about 53K product pages)

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Automated crawl finds dark patterns across 11K shopping sites

application: Put a reject option on the first layer of the cookie banner with the same prominence as accept, and do not hide refusal behind a settings screen.
do: Put 'Reject all' on the first cookie banner screen, as prominent as 'Accept all'.
dont: Hide the reject option behind a 'Manage settings' screen.
finding: Just 11.8% of the scraped consent designs met minimal legal requirements derived from EU law. In the experiment, dropping the opt-out button from the first layer lifted consent by 22-23 percentage points, while showing granular controls up front cut it by 8-20 points; banner versus barrier style made no difference.
limitation: Experiment used only 40 participants and UK sites using five CMPs; the paper reflects 2019-era designs and does not assess later regulatory changes.
measurement: Consent rate by banner variant; presence of first-layer reject button; clicks required to refuse all non-essential cookies
method: Scrape of consent pop-ups from the five most popular consent management platforms on top UK sites, plus a field experiment on the eight most common designs
plain: Only 11.8% of cookie pop-up designs checked on UK sites met minimum EU legal rules. In a test, taking the reject button off the first screen raised acceptance by over 20 percentage points.
publisher: arXiv (Nouwens et al., MIT / UCL / Aarhus; ACM CHI 2020)

stat.text: of consent pop-up designs on 680 UK sites met minimal EU legal requirements (Nouwens et al., ACM CHI 2020)

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Consent pop-up designs on UK sites and how they sway choices

visual.cap: A visitor sees the cookie banner

application: When A/B testing a consent banner, report interaction and acceptance rates by layout and nudge variant so a design that inflates consent through steering is flagged rather than shipped as a win.
do: Report acceptance rates by banner layout and nudge whenever you test a cookie banner.
dont: Ship a banner variant just because it raises consent, if it does so by steering people.
finding: Small implementation details strongly changed whether people engaged with consent notices: notices at the lower left drew more interaction, a single yes/no choice led more people to accept tracking than per-category or per-vendor choices, and nudging had a large effect on outcomes.
limitation: Tested on a single German site; the abstract gives no effect sizes, so the magnitude of each effect must be read from the full paper.
measurement: Banner interaction rate by position; acceptance rate by choice format; proportion of users ignoring the notice
method: Analysis of common consent-notice UI properties followed by three field experiments on a German website
plain: In live tests with over 80,000 visitors to one German site, small changes to a cookie notice's position, choices and nudges strongly changed how many people accepted tracking.
publisher: arXiv (Utz et al., Ruhr-Uni Bochum / U. Michigan; ACM CCS 2019)
sample: More than 80,000 unique users of one German website
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Field experiments on cookie notice position, choices and nudges

application: Map each step of checkout and subscription flows against the CMA's three categories and remove preselected add-ons, partitioned prices and unverified scarcity claims.
do: Leave optional paid add-ons unticked at checkout so shoppers choose them on purpose.
dont: Pre-select paid extras or make scarcity claims you can't back up.
finding: The CMA groups 21 practices into choice structure (e.g. defaults, sludge, drip pricing), choice information and choice pressure (e.g. scarcity and popularity claims), and argues they can distort buying, weaken competition and entrench market power. It cites a 58-study meta-analysis in which a preselected option was on average 27% more likely to be picked than with no default.
limitation: Explicitly not legal guidance; the CMA notes evidence is mostly lab or experimental rather than measured market outcomes, and evidence strength ratings are indicative.
measurement: Share of add-ons preselected at checkout; difference between first-shown and final price; count of scarcity/popularity claims per session
method: Discussion paper drawing on peer-reviewed research, authority reports and CMA case studies, with a companion evidence review rating each practice on a 1-5 star evidence scale
plain: The UK competition regulator lists 21 design tactics, such as pre-ticked options, hidden fees and pressure claims, that can push shoppers into choices. In studies it cites, a pre-selected option was on average 27% more likely to be picked.

stat.text: more likely to be picked when an option is pre-selected (58-study meta-analysis cited by the UK CMA)

strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: UK CMA taxonomy of 21 online choice architecture practices

application: Run a privacy UX audit across sign-up, settings, rights requests and account deletion, tagging any screen that fits one of the six EDPB pattern families.
do: Make withdrawing consent and deleting an account take no more steps than giving consent or signing up.
dont: Scatter privacy settings across menus or make account deletion a maze.
finding: The guidelines define six families of deceptive design (overloading, skipping, stirring, obstructing, fickle, left in the dark) and walk through the account lifecycle from sign-up to deletion, tying each to GDPR fairness, transparency, consent withdrawal and data-protection-by-design duties.
limitation: Focused on social media platforms and GDPR; the list is not exhaustive and breaches are judged case by case, so it does not measure prevalence or user impact.
measurement: Steps to withdraw consent vs. give it; steps to delete account vs. create it; time to locate privacy settings in task tests
method: Not stated (regulatory guidance applying GDPR provisions to interface use cases)
plain: EU data regulators describe six families of deceptive design, such as burying privacy settings or making account deletion hard, and tie each to duties under GDPR, from sign-up to deletion.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: EU data protection board's guide to deceptive social media design

application: Prioritise fixing low-visibility patterns first (preselected options, hidden fees, cancellation friction) since users are least likely to detect them on their own.
do: Fix pre-ticked options, hidden fees and cancellation hurdles first, as shoppers rarely spot them.
dont: Assume shoppers will notice and avoid manipulative designs on their own.
finding: The OECD sorts dark patterns into seven types including obstruction, sneaking, social proof and urgency, and notes reported prevalence varies widely by method (e.g. a 2022 EC study found at least one dark pattern on 97% of 75 popular EU shopping sites and apps). It finds hidden information, hard-to-cancel flows and preselection are both effective and hard for consumers to notice, while confirmshaming and scarcity cues are easier to spot.
limitation: No new empirical data; it aggregates studies whose definitions and samples differ, so prevalence figures are not directly comparable.
measurement: Number of preselected options in key flows; cancellation steps vs. sign-up steps; incidence of hidden or late-disclosed fees
method: Literature review of academic studies, enforcement actions, regulator sweeps, consumer surveys and behavioural experiments
plain: An international review of dark-pattern research (OECD) finds hidden information, hard-to-cancel flows and pre-ticked options work on shoppers and are hard to notice. A 2022 EU study found at least one on 97% of 75 popular shopping sites and apps.

stat.text: of 75 popular EU shopping sites and apps had at least one dark pattern (2022 European Commission study cited by the OECD)

strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: OECD review of dark commercial pattern prevalence and harm

application: Rewrite decline buttons and opt-out copy to neutral language (no guilt or mockery) and give Reject all equal size, colour and placement to Accept all.
do: Give Reject all the same size, colour and position as Accept all.
dont: Word the decline button to shame people, like 'No, I prefer worse content'.
finding: The regulators single out harmful nudges and sludge, confirmshaming, biased framing, bundled consent and data-sharing defaults, and expect refusing non-essential cookies to be as easy and as prominent as accepting. A cited study of 300 news-site cookie notices found all allowed one-click acceptance but only 15 allowed one-click refusal.
limitation: UK-specific regulatory position; it presents expectations and cited figures rather than new testing, and acknowledges not every nudge or default is harmful.
measurement: Clicks to refuse vs. accept cookies; count of shame-based or loaded decline labels; share of privacy settings defaulting to sharing
method: Position paper building on existing ICO/CMA guidance, enforcement cases, academic research and the ICO Public Awareness Survey
plain: UK privacy regulators say saying no to optional cookies must be as easy and visible as saying yes, and decline buttons shouldn't guilt-trip or mock people.
publisher: UK ICO and CMA (Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum)

stat.text: of 300 news-site cookie notices allowed one-click refusal (all 300 allowed one-click acceptance), in a study cited by the UK ICO and CMA.

strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: UK ICO and CMA position on privacy-harming design choices

visual.cap: A visitor decides about optional cookies

application: Benchmark cancellation against sign-up: same channel, same or fewer steps, no forced call or chat, and charges stop immediately on confirmation.
do: Let people cancel online in no more steps than it took to sign up.
dont: Force a phone call or chat to cancel a plan that was bought online.
finding: The final rule required sellers of recurring plans to disclose key terms before billing, obtain express informed consent, avoid misrepresentation, and offer a cancellation route as simple as enrolment. The FTC reported subscription complaints averaging nearly 70 per day in 2024, up from 42 per day in 2021.
limitation: The rule was vacated in full by the US Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 on procedural grounds, so it is not binding law; it remains a useful design benchmark, not proof of user outcomes.
measurement: Steps to cancel vs. steps to subscribe; cancellation completion rate; subscription-related support complaints per week
method: Not stated (rulemaking announcement following public comment)
plain: A US rule would have made cancelling a subscription as easy as signing up. A court struck it down in 2025, but it's still a useful yardstick for fair cancellation.
sample: Over 16,000 public comments on the proposed rule

stat.text: subscription complaints a day reached the FTC in 2024, up from 42 a day in 2021.

strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: FTC's 2024 click-to-cancel rule for subscriptions

application: Implement the banner in the page flow (not a fixed overlay), with equal accept/reject buttons, a server-side fallback that works without JavaScript, and a confirmation message that receives focus.
do: Place the cookie banner in the page flow with matching accept and reject buttons.
dont: Pin the banner over the page where it can hide the field or link someone is on.
finding: The component asks services to let users accept or reject non-essential cookies, set none until accepted, remember the choice for a year, and confirm the decision; examples show accept and reject as matching buttons side by side. It must not be sticky or fixed so it avoids obscuring focused content under WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11.
limitation: Implementation guidance for UK government services; it does not provide evidence on consent rates and does not explicitly mandate equal visual weight.
measurement: Non-essential cookies set before consent (should be zero); banner reappearance after a saved choice; keyboard and screen reader task success on the banner
method: Not stated (design-system guidance; notes open research question on focus styling)
plain: The UK government's cookie banner offers matching Accept and Reject buttons, sets no optional cookies until people agree, and sits in the page so it never covers what they're using.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GOV.UK pattern for an accessible, neutral cookie banner

application: Audit every checkout field: confirm errors never appear before the user has typed, trigger on blur or at expected length for ZIP/card/CVV, re-check on each keystroke once an error shows, and add a valid-state checkmark.
do: Validate when people leave a field, clear errors once fixed, and show a tick when an entry is valid.
dont: Flash an error before someone has finished typing.
finding: Baymard's benchmark found roughly 31% of sites give no inline validation at all (the page also cites 32% elsewhere). Testing showed validation works best when it runs on leaving a field (or once a fixed-length value is complete), clears the moment input becomes valid, and shows a positive confirmation for correct entries.
limitation: No participant count or benchmark sample size is given, the two prevalence figures conflict, and results come from ecommerce checkouts, so timing rules may not transfer unchanged to long application forms.
measurement: Validation errors per form submission; share of fields with stale error messages after correction; checkout completion rate
method: Large-scale usability testing on live ecommerce sites plus Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: Check a field when someone moves on from it, not while they are still typing. Clear the error as soon as it is fixed, and show a tick for correct entries.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: When to fire, clear and confirm inline field validation

visual.cap: A shopper types their email at checkout

application: Replace any 'all fields are required' banner with per-field asterisks or 'Required' text in high-contrast colour, add the HTML required/aria-required attribute, and label truly optional fields as optional.
do: Put a marker on every required field and label optional ones '(optional)'.
dont: Rely on one 'all fields are required' line at the top of the form.
finding: Budiu argues each mandatory field should carry its own marker (an asterisk or the word Required) because a single instruction at the top of the form is easily missed or forgotten; optional fields can additionally be labelled optional. Markers must have adequate contrast and be exposed to screen readers as required.
limitation: Guidance draws on examples and principles rather than a reported study, so it does not quantify the effect of marking on errors or completion.
measurement: Submission attempts with missing required fields; time to complete form; screen-reader announcement of required state (pass/fail)
method: Not stated
plain: Mark each required field on its own, with an asterisk or the word 'Required'. A single note at the top saying all fields are required is easy to miss or forget.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Mark every required field explicitly, not with a blanket note

application: Swap calendar pickers for day/month/year fields when asking for known dates, accept typed month names and abbreviations, remove auto-tab between boxes, and add bday-day/bday-month/bday-year autocomplete.
do: Use separate day, month and year boxes for known dates, and accept month names.
dont: Make people scroll a calendar back years to find their birth date.
finding: For memorable dates such as a birth date, GOV.UK uses separate day, month and year boxes inside a fieldset, with a numeric keypad, no automatic focus jumping and bday autocomplete tokens. After a service saw hundreds of users get errors for typing month names, accepting names like 'jan' cut those errors sharply.
limitation: The error reduction is described qualitatively with no figures, and the component is explicitly not meant for dates users must look up on a calendar, so it does not settle picker design for booking flows.
measurement: Date-field validation error rate; share of date-of-birth fields autofilled; time to complete date question
method: Service research cited from the Apply for teacher training service
plain: For dates people already know, like a birthday, three small boxes for day, month and year work better than a calendar. Accepting words like 'jan' cut errors for one service.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Three-box date entry for dates people already know

application: Check the OTP screen uses type=text, inputmode=numeric and autocomplete=one-time-code, and rewrite the SMS template to the origin-bound @domain #code format.
do: Use inputmode=numeric with autocomplete=one-time-code, and end the SMS with the @domain #code format.
dont: Use a number-type field for codes, which can drop a leading zero.
finding: Kitamura recommends a text input with numeric inputmode and autocomplete set to one-time-code rather than a number field, which can drop leading zeros; ending the SMS with @domain and #code lets browsers extract and auto-fill the code, and the WebOTP API can read it programmatically. It also cautions that SMS codes are not phishing-resistant.
limitation: Technical guidance without user testing data; browser support for autofill and WebOTP varies and the page has not been updated since 2020.
measurement: OTP autofill rate; OTP step completion time; failed or resent code rate
method: Not stated
plain: With the right setup, phones can fill in a text-message code automatically. A plain text box set to show the number keypad also avoids number fields that drop a leading zero.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Markup and message format for one-time SMS codes

visual.cap: A shopper gets a sign-in code by text

application: Restructure checkout and sign-up forms into one column, keeping only tightly related field groups on a shared row, and consider a single full-name field or address lookup to remove paired fields.
do: Stack fields in a single column, sharing a row only for linked fields like city, state and ZIP.
dont: Spread unrelated fields across two or more columns.
finding: Baymard found 16% of benchmarked sites use extensive multicolumn forms, and testers on them more often skipped required fields or filled irrelevant ones, even with column separators or autofill present. Placing two or three fields on one row is acceptable only when they form one logical unit, such as city/state/ZIP or card expiry and security code.
limitation: No participant numbers or quantified error rates are reported, and findings are from ecommerce checkouts rather than dense data-entry or enterprise forms.
measurement: Skipped required field errors; checkout completion rate; average form completion time
method: Multiple rounds of checkout usability testing plus Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: Forms laid out in one column are easier to follow. On side-by-side layouts, testers more often skipped required fields or filled in ones that did not apply.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Single-column forms beat side-by-side field layouts

application: Add tested, localised masks to phone, date and card number fields (with visible empty placeholders), fall back to an unrestricted field in unverified countries, and test editing, deleting and pasting behaviour.
do: Use a tested, localised mask that formats phone, date and card fields as people type.
dont: Rely on a format example alone, or force a mask that blocks pasting or editing.
finding: In testing, 89% of participants typed restricted data in a format other than the example shown, so displaying an example alone did not prevent errors; meanwhile 64% of sites lacked masks or implemented them poorly. Well-built masks reduced hesitation and validation errors, especially on mobile, but must be localised per country.
limitation: Sample sizes are not given and the study is from 2017; poorly built masks can block completion, so the benefit depends heavily on implementation quality.
measurement: Format-related validation errors; phone/card field completion time; paste and edit failure rate in QA
method: Large-scale checkout usability testing with eye-tracking, plus benchmark audits of ecommerce checkouts
plain: Showing an example format is not enough: most testers typed phone numbers, dates and card numbers their own way anyway. A well-built mask that formats as they type cut hesitation and errors.

stat.text: of test participants typed restricted data in a different format from the example shown (Baymard checkout testing, 2017).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Input masks outperform format examples for restricted fields

application: Audit field widths so CVV, ZIP and year inputs are visibly short, names and emails share a consistent medium width, and no field implies a length the data never reaches.
do: Size short fixed-length fields, like security code or postcode, to fit their answer.
dont: Make every field the same full width regardless of what it holds.
finding: Testers presented with fields far wider or narrower than the expected answer sometimes doubted whether they had understood the label, especially for unfamiliar items like CVV. Holst proposes sizing fixed-length fields to their exact length, using one consistent default width for typical variable fields, and custom widths for atypical ones like postal codes.
limitation: A 2010 article with no reported sample or quantified effect; character-width ranges come from the forms studied then and may not reflect responsive layouts today.
measurement: Hesitation time on short-code fields; CVV/ZIP entry error rate; count of fields whose width mismatches expected length
method: Checkout usability study (details not described on page)
plain: The size of a box hints at what goes in it. When a box was far wider or narrower than the answer, such as a short security code, testers doubted they had understood the question.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Field width as a silent hint about expected input

application: Scan checkout, account and contact forms for missing or wrong autocomplete values (name, email, tel, street-address, postal-code, shipping/billing prefixes) and fix them.
do: Add the right autocomplete value to every name, email, phone and address field.
dont: Leave checkout fields unmarked so the browser can't fill them and people retype everything.
finding: SC 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) requires that any field collecting information about the user has a programmatically determinable purpose when that purpose appears in WCAG's Input Purposes list and the technology supports it. In HTML this is typically met with autocomplete tokens, helping people with memory, cognitive or motor impairments rely on autofill.
limitation: The criterion only covers data about the user and requires exposed purpose, not that browsers actually autofill; it does not measure conversion or completion impact.
measurement: Share of user-data fields with valid autocomplete tokens; autofill usage rate; form completion time
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Name, email, address and phone fields should tell the browser what they're for, so it can fill them in. That helps people who struggle with memory, typing or fine movement.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Expose personal-data field purposes so browsers can autofill

application: Cut password rules to a minimum length, state any rule up front, remove character and max-length restrictions, offer a strength meter as encouragement, and keep guest checkout open for emails with existing accounts.
do: Ask only for a minimum length, state any rule up front, and keep guest checkout open.
dont: Demand mixes of capitals, numbers and symbols, or reveal the rules only after an error.
finding: Baymard's benchmark found 82% of ecommerce sites impose needlessly complex password rules; the main damage appears on return visits, where forgotten passwords and slow reset emails led to checkout abandonment of up to 19% among existing-account testers in some tests. Baymard advises requiring only a minimum length (around 6 to 8 characters) backed by server-side security controls.
limitation: Participant and site counts are not reported, the abandonment figure comes from specific tests on sites like Amazon and ASOS, and appropriate rules may differ for high-security industries.
measurement: Password reset requests per sign-in attempt; checkout abandonment at sign-in; account creation completion rate
method: Multiple rounds of usability testing plus Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: Complicated password rules hurt most when shoppers come back: they forget the password, wait for reset emails, and some give up on the order. A minimum length is usually enough.

stat.text: of ecommerce sites in Baymard's benchmark impose needlessly complex password rules.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Complex password rules hurt repeat sign-in more than signup

application: Replace dropdowns that hold a short set of options (e.g. shipping speed, size, plan) with visible vertical radio lists, and make each label part of the click target.
do: Show short sets of options, like delivery speed, as a vertical list with clickable labels.
dont: Hide three or four options inside a dropdown.
finding: Nielsen sets radio buttons for picking exactly one of several mutually exclusive options and checkboxes for independent choices, with options listed vertically and labels clickable. He favours radio buttons over dropdowns where space allows because every option stays visible for comparison, lowering cognitive load and pointing difficulty.
limitation: A 2004 guideline without reported test data; its advice to always preselect a radio default is disputed by some newer design systems and does not address mobile-native pickers.
measurement: Selection error rate; time to choose an option; click/tap count per selection
method: Guideline synthesis drawing on GUI standards and prior NN/g user testing
plain: When people must pick one of a few options, a visible list of round radio buttons lets them compare every choice at once. A dropdown hides the choices until it is opened.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Choosing radios, checkboxes or dropdowns for selections
