application: Report SUS results as percentile ranks or letter grades against the 68 average rather than as a percent, and pair SUS with observed task metrics.
finding: SUS is a 10-item, five-point questionnaire scored to a 0-100 range; across about 500 studies the mean is 68, which sits at the 50th percentile, so raw scores should not be read as percentages. Post-test SUS correlates only weakly with task completion and time (r of about .24).
limitation: Benchmark reflects the mix of products in MeasuringU's database as of 2011; SUS signals perceived usability but does not identify which interface problems to fix.
measurement: SUS score (0-100); SUS percentile rank; learnability subscale (items 4 and 10)
method: Aggregation of SUS scores from prior usability evaluations into a normative database
strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Scoring and benchmarking the System Usability Scale

application: For each key product goal, define the user behavior that signals progress and pick one tracked metric per goal before launching a redesign.
finding: Rodden, Hutchinson and Fu argue web products need user-centered metrics tied to product goals, and present HEART as a process for mapping goals to metrics drawn from large-scale behavioral data. They report it generalized across many Google products and could be adapted elsewhere.
limitation: The abstract page reports team examples rather than controlled evidence that HEART-driven decisions improve outcomes; the downloadable PDF link on the page points to a third-party host.
measurement: Task success rate; retention rate; adoption of new features
method: Framework proposal illustrated with practical examples from Google product teams (CHI 2010 paper)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Google's HEART framework for user-centered product metrics

application: Set up a recurring live-service review that triangulates analytics, support tickets and survey feedback, then schedule usability sessions on the problems those sources surface.
finding: For live services, GDS recommends combining analytics and back-office data, support-ticket analysis and surveys with interviews, visits, usability tests and A/B tests of new or changed features. Research must cover a broad range of users, including people with low digital access and assistive technology users, plus frontline staff.
limitation: Lists methods without detailing how to run them or offering evidence of their relative effectiveness.
measurement: Support tickets per transaction; completion rate from analytics; A/B variant conversion
method: Not stated
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Which research methods to run once a service is live

application: Add Adjusted Wald confidence intervals to every completion rate and geometric means to task times in usability test reports.
finding: For small UX samples, use t-based intervals for means, log-transform task times before building intervals, and use the Adjusted Wald interval for completion rates; the geometric mean beats the median for task time below roughly 25 users. Intervals at these sizes are typically wide, often 20 to 30 percentage points.
limitation: Small samples still only detect large effects; the guidance does not make underpowered comparisons conclusive.
measurement: Completion rate with Adjusted Wald CI; geometric mean task time; mean rating with t-based CI
method: Statistical guidance drawing on prior simulation and methods research
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Statistics that hold up with 5 to 30 test users

application: Replace or supplement NPS with a question about actual recent referrals plus an open prompt asking how the experience could improve, and report response rates alongside any score.
finding: Spool argues NPS bucketing distorts data (all 6s score the same -100 as all 0s), the 11-point scale invites inconsistent answers, the question predicts future behavior rather than recording past behavior, and the score is easy to game. He suggests open-ended follow-ups, experience questions, and past-referral questions instead.
limitation: Opinion essay built on illustrative examples and anecdotes, not a controlled study of NPS validity.
measurement: Reported referrals in a recent period; mean satisfaction rating; survey response rate
method: Expert critique using worked numeric examples and anecdotes from the author's qualitative studies
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: The case against Net Promoter Score in UX

application: Before restructuring site navigation, run an open card sort to draft categories, then tree-test the draft with randomized tasks and fix the paths where users diverge.
finding: The ONRR team ran card sorting and tree testing with tools they already had; most cards grouped clearly, but vague card labels caused confusion. Tree testing showed full agreement on some paths and divergence on others, prompting a new top-level category and cross-listing of some content.
limitation: Single agency case with 11 participants per study; the team itself noted sessions ran short and a larger sample would have helped.
measurement: Card agreement rate; tree-test path success per task; task path divergence
method: Moderated open card sort using GitHub project boards, followed by moderated tree testing with a clickable prototype and randomized task order
sample: Card sort: 11 participants, 56 cards; tree test: 11 participants (4 external, 7 internal), 10 tasks; ONRR website redesign
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Low-cost card sorting and tree testing on a federal site

application: Add a highlighter test of key product-page or checkout copy, asking users to mark clear text one color and confusing text another.
finding: 18F groups card sorting, content highlighter tests, multivariate testing, success metrics, think-aloud usability testing and visual preference tests as validation methods, noting each method's purpose and US Paperwork Reduction Act implications. Multivariate tests must run until results are statistically significant.
limitation: Short method summaries without evidence on effectiveness; PRA guidance applies only to US federal work; guide is archived.
measurement: Proportion of copy flagged confusing; task success in think-aloud tests; variant conversion in multivariate tests
method: Not stated
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: 18F's toolkit for validating designs with users

application: Audit an existing post-purchase survey by mapping every question to a decision it informs and deleting the ones that map to nothing.
finding: Start with a clear research question, confirm a survey suits it, and plan analysis before launch; cut any question whose answer would not change your work. Write neutral, plain-language questions, weigh open versus closed formats, gain explicit opt-in consent, and pilot the survey with real users.
limitation: The post cites no studies or data; it is one practitioner's advice, partly framed around UK data-protection law.
measurement: Survey completion rate; item non-response rate; share of questions mapped to a decision
method: Practitioner guidance from a government user researcher
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Practical rules for designing a user survey

application: Before a redesign, run a baseline benchmark with randomized task order and confidence intervals so post-launch results can be compared directly.
finding: Benchmarks should recruit representative users, combine completion, time, errors and satisfaction, counterbalance task order, pilot first, and size samples by margin of error (roughly 20 users for a 20% margin, about 80 for 10%). Sauro estimates about 10% of remote participants speed through for the incentive and should be screened out.
limitation: Experience-based tips; the speeder estimate and sample-size rules are not backed by a described dataset on the page.
measurement: Task completion rate; time on task including failed attempts; post-task Single Ease Question
method: Practitioner guidance drawing on MeasuringU benchmarking experience
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: How to run a repeatable usability benchmark

application: Define pass/fail criteria for each checkout task in advance and compare results against a 78% baseline with Adjusted Wald intervals.
finding: Across nearly 1,200 tasks, the average completion rate is 78%, a reasonable default target; success criteria should be defined before testing. About 14% of users who fail a task still rate it very easy, so difficulty ratings cannot replace observed success.
limitation: Benchmark is an average across mixed domains from 2011 and may not fit a specific product type or task difficulty.
measurement: Task completion rate; Adjusted Wald 95% confidence interval; post-task difficulty rating
method: Analysis of MeasuringU task database plus cited usability-metrics research
strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Task success rates: benchmarks and interpretation

application: Audit every custom gesture (pinch-zoom on product images, swipe carousels, swipe-to-dismiss) and confirm each has a visible tap control such as +/- zoom buttons or previous/next arrows.
do: Add tap controls, such as + and − or arrows, next to every custom gesture.
dont: Make pinch or swipe the only way to zoom, scroll a carousel or dismiss something. (WCAG 2.5.1, Level A.)
finding: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures (Level A) requires that anything operated by a multipoint gesture (e.g. two-finger pinch) or a path-based gesture (e.g. a directional swipe) can also be done with one pointer and no path, such as a tap, unless the gesture is essential. Browser- or OS-provided gestures are out of scope, and keyboard support alone does not satisfy it.
limitation: Defines a minimum conformance bar; it does not show how many users discover or prefer gestures versus buttons, nor does it cover unconstrained dragging (handled by SC 2.5.7).
measurement: Share of gesture-driven functions with a single-tap alternative; task success for users with motor impairments or switch/eye-gaze input; number of 2.5.1 failures per audit
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Anything you can do by pinching or swiping should also work with a simple tap, like zoom buttons or arrows. Some people can only use one finger or a pointer.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Single-tap fallbacks for pinch and swipe gestures

visual.cap: Someone using one finger wants a closer look

application: For sliders, sortable lists, kanban boards and drag-to-pan maps, add tap-on-track positioning, up/down move buttons or directional controls, and retest with a single pointer only.
do: Pair drag controls with tap options such as 'Move up' buttons or tapping a point on a slider.
dont: Make dragging the only way to reorder, adjust or move something. (WCAG 2.5.7, Level AA.)
finding: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (Level AA) requires that any function using a drag can also be achieved with a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the behavior is native to the user agent (e.g. touch scrolling, unmodified pull-to-refresh). Custom scroll implementations that override native scrolling fall within scope.
limitation: A conformance requirement rather than user research; it does not quantify how often drag-only controls block users or which alternative pattern performs best.
measurement: Number of drag-only interactions found; completion rate of reorder/slider tasks using tap only; time on task with and without dragging
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: If something works by dragging, like a slider or reordering a list, there must also be a way to do it with taps. Dragging is hard for many people.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Tap alternatives for drag-based controls

visual.cap: Someone reorders their saved list

application: Test key flows (browse, product page, checkout) in both portrait and landscape on real phones and remove any orientation lock or 'please rotate your device' gate that is not strictly essential.
do: Let every screen work in both portrait and landscape.
dont: Show a 'please rotate your device' block unless the orientation is truly essential. (WCAG 1.3.4, Level AA.)
finding: WCAG SC 1.3.4 Orientation (Level AA) requires that content not restrict its view or operation to a single display orientation unless that orientation is essential (examples given include a piano app or check capture). Forced rotation particularly harms people whose devices are mounted in a fixed position, such as on a wheelchair.
limitation: Covers orientation locking only; it says nothing about whether the landscape layout is usable or well designed, and gives no data on how many users rotate devices.
measurement: Count of screens with orientation locks; task completion in landscape vs portrait; layout defects per orientation
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: A site or app should work whichever way the phone is held. Some people have their device mounted and can't turn it.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Don't lock screens to portrait or landscape

application: If the product has five or fewer top-level destinations, expose them in a persistent bottom tab bar; if a hamburger is unavoidable, add in-page cross-links to offset its lower discoverability.
do: Show up to about five main sections in a visible bottom bar.
dont: Hide every main section behind a hamburger or an unlabeled swipe.
finding: Raluca Budiu compares mobile navigation patterns: visible tab and navigation bars work for a small set of options (roughly four or five before targets get too small), while hamburger menus fit many options but are the least discoverable because users must choose to open them. Unlabeled swipe-to-open menus are likely to go unnoticed by most users.
limitation: A pattern primer illustrated with app screenshots, not a reported study; it gives no measured discoverability or task-success rates and predates current OS gesture conventions.
measurement: Navigation discoverability (first-click success); use rate of secondary sections; time to reach a target category
method: Not stated
plain: On phones, a visible bar of a few options is easy to find, while a hamburger menu hides everything until someone thinks to open it.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Trade-offs of tab bars, hamburgers and hub navigation on mobile

visual.cap: A new visitor looks for their orders

application: Check every checkout field for the right type/inputmode (tel, numeric, email), turn off autocorrect and autocapitalize on names, addresses and emails, and verify consistency across all checkout steps.
do: Set each field's type so the right keyboard opens, and switch off autocorrect for names, addresses and emails.
dont: Let autocorrect 'fix' a surname or email address as the shopper types.
finding: In the 2015 benchmark, 54% of sites did not invoke an optimized keyboard for phone, ZIP or card-number fields, and 79% left auto-correct switched on for fields like name, address and email, which in testing led users to submit corrupted data unnoticed. Sites getting two or more of five keyboard guidelines wrong fell only from 69% to 60% between 2013 and 2015.
limitation: Small, US-only, ecommerce-only sample measured in 2015; it does not show current adoption rates or quantify the conversion impact of keyboard fixes.
measurement: Share of fields with the correct keyboard invoked; typo/validation error rate per field; checkout form completion rate on mobile
method: Benchmark of touch keyboard implementations repeated in 2013 and 2015, informed by observations from Baymard's mobile ecommerce usability test sessions
plain: Phones should open the right keyboard for each box, like a number pad for phone numbers, and stop autocorrect changing names and emails. Otherwise people send wrong details without noticing.
sample: 48 leading US mobile ecommerce sites (described as over $50M in online sales), audited in 2013 and 2015

stat.text: of 48 large US mobile shops left autocorrect on for fields like name, address and email (Baymard, 2015).

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Mobile sites still misconfigure touch keyboards in forms

application: Make guest checkout a clearly visible, collapsed-header option at account selection, and use ZIP-based city/state lookup to cut typing on mobile.
do: Keep field labels clear on their own and fill in the city from the postcode.
dont: Split phone numbers or postcodes into several small boxes.
finding: The article reports the touch keyboard covering close to half the screen in portrait and about 70-80% in landscape, so users easily lose their place in forms; 60% of test subjects had serious trouble finding and selecting the guest checkout option. It recommends context-independent field labels, single fields for single entities like phone and ZIP, and auto-detecting data such as city from ZIP.
limitation: Dated (2013) with an unstated number of test participants; percentages come from a mix of tests and audits and do not establish causal effects on conversion.
measurement: Guest checkout selection success rate; fields typed per order; mobile checkout abandonment rate
method: Usability test sessions of mobile checkouts plus benchmarks of top mobile and desktop ecommerce sites; protocol details not described
plain: On phones the keyboard covers close to half the screen, so people lose their place in forms. Many testers also struggled to find the guest checkout option.
sample: Participant count not stated; benchmarks of the top 50 mobile-optimized and top 100 desktop ecommerce sites

stat.text: of test subjects had serious trouble finding and selecting the guest checkout option (Baymard mobile checkout testing, 2013).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.

application: Audit the bottom bar of an app or mobile web app: remove action buttons (e.g. 'Add' or 'Share') from it, cap it at five destinations, and keep it persistent across sections.
do: Keep the tab bar to a few main sections and keep it in place across the app.
dont: Put action buttons like 'Add' or 'Share' in the tab bar.
finding: Apple says tab bars are for moving between top-level app areas, not for triggering actions (use a toolbar for those), with three to five tabs typical on iPhone. Tabs should stay visible across areas and remain present even when their content is unavailable, and badges can flag new information quietly.
limitation: Platform convention guidance without published user research; following it ensures iOS consistency but does not prove performance gains on mobile web.
measurement: Number of tab bar items; share of tab bar items that are actions rather than destinations; tab-switch task success
method: Not stated
plain: On iPhone, the bottom tab bar is for switching between main sections, usually three to five. Actions like 'Share' or 'Add' belong in a toolbar instead.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Apple's rules for iOS tab bars

visual.cap: The bar at the bottom of an iPhone app

application: On notched/Dynamic Island phones, check that sticky add-to-cart bars and bottom CTAs respect safe-area insets (e.g. env(safe-area-inset-bottom)) and don't sit under the Home indicator.
do: Keep sticky buttons and key controls inside the screen's safe area, clear of the Home indicator.
dont: Put a tappable control right on the bottom edge where the phone's own swipe gestures take over.
finding: Apple directs designers to keep content inside safe areas that exclude system bars and hardware cutouts like the Dynamic Island, to avoid interactive controls at the bottom edge where system gestures can override custom ones, and to avoid hard-to-reach far corners. It also asks apps to support both orientations and keep touch targets at least 44x44 points.
limitation: Platform guidance rather than a study; it gives no data on mis-tap rates or reach and is written primarily for native iOS apps, not browsers.
measurement: Number of controls overlapping safe-area insets; mis-tap rate on bottom CTAs; touch target size compliance (44pt)
method: Not stated
plain: Phone screens have notches, rounded corners and system swipe areas. Buttons placed there can be hidden or hijacked by the phone itself, so keep key controls inside the safe area.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Safe areas, edge gestures and reach in Apple layouts

application: Support both pinch and double-tap zoom on product images, load a higher-resolution image when zoom starts, and show a brief, fading hint that zoom is available.
do: Support pinch and double-tap zoom, and show a brief hint that zoom works.
dont: Lock product photos so pinching or double-tapping does nothing.
finding: Testers routinely tried pinch, double-tap and swipe on product images, yet 40% of benchmarked sites supported none of these image gestures, and some participants left to shop elsewhere when they couldn't inspect details. Only half of the sites that did support zoom told users it was available.
limitation: 2016 US-only benchmark with an unstated number of test participants; the abandonment observations are qualitative and not quantified.
measurement: Image zoom usage rate; product page exit rate after image interaction; share of image interactions that are unsupported gestures
method: Qualitative 1:1 mobile usability testing plus a benchmark of mobile ecommerce sites
plain: On phones, people pinch, double-tap and swipe product photos to see details. Many shops ignore these gestures, and some testers left to shop elsewhere when they couldn't zoom in.
sample: Benchmark of 50 top-grossing US mobile ecommerce sites; test participant count not stated

stat.text: of 50 top-grossing US mobile shops in Baymard's 2016 benchmark supported none of the common image gestures.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.

application: Map each tappable action by frequency and severity: add undo for frequent actions like remove-from-cart, and confirmation or hold-to-confirm only for rare, high-stakes actions like placing an order or deleting an account.
do: Add an undo for frequent actions like removing an item, and a confirm step only for big ones like placing an order.
dont: Let a stray tap delete something or submit an order with no way back.
finding: Baymard observed frequent accidental taps on touch devices, often from users reading with a finger, shifting grip or scrolling, sometimes causing premature submissions or lost data. It weighs three responses: accept the error, require proof of intent (confirm, hold, two-step), or make the action reversible, choosing by how frequent and how severe the action is.
limitation: Qualitative; reports no accidental-tap rates, sample sizes or abandonment figures, so it can't show how much any strategy reduces errors.
measurement: Undo usage rate; unintended submission or navigation events; abandonment after accidental actions
method: Observations from Baymard's mobile ecommerce usability testing
plain: People often tap things by accident while reading or scrolling on a phone. Make common actions easy to undo, and ask for confirmation only on rare, serious ones.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Choosing how to guard against accidental taps

application: Audit category and product templates. Each breadcrumb should reflect the taxonomy rather than the referring path, every crumb except the last should link to a real page, and mobile trails should fit on a single line.
do: Show the site path, such as Home › Lighting › Lamps, linking every level except the current page.
dont: Show the visitor's click history, or let the trail wrap over several lines on a phone.
finding: Breadcrumbs should add to global and local navigation, not replace it. They should show where a page sits in the site hierarchy, not the user's click history, with one canonical path on polyhierarchical sites and the current page as a final, unlinked item. On mobile, avoid trails that wrap onto several lines and consider showing only the last one or two levels.
limitation: Expert guidance with illustrative site examples. The page reports no study data, so it does not quantify how breadcrumbs affect findability or conversion.
measurement: Breadcrumb click-through rate from deep-entry pages; share of trails that wrap on mobile viewports; upward-navigation task success
method: Not stated
plain: Breadcrumbs should show where a page sits in the site, not the clicks someone took to get there, ending with the current page. On phones, keep the trail to one line.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Eleven rules for hierarchy-based breadcrumb trails

application: Measure how much of a phone viewport the sticky header covers. Shrink it, make its background opaque, and test a reveal-on-scroll-up variant if it takes up a large share of the screen.
do: Keep sticky headers short and opaque, and on mobile bring them back when people scroll up.
dont: Let a tall sticky header cover a large part of a phone screen.
finding: Sticky headers should stay short, sit on an opaque background with clear contrast, and avoid distracting motion. On mobile, a header that reappears when the user scrolls up is a good compromise. Illustrative measurements on an iPhone 11 Pro ranged from a 13:1 content-to-header ratio on one site to 2:1 on another, showing how much space a bloated header can take.
limitation: The ratios are single-site examples on one device, not a benchmark. The page reports no user testing showing that sticky headers improve task outcomes.
measurement: Header height as a percentage of viewport; header navigation/search usage after scroll; content-to-chrome ratio on mobile
method: Not stated
plain: A header that stays at the top while people scroll should be short and solid. On phones, one that reappears only when they scroll back up leaves more room for the page.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Making persistent headers earn their screen space

visual.cap: A shopper scrolls a list on a phone

application: Review each mega-menu panel. Group links under clear subheadings, sort them vertically within columns, and remove any image that doesn't link to an actual category.
do: Group mega-menu links under subheadings and sort them down each column.
dont: Sort links alphabetically across rows, or add images that don't link to a category.
finding: Mega menus become hard to use when their panel divisions are unclear, when images decorate rather than represent real options, and when items are sorted alphabetically across rows, because users scan down columns and may read hidden ordering as random. Long lists should be grouped under subheadings and sorted down left-aligned columns.
limitation: Based on two example sites from 2010, with no reported data. The author's estimate of lost usage is speculative, and the guidance predates modern responsive and touch menus.
measurement: Time to locate a target link in the mega menu; misclick rate within panels; first-click accuracy on menu tasks
method: Informal expert critique of two live mega menus, referring to earlier NN/g usability studies without details
plain: In big drop-down menus people read down columns, so sort links top to bottom and group them under clear subheadings. Pictures should be real options, not decoration.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Common mega-menu layout mistakes and fixes

application: Before relaunching a navigation, build the proposed menu tree in a spreadsheet and test 8–10 key findability tasks on it, including a warm-up task. Compare success and directness against the current tree.
finding: Tree testing checks whether people can find items in a text-only category hierarchy, with no visual design involved. Tasks should not repeat the target label, and tests work best after card sorting and before design work. Key outputs are success rate, time on task and directness. Comparing alternative label wordings calls for separate trees tested with different participants.
limitation: Describes how to run the method but gives no concrete sample sizes or benchmark scores. It notes that common tools only accept leaf nodes as correct answers.
measurement: Task success rate; directness (first-path accuracy); time on task
method: Not applicable (method guide describing task-based tree testing)
sample: Not stated on page (qualitative needs few participants; quantitative needs a larger sample, no numbers given)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Validating category labels with tree tests

application: Check that the main navigation highlights the active category on category and product pages. Add a roughly 300–500 ms hover delay to drop-down menus, and make top-level navigation headers clickable.
do: Highlight the current category in the main menu and add a short delay before drop-downs open.
dont: Let drop-down menus fly open the instant the pointer crosses them.
finding: Baymard rated 61% of desktop and 65% of mobile sites mediocre or worse on homepage and category navigation, with category taxonomy scoring lowest. In the benchmark, 96% of sites failed to highlight the user's current scope in the main navigation, and 62% lacked a hover delay on drop-down menus.
limitation: Scores are expert judgements against Baymard's own guideline set, not measured conversion impact. The article covers only 10 of 47 navigation guidelines, and the rest are paywalled.
measurement: Presence of current-scope highlighting; accidental drop-down open rate; category page reach from homepage
method: Manual expert review and scoring against Baymard guidelines, supported by qualitative usability testing
plain: Most big shops scored mediocre or worse for homepage and category navigation. Almost all failed to highlight which section the shopper was in, and many menus dropped open as the pointer passed over.
sample: 17,000+ UX performance scores across 180+ leading US and European ecommerce sites; usability test participant count not stated

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's navigation benchmark (180+ sites) failed to highlight the user's current section in the main menu.

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Benchmark of ecommerce homepage and category navigation flaws

application: Remove breadcrumbs from checkout and other linear flows, place them before the main landmark, and wrap them in a nav labelled for screen readers.
do: Use breadcrumbs on multi-level browsing pages and remove them from checkout.
dont: Show breadcrumbs inside a step-by-step checkout as if they were progress steps.
finding: GOV.UK recommends breadcrumbs only for multi-level sites. They should not be used on flat sites or to show progress through a linear transaction. They sit above the main element so the skip link bypasses them, use a labelled nav element, end at the parent section rather than the current page, and can collapse to the first and last items on mobile.
limitation: Implementation guidance from one government design system. It reports no research findings, and its end-at-parent convention differs from NN/g's advice to show the current page.
measurement: Breadcrumb presence on linear flows (should be zero); skip-link bypass verified; nav landmark labelled
method: Not stated
plain: Use breadcrumbs only on sites with several levels, never as a progress marker in a step-by-step flow like checkout. Place them before the main content so the 'skip' link jumps past them.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GOV.UK breadcrumb component rules and placement

application: Cut the primary navigation down to the handful of sections users most need. Move exhaustive link lists to the footer or a sitemap, and put external links last.
do: Keep the top menu to a handful of key sections and move the full list to the footer.
dont: Turn the main menu into a complete sitemap.
finding: Service navigation should hold only the most useful top-level sections, such as getting help, contact or account management, rather than acting as a complete site map. The service name should link to the service's home or start page, and any external links should come after internal ones with a warning when they open a new window.
limitation: Gives no research methods, participants or findings. The rationale lives in GitHub discussions rather than on the page.
measurement: Number of primary navigation items; click share per nav item; findability success for account/help tasks
method: Not stated
plain: The top menu should hold only the few sections people most need, such as help, contact or their account, not every page on the site. Long lists of links belong in the footer.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Choosing which links go in a service's top navigation

visual.cap: A customer wants to check their account

application: Inspect breadcrumb markup. Confirm it sits in a labelled nav landmark and that the current-page item exposes aria-current=page to assistive technology.
do: Wrap breadcrumbs in a labelled nav element and mark the current page with aria-current.
dont: Build the breadcrumb trail as plain text with no navigation label.
finding: A breadcrumb trail is a hierarchical list of links to parent pages placed inside a navigation landmark, which must be labelled with aria-label or aria-labelledby. The current page's link takes aria-current set to page. No custom keyboard handling is required because the trail relies on standard link behaviour.
limitation: Covers semantics only, not visual design, placement or whether breadcrumbs help users. It is authoring guidance, not a normative WCAG requirement.
measurement: Labelled nav landmark present; aria-current on current item; screen reader announcement check
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Breadcrumbs, the trail of links showing where a page sits, should be marked up as a labelled navigation area, with the current page flagged so screen readers announce it.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Accessible markup contract for breadcrumb trails

application: Audit mega-menu and dropdown code. Replace role=menu or menubar on site navigation with disclosure buttons that toggle aria-expanded, and verify that Escape closes the panel and returns focus.
do: Build drop-downs from buttons that toggle aria-expanded and close on Escape.
dont: Put role=menu on ordinary site navigation.
finding: The APG builds dropdown site navigation from disclosure buttons with aria-expanded and aria-controls, deliberately avoiding the ARIA menu role because typical site navigation doesn't need that widget's complex keyboard model. Escape should close an open dropdown and return focus to its button, which the page ties to WCAG 1.4.13, and the active link carries aria-current=page.
limitation: The page says the example code is not production-ready and must be tested with assistive technologies. It is not evidence of measured user performance.
measurement: Presence of role=menu on site nav (should be absent); Escape closes and restores focus; aria-expanded state accuracy
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Drop-down site menus work better for keyboard and screen reader users when built as simple show-and-hide buttons, not complex app-style menus. Escape should close the menu and return to its button.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Building dropdown site navigation without the ARIA menu role

application: Confirm that every category and content page can be reached through at least two mechanisms, such as the main menu plus site search or an HTML sitemap, while treating checkout steps as exempt.
do: Make every category and content page reachable through both the menu and site search.
dont: Leave pages that can only be found through one buried link.
finding: SC 2.4.5 Multiple Ways (Level AA) requires at least two ways to locate any page within a set of pages, except for pages that are a step in or the result of a process, such as checkout steps or search results. Sufficient combinations include search, a site map, a table of contents, related links or links from the home page.
limitation: Sets a minimum conformance bar. It does not say which combination of navigation methods works best for users or how to label them.
measurement: Pages reachable by two or more mechanisms (%); sitemap/search coverage of indexable pages; orphan page count
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: People should have at least two ways to reach any page, such as the menu plus site search, or a site map. Checkout steps and search results don't need this.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: WCAG requirement for more than one route to each page

application: Audit the slowest interactions on PLP filters, add-to-cart and checkout steps in field data and ensure each paints visible feedback within 200 ms at p75 on mobile.
do: Make filters, add-to-cart and checkout buttons show a visible change within 200 ms.
dont: Let a tap sit with no visible response while scripts finish running.
finding: INP reports roughly the slowest click, tap or key-press latency during a page visit (input to next painted frame), with one worst interaction discarded per 50 on very interactive pages; at the 75th percentile, 200 ms or under is good and above 500 ms is poor. The page cites Chrome usage data indicating about 90% of time on a page happens after it has loaded.
limitation: Defines and explains the metric; it does not show that improving INP changes conversion, and it omits scroll, hover and zoom responsiveness.
measurement: p75 INP (mobile and desktop); share of page loads with INP under 200 ms; slowest interaction target element
method: Not stated
plain: This score checks how long a page takes to visibly react after a click, tap or key press, using roughly the slowest reaction in a visit. 200 milliseconds or less counts as good.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: INP explained: how responsiveness is scored across a visit

visual.cap: A shopper taps Add to basket
visual.note: Illustration. 200 ms (good) and 500 ms (poor) are Google's INP thresholds; the screens are made up.

application: For the top landing and product templates, record LCP sub-part timings from field data and fix whichever delay phase exceeds about a tenth of total LCP, starting with hero image discovery and priority.
do: Make the main product image findable in the page code and never lazy-load it.
dont: Lazy-load the hero image or start fetching it only after scripts run.
finding: The guide splits LCP into server response time, resource load delay, resource load duration and element render delay, suggesting the two delay phases stay under about 10% each while TTFB and download take roughly 40% each, against a target of 2.5 s or less for 75% of visits. It stresses making the LCP resource discoverable in the HTML and never lazy-loading the hero image.
limitation: Percentages are offered as rough guidelines, not tested targets; it gives no figures for the cited internal research and no business-outcome evidence.
measurement: p75 LCP; LCP resource load delay as % of LCP; element render delay as % of LCP
method: Not stated
plain: When the main picture loads slowly, the delay can come from four places: the server, waiting to start the download, the download itself, or drawing it. Measure each to find the real culprit.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Breaking LCP into four sub-parts to find the bottleneck

application: Check every product image, promo banner, cookie notice and review widget for reserved dimensions or aspect-ratio boxes, and move non-essential injected content below the fold or behind a user action.
do: Set width and height or an aspect ratio on every image, banner and embed.
dont: Inject promo bars or cookie notices above content after the page has drawn.
finding: Target a unitless CLS of 0.1 or lower for three quarters of visits (above 0.25 is poor); the main culprits are unsized images and embeds, injected content such as ads and banners, and web-font swaps. Shifts occurring within half a second of a user action are not counted, and field CLS covers the whole page lifetime while lab tools mostly capture initial load.
limitation: Gives technical remedies only; it includes no user data on how shifts affect errors, trust or sales.
measurement: p75 CLS; count of unsized images and embeds; largest shifting element per template
method: Not stated
plain: Pages jump when images, ads, banners or fonts arrive without space saved for them. Reserving that space keeps the page still while it loads.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Practical fixes for unexpected layout shifts

visual.cap: A shopper is about to tap a product
visual.note: Illustration. Product names and prices are made-up examples.

application: Profile the PLP under CPU throttling, locate long tasks tied to scroll or lazy-load callbacks, and break them up so taps on product tiles respond promptly.
do: Break long scripts tied to scrolling or lazy-loading into smaller pieces.
dont: Run heavy work on every scroll update while shoppers are trying to tap.
finding: A long main-thread task triggered by an Intersection Observer state update on the listing page was split by yielding before the update, cutting p75 INP by about half (from close to 1,400 ms to roughly 650 ms over six months). An A/B test showed a 1% per-session lift in click-through from listing to product detail pages.
limitation: Single-company case study published by Google; baseline figures are not fully consistent across readings and test duration and sample size are not reported.
measurement: p75 INP on PLP; longest main-thread task duration; PLP-to-PDP click-through rate per session
method: Case study: field INP from CrUX via PageSpeed Insights, lab profiling in Chrome DevTools with 4x CPU throttling; CTR impact assessed with an A/B test
plain: A large Turkish shop found one long background task made its product list slow to react to taps. Splitting it up roughly halved the delay, and an A/B test showed slightly more clicks into products.
sample: Trendyol product listing page, mobile; INP tracked over six months; A/B test duration not stated

stat.text: per-session lift in listing-to-product click-through in Trendyol's A/B test after halving listing-page INP (Google web.dev case study).

strengthWhy: Single-site case study without a control group.
title: Trendyol halves listing-page INP by yielding to the main thread

application: Run a controlled split test of a performance-only variant on a key landing page so speed and stability gains can be tied to revenue rather than assumed.
do: Split-test a speed-only version of a key page so gains are measured, not assumed.
dont: Quote this one-page result as the uplift your own site will get.
finding: The optimized variant cut CLS by about 93% and also improved TTFB and FCP, and the team reported revenue per visitor up 53.37% and conversion rate up 33.13% versus the original, with exit rate down about 35%.
limitation: One page at one retailer; metric definitions, sample size and significance are not given, and the page is ambiguous about whether results come from the landing page or homepage.
measurement: CLS and TTFB by variant; conversion rate by variant; revenue per visitor by variant
method: A/B test: 50/50 traffic split between an optimized and an original version of one high-traffic landing page, run for one month with no visual or functional differences
plain: A Japanese retailer tested a version of one page tuned for speed and stability against the original. The tuned version reported much higher revenue per visitor, though details of the test are thin.
sample: One Rakuten 24 landing page, one month; visitor counts and geography not stated

stat.text: higher revenue per visitor reported for Rakuten 24's speed-optimised page versus the original (Google web.dev case study; sample size not given).

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Rakuten 24 A/B test of a Core Web Vitals-optimized page

application: Test the store on a throttled or dropped connection and confirm the cart stays browsable, the buy action is clearly disabled with an explanation, and queued actions sync visibly when the network returns.
do: Keep browsing and the basket usable offline and explain why the buy button is disabled.
dont: Block the whole screen with a loader or describe the problem in technical terms.
finding: Apps should decide how long to wait before treating a connection as failed, tell people promptly what state they are in and what still works, show when data was last refreshed, and disable only connection-dependent actions (such as buying) while keeping browsing available. It advises against full-screen blocking loaders, recommends queuing tasks, and suggests plain action-oriented wording instead of the jargon term for being disconnected.
limitation: Expert guidance from 2016 illustrated with app examples; it cites no user research and predates current PWA and service-worker practice.
measurement: Error or abandonment rate on poor connections; share of offline sessions with a clear status message; time to sync after reconnect
method: Not stated
plain: When the connection drops, tell people straight away, show what still works and when information was last updated, and switch off only actions that need a connection, like paying.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Designing honest offline and flaky-network states

visual.cap: A shopper's train enters a tunnel
visual.note: Illustration. Product names and prices are made-up examples.

application: Audit add-to-cart, coupon apply and payment submit for instant visual confirmation, and add progress messaging to any step that can take more than about a second.
do: Show an instant confirmation when people add to cart, apply a coupon or pay.
dont: Leave a tapped button unchanged while the request runs in the background.
finding: The first usability heuristic is framed as communication: every action should get immediate feedback, longer waits need progress indication, and back-end facts like low stock or distance to free shipping should surface only when they affect the user's decision. A cited eyetracking clip shows a user hesitating and looking for a loader when a tap produced no visible response.
limitation: Principle-based article; it presents no measured effect of status feedback on task success or conversion.
measurement: Repeat taps on the same control; time to visible feedback after action; task abandonment during waits
method: Heuristic explanation with product examples; references a clip from an NN/g mobile eyetracking study (details not reported)
plain: Every tap should get an instant, visible response, and longer waits need progress. Without it, people hesitate and hunt for signs that anything happened.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Why showing system state builds control and trust

visual.cap: A shopper taps Add to basket

application: Inventory transition durations in the design system, cap routine UI motion at 400 ms, set entrance and exit curves explicitly, and wire up prefers-reduced-motion.
do: Keep routine animations between 100 and 400 milliseconds and respect people's reduced-motion setting.
dont: Use long, slow animations for things people see many times a day.
finding: Small feedback such as toggles suits around 100 ms, larger view changes like modals 200 to 300 ms, and most UI motion should stay within 100 to 400 ms, with appearing elements given slightly more time than disappearing ones. Ease-out is the usual choice for entrances and ease-in for exits; frequently seen animations should be shorter, and reduced-motion preferences must be honoured.
limitation: Recommendations come from expert synthesis rather than a new controlled study; ranges are not validated against task performance.
measurement: Animation durations versus 100 to 400 ms range; share of animations respecting reduced-motion; perceived responsiveness ratings in testing
method: Expert guidance drawing on published motion design literature (Head 2016; Saffer 2014; Pratt et al. 2010) and product examples
plain: Small feedback, like a switch flipping, should take about a tenth of a second, and bigger changes like a pop-up opening about 0.2 to 0.3 seconds. Most interface motion should finish within 0.4 seconds.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Timing and easing rules for interface animation

application: Review favourite, add-to-cart and password-field interactions to confirm each gives a nearby, short response that reports status or prevents an error, and strip purely decorative motion.
do: Show a short response next to the button that confirms the action or helps prevent an error.
dont: Add decorative motion that tells people nothing.
finding: A microinteraction pairs a single trigger, from either the user or a system condition, with a small contextual response placed near that trigger. They earn their place by communicating status, preventing errors or enabling undo, and should stay brief and subtle so they support rather than distract from the main task.
limitation: No user testing or data; it argues for purpose over decoration but does not measure impact on usability or engagement.
measurement: Inline validation error recovery rate; undo usage after destructive actions; misclick or repeat-action rate
method: Not stated (editorial piece drawing on Saffer's 2014 book and the author's observations)
plain: Tiny responses, like a heart filling in when you tap 'save', should appear right next to what you touched and tell you something useful, such as that it worked.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Microinteractions as purposeful trigger-and-response moments

visual.cap: A shopper taps 'Save' on a product

application: Replace ad hoc animation values with named easing and duration tokens, using decelerate curves for entrances and accelerate curves for exits, and pick the transition pattern that matches the navigational relationship.
do: Use named easing and duration tokens instead of one-off animation values.
dont: Use one easing curve and duration for entering, leaving and large movements alike.
finding: Material defines standard and emphasized easing families, each with separate variants for on-screen movement, entering (decelerate) and exiting (accelerate), plus a duration scale from 50 ms up to 1000 ms that should grow with the size or travel of the animated area. It also specifies spring presets in fast, default and slow speeds, split between spatial motion and non-overshooting effects such as colour and opacity, and four transition patterns: container transform, shared axis, fade through and fade.
limitation: Implementation documentation for one design system; it explains how to apply tokens, not evidence that these values improve user outcomes.
measurement: Share of animations using system tokens; duration versus element travel distance; transition pattern consistency across flows
method: Not applicable (design system documentation)
plain: Material Design gives named speed and easing settings for animation: things entering slow down as they arrive and things leaving speed up. Bigger movements get longer durations.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Material motion tokens: easing curves, durations and springs

application: Audit the PDP gallery on both breakpoints and replace dot or text indicators with tappable thumbnails, including in the full-screen overlay, and add a partial-thumbnail cue where the row is truncated on mobile.
do: Show tappable thumbnails under the main image, with a partly cut-off one hinting at more.
dont: Replace thumbnails with dots that reveal nothing about each image.
finding: Every desktop benchmark site used gallery thumbnails, but only 24% of mobile benchmark sites did, with many swapping to dots or text to save space. When indicators replaced thumbnails, half of desktop testers struggled to discover the additional images, and dots gave no preview of what each image contained (e.g., scale shots or video).
limitation: Participant counts are not published, and the study measures discoverability and errors rather than demonstrating a conversion or revenue effect.
measurement: Share of PDP sessions viewing 2+ gallery images; mis-tap rate on gallery indicators; overlay open-and-immediate-close rate
method: Large-scale desktop and mobile usability testing combined with Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: Small preview pictures under a product photo tell people there are more images and what each shows. Dots don't, and half of desktop testers struggled to find extra images when dots replaced thumbnails.

stat.text: of mobile sites in Baymard's benchmark use gallery thumbnails, while every desktop site did.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Thumbnails Beat Dots for Signalling Extra Product Images

application: For visual categories, implement Quick View as a centered overlay over a dimmed, visible list, make the Back button close it, and place a prominent product-page link above the fold; use comparison tools instead for spec-driven categories.
do: Offer quick view for visual products as an overlay with a clear link to the full product page.
dont: Let the Back button skip past the quick view and lose the shopper's place in the list.
finding: Benchmark data show only half of sites selling visually driven products offer Quick Views; 2022 testing found shoppers of items like apparel valued seeing price, size availability, a few images and add-to-cart without leaving the list, reversing Baymard's poorer 2014-2015 results. Quick Views were far less useful for spec-heavy products, and some mobile users mistook the overlay for the full product page.
limitation: No sample sizes are given, and the guidance changed between test rounds, so results may depend on implementation quality and category; it does not show Quick Views lift sales.
measurement: Quick View open rate per list session; add-to-cart rate from Quick View vs PDP; Back-button exits from Quick View that leave the list
method: Large-scale product list usability testing (including 2022 desktop testing and recent mobile sessions) plus Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: A quick view lets shoppers peek at price, sizes and photos without leaving the product list. It helped for clothes but not for products bought on specs, and some phone users mistook it for the full page.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: When Quick Views Help and When They Hurt

application: Show the rating breakdown as horizontal bars where each bar filters reviews by that star level, keep the rating filter visible by default, make selections mutually exclusive, and hide the breakdown when a product has five or fewer reviews.
do: Show star-level bars that each filter the reviews when tapped.
dont: Show only the average star score with no breakdown.
finding: In testing, 95% of participants relied on reviews and 53% deliberately looked for negative ones, and the ratings distribution was the most-used part of the reviews section. In the benchmark, 43% of sites lacked a distribution summary entirely, and among those with one, 39% missed at least one key design detail.
limitation: Survey preferences (e.g., choosing more ratings over a higher average) are stated preferences from US respondents and do not prove purchase behaviour elsewhere.
measurement: Interaction rate with rating distribution bars; share of review sessions using star filters; PDP conversion after review engagement
method: Product page usability testing, a benchmark of top-grossing ecommerce sites, and two US consumer surveys
plain: Nearly everyone in testing relied on reviews, and about half went looking for bad ones on purpose. A star breakdown, where tapping a bar shows those reviews, was the most-used part of the review section.
sample: Benchmark of 60 top-grossing sites; 670 US participants across two surveys; usability test participant count not stated

stat.text: of Baymard test participants deliberately looked for negative reviews (95% relied on reviews).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Five Rules for a Usable Star-Rating Breakdown

application: Audit best-selling and high-revenue PDPs for image resolution and maximum zoom depth, and on mobile load a higher-resolution asset once the user starts zooming.
do: Load a sharper image as soon as someone starts zooming.
dont: Use low-resolution photos that turn blurry when zoomed.
finding: In testing, 56% of users began their product page visit by exploring the images, yet the benchmark found a quarter of sites offered images inadequate for visual evaluation, with low resolution at 14% and insufficient zoom at 11%. Poor images led some users to abandon and could damage perception of the whole brand.
limitation: The study sample size is not given, and abandonment was observed in sessions rather than quantified; it does not establish a specific resolution threshold.
measurement: Zoom interaction rate per PDP view; PDP exit rate after gallery use; A/B conversion lift from upgraded imagery on high-traffic SKUs
method: Large-scale usability testing from Baymard's research database combined with a benchmark of ecommerce sites' popular categories and products
plain: Many shoppers start a product page by looking at the photos. Blurry images, or zoom that can't get close, made some testers give up and think less of the whole brand.

stat.text: of Baymard test participants began their product page visit by exploring the images.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Low-Res Images and Weak Zoom Erode Product Trust

application: For temporarily unavailable SKUs, keep the buy button active with an extended delivery estimate and an explanatory note, show alternatives nearby, and for discontinued items replace the buy area with clearly labelled substitutes.
do: Keep the buy button active for temporarily unavailable items, with a clear later delivery estimate.
dont: Offer only a back-in-stock email that requires creating an account.
finding: Baymard reports that 30% of users shown an out-of-stock notice are likely to leave and shop elsewhere, while 68% of benchmarked sites do not allow ordering temporarily unavailable items. Back-in-stock email alerts and wishlists tested poorly as the sole option, especially when they required creating an account.
limitation: Sample sizes are not stated, and some figures (such as account-wall drop-off) are anecdotal from clients rather than controlled measurements.
measurement: Exit rate on out-of-stock PDPs; orders placed for backordered items; click-through to suggested alternatives
method: Product page usability testing, Baymard's product page benchmark, supporting checkout research and a cart-abandonment survey, plus anecdotal audit-client observations
plain: When a product shows as out of stock, many shoppers leave to buy elsewhere. If it's only temporary, let people order it anyway with a later delivery date.

stat.text: of users shown an out-of-stock notice are likely to leave and shop elsewhere, according to Baymard.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Let Shoppers Buy Out-of-Stock Items with Longer Delivery

application: Restructure long spec sheets into titled groups in a single column with alternating row shading, and add a key-specs summary at the top for sheets longer than two viewports while repeating those specs in place.
do: Group specs under titled sections in a single column with alternating row shading.
dont: Lay specs out in several columns that look like a product comparison.
finding: The benchmark found half of sites had hard-to-scan spec sheets: 23% did not group specs into sections, 23% lacked visual aids like row shading, and 20% used multi-column layouts that some testers misread as a product comparison. Eye-tracking indicated alternating horizontal shading helped users match labels to values more quickly.
limitation: Participant numbers for the usability and eye-tracking work are not published, and the study does not quantify conversion impact.
measurement: Time to locate a target spec in moderated tests; spec section expand/scroll depth; spec-related pre-sale support contacts
method: Large-scale Product Details Page usability testing, an eye-tracking study, and Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: Long product spec lists are hard to scan. Grouping specs under headings in one column with alternating row shading helps people match each label to its value.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Making Product Spec Sheets Scannable

visual.cap: A shopper checks a laptop's battery life
visual.note: Illustration. Specs are made-up examples.

application: Check that each PDP shows the current price prominently in the buy box, places any discount directly beside it with both original and sale prices, states the saving, and mentions each promotion only once.
do: Show the sale price large in the buy area, with the original price and saving right beside it.
dont: Mention the same promotion in several places so shoppers wonder whether deals stack.
finding: The benchmark found 18% of desktop and 11% of mobile sites make the price needlessly hard to find, 14% of desktop sites separate promotions from the price, and 19% describe the same offer more than once, leaving users unsure whether deals stack. Testing showed a large, bold or coloured price in the buy area attracted attention most reliably.
limitation: Overall sample sizes are not reported, and the recommendation on absolute vs percentage discounts relies on external research rather than this study.
measurement: Time to locate price in usability tests; add-to-cart rate on discounted SKUs; promo-related support queries
method: Large-scale desktop and mobile product page usability testing and benchmarking of ecommerce sites
plain: Shoppers struggle to tell what they'll pay when the price is small, the discount sits elsewhere, or the same deal is mentioned twice. A large, bold price in the buy area drew attention most reliably.
sample: Not stated on page (one cited site test: 67% of participants struggled to find the price)

stat.text: of desktop sites in Baymard's benchmark describe the same offer more than once.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Four Ways Sale Pricing Confuses Shoppers on PDPs

visual.note: Illustration. Product names and prices are made-up examples.

application: Audit recommendation and 'you may also like' modules so every card shows image, untruncated title, price, rating with count, variation swatches, and brand on multi-brand stores, with parity on mobile.
do: Give every suggestion card an image, full title, price, rating with review count and available options.
dont: Cut product titles short or drop the rating to squeeze more cards into a row.
finding: Users tended to overlook product suggestions that lacked enough detail, and 68% of desktop benchmark sites omitted at least one essential attribute; for example, 55% truncated titles and half left out the average rating. Baymard identifies six needed attributes: a quality thumbnail, full title, price, rating average with count, available variations, and brand.
limitation: No participant or site counts are given, and the study does not measure how much each attribute changes click-through or attach rate.
measurement: Click-through rate on cross-sell modules; attach rate of suggested items; share of cards meeting all six attributes
method: Large-scale desktop and mobile usability studies and Baymard's product page benchmark
plain: Suggested products get skipped when their cards leave out details. Testers overlooked suggestions missing things like the full name or the star rating.

stat.text: of desktop sites in Baymard's benchmark left at least one essential detail off their suggestion cards.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: What Cross-Sell Cards Must Show to Get Clicked

visual.cap: A shopper scans 'You may also like'
visual.note: Illustration. Product names, ratings and prices are made-up examples.

application: Ensure product lists offer price (both directions), highest-rated, best-selling and newest sorts, add category-specific sorts where relevant, drop alphabetical sorting, and always display the active sort beside a visible label.
do: Offer price low-to-high and high-to-low, top rated, best-selling and newest, and show the active sort.
dont: Offer alphabetical sorting or a 'Sort by' placeholder that hides the current order.
finding: Testing showed shoppers regularly looked for sorting by price, user rating, best-selling and newest, yet 64% of benchmarked sites lacked at least one; on desktop, 36% had no rating sort and 52% no best-seller sort. Alphabetical sorting was almost never used, and 30% of sites used a 'Sort By' placeholder that hid which sort was active.
limitation: Sample sizes are not reported, and the study shows which sorts users seek rather than their effect on conversion.
measurement: Sort usage rate per list session; distribution of sort types chosen; list-to-PDP click-through after sorting
method: Large-scale usability testing across desktop, mobile site and mobile app sessions, plus Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: Shoppers expect to sort lists by price, rating, best-selling and newest, but most shops miss at least one. A 'Sort by' box that hides the current choice leaves people unsure how the list is ordered.

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's benchmark lacked at least one of the four sort options shoppers looked for.

application: For best-sellers and complex products, rewrite descriptions into 2-6 highlight blocks covering unique selling points, each with an image or icon and short headline, and move secondary features to a separate list.
do: Turn key selling points into 2–6 highlight blocks, each with an image, short headline and short paragraph.
dont: Paste every feature into one long bullet list.
finding: All test users consulted the product description at some point, but plain text blocks were often seen as dull and long bullet lists turned into feature dumps that users skimmed past. Descriptions broken into highlights (image, headline and short paragraph per feature) led users to explore features more fully, yet only 22% of benchmarked sites used this structure.
limitation: Sample size is not stated, and engagement was observed qualitatively; the article does not quantify conversion impact or test simple low-consideration products.
measurement: Scroll depth through description section; time on description; PDP add-to-cart rate before vs after restructuring
method: Product Details Page usability testing, with a benchmark of sites' top-5 selling products
plain: Everyone in testing read the product description, but plain text blocks felt dull and long bullet lists got skimmed. Splitting it into a few feature highlights, each with a picture and headline, led people to explore more.

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's benchmark structured product descriptions as feature highlights.

title: Feature Highlights Make Product Descriptions Engaging

application: Count the filter types on each product list; if more than about six, move from a top toolbar to a left sidebar or ensure an 'All filters' entry point is impossible to miss.
do: Use a left sidebar when a list has more than about six filter types.
dont: Cram eight or more filters into a top bar of closed drop-downs.
finding: Horizontal filter toolbars hide each filter's options until clicked, which makes it harder to scan available values and counts than in a sidebar, and they strain once a list needs more than roughly 6-8 filter types. Baymard's benchmark puts horizontal toolbar adoption at 24% of sites, a share it reports as steady since 2020.
limitation: No participant count or task data is published, so the size of the usability penalty versus sidebars is not quantified.
measurement: Filter usage rate per list page; time to first filter applied; filter-to-product-click rate
method: Large-scale usability testing plus Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: Filter bars across the top hide each filter's choices until you click. A sidebar shows the options at a glance and copes better when there are many filters.

title: Why sidebar filters usually beat horizontal filter bars

application: Trigger a sample of nonsense and near-miss queries and check that the empty-results page offers category links, alternate query suggestions with product previews, and a visible chat or phone option.
do: Show related categories, suggested searches with products, and a chat or phone link on the no-results page.
dont: Show only generic tips like 'check your spelling' and nothing else.
finding: Roughly half of benchmarked ecommerce sites fail to give shoppers useful ways forward after a search returns nothing, and generic search tips on their own are rarely read or acted on. Better pages link to related (ideally pre-filtered) categories, offer alternative queries with product previews, and surface recommendations, popular items and support contacts.
limitation: The page does not tie the ~50% figure to a stated number of sites or test participants, and it does not measure revenue impact of each recovery tactic.
measurement: Zero-results rate; exit rate from no-results page; click-through from no-results page to product list
method: Large-scale on-site search usability testing and Baymard's ecommerce search UX benchmark
plain: When a search finds nothing, about half of shops leave people stuck. Better pages offer related categories, other search ideas with product previews, and a way to get help.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Turning zero-results pages into recovery paths

application: Add an applied-filters row above the product grid with one chip per selection, an 'x' on each and a Clear All link; on mobile use a horizontally scrolling chip row with the last chip visibly cut off.
do: Add a row of applied-filter chips with an 'x' on each and a 'Clear all' link.
dont: Show only a count like '3 filters' without naming them.
finding: Without a consolidated list of active filters, users struggle to confirm what is applied, to remove selections quickly, and to understand why a list looks small, sometimes concluding the store lacks suitable products. Baymard's benchmark reports 28% of sites offer no such overview, and that showing just a count of applied filters is not a substitute for naming them.
limitation: Desktop testing did not settle which overview placement performs best, and no sample sizes or conversion effects are reported.
measurement: Filter removal rate; filter-session product-click rate; share of sessions abandoning after filtering
method: Large-scale desktop and mobile usability testing plus Baymard's UX benchmarks
plain: Show every filter someone has applied as a removable chip above the results. Without it, people can't tell why the list looks small and may think the shop has nothing for them.

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's benchmark show no overview of applied filters.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Showing active filters as a removable summary

application: Mine search and autocomplete logs for the most frequent misspellings, map them to correct terms, and test that typing a near-miss (e.g. a dropped letter) still shows correct suggestions on mobile.
do: Map common misspellings to the right terms so suggestions still appear.
dont: Let one dropped letter wipe out every suggestion.
finding: Nearly every test participant leaned on autocomplete, yet small misspellings often caused suggestions to vanish or turn irrelevant, leading some users to spend 30+ seconds fixing the query, switch to category browsing, or leave. Baymard's benchmark found 69% of sites do not return useful autocomplete suggestions for slightly misspelled queries.
limitation: The number of participants and benchmarked sites is not given, and how often each user reaction occurs is not quantified.
measurement: Autocomplete suggestion click rate on misspelled inputs; query reformulation rate; search exit rate
method: Qualitative usability testing across desktop, mobile web and mobile apps, plus Baymard's search benchmark
plain: People rely on search suggestions, but a small typo often makes them disappear. Some then spend half a minute fixing it, switch to browsing, or leave.

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's benchmark don't return useful autocomplete suggestions for slightly misspelled queries.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Keeping autocomplete working through typos

application: Audit the first 20 desktop / 10 mobile results of key categories and ensure every product type above about 10% of the list appears there under the default sort.
do: Default to a 'Featured' order that mixes the main product types near the top.
dont: Default a category to 'Price: low to high', so it opens with only accessories.
finding: Shoppers judge a category's range from its first few products, so defaults like price, alphabetical or pure bestseller can make a catalog look narrow, overpriced or cheap. Baymard reports 24% of benchmarked desktop sites fail to convey selection breadth via their default sort, and recommends a diversity-weighted 'Relevance' or 'Featured' order.
limitation: No participant counts or A/B results are given, so the conversion effect of a diversity-based sort is not demonstrated.
measurement: Category bounce rate; scroll depth on product lists; sort-change rate
method: Large-scale, multi-round desktop and mobile usability testing plus Baymard's UX benchmark
plain: Shoppers judge a shop's range from the first few products. Sorting by price or name by default can make the range look narrow, too pricey or too cheap.

stat.text: of desktop sites in Baymard's benchmark fail to show their range through the default sort.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Default sort order that shows catalog breadth

application: Search a broad term, sort by lowest price, and check whether accessories dominate; if so, offer category-scoped sort choices or prompt for a department first.
do: Offer sort options scoped to a category, like 'TVs by screen size'.
dont: Let 'lowest price' on a search for 'TV' fill the top with cables and wall brackets.
finding: Sorting a broad search result set by price or rating tends to float accessories and low-relevance items to the top, which confused test participants; Baymard says only 10% of sites address this. It proposes asking for a department before sorting or offering scoped sort options such as sorting TVs by screen size.
limitation: An older article with no published sample sizes; the faceted sorting pattern is proposed rather than validated with comparative testing.
measurement: Product clicks after sort change; sort-then-refine rate; search exit rate after sorting
method: Baymard ecommerce search usability study and search benchmark; scope figure from its homepage and category usability study
plain: Sorting broad search results by price or rating often floats accessories to the top. Ask which department first, or offer sorting within a category.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Pairing sort options with a category scope
