application: Before building facets, list the attributes customers actually use to choose (from search logs or interviews) and confirm every product has clean metadata for each one.
do: List the attributes customers really choose by, and check every product has data for them.
dont: Add dozens of filter options that are mostly empty or irrelevant to buyers.
finding: A filter removes items that fail one criterion, while faceted navigation combines several filters across different attributes, making large collections easier to explore. Facets bring extra design effort, require metadata on every item, and add interaction cost, so they only pay off when they reflect the attributes users care about.
limitation: Definitional piece with no user study or data; it does not show when facets measurably outperform simple filters.
measurement: Facet usage per attribute; metadata completeness per facet; time to find a target item
method: Not stated (explanatory article using recipe-site examples)
plain: A simple filter removes items that don't match one thing. Combined filters across many attributes help with big ranges, but only if every product has clean data and the attributes matter to shoppers.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: When simple filters suffice and when facets earn their cost

application: On mobile product lists, test whether filter changes show live updates and a visible result count without leaving the list; replace icon-only filter buttons with a text label.
do: Open filters in a side tray with a visible, updating result count and a 'Filter' text label.
dont: Send people to a separate full screen where they can't see what each filter does.
finding: Sending mobile users to a separate filter screen forces back-and-forth to see the effect of each choice; a partial overlay tray lets results stay visible and update as filters change. The article advises opening it from the right, keeping the result count pinned, and using text labels such as 'Filter' rather than icons.
limitation: Qualitative critique of a few designs without a sample or measured outcomes; it does not compare the tray against full-screen filter panels in testing.
measurement: Mobile filter usage rate; filters applied per session; filter-to-zero-results rate
method: Design review of iStockphoto, Amazon and eBay mobile designs informed by the author's usability testing; no formal study reported
plain: On a phone, a filter panel that slides over part of the list lets people see results change as they choose. A separate filter screen makes them jump back and forth to check.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Mobile filter trays that keep results in view

visual.cap: A shopper narrows a list on a phone

application: Check the no-results template for a prominent heading, the original query pre-filled in an editable box, a did-you-mean suggestion, and no humorous illustration.
do: Show a clear heading, the search pre-filled for editing, and a 'did you mean' link.
dont: Use a cartoon or a joke on the empty results page.
finding: Users frequently overlook small no-results messages, so the empty state must be visually unmistakable, offer next steps (an editable query box, spelling fixes, related queries, tips), and avoid jokey imagery that can read as mocking an already frustrated user.
limitation: Based on illustrative observations rather than a quantified study; it does not report how much each guideline reduces abandonment.
measurement: Zero-results exit rate; query reformulation rate after zero results; spelling-suggestion click rate
method: Qualitative observation from the author's research, including an eyetracking recording of one user on a no-results page
plain: People often miss small 'no results' messages. Make the empty page obvious, keep their search editable, offer spelling fixes, and avoid jokey pictures that can feel like mockery.
sample: Not stated on page (eyetracking example shows a single user)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Three rules for empty search results pages

application: Inspect the site search autocomplete for role=combobox, aria-expanded, aria-controls and aria-activedescendant, then verify arrow, Enter and Escape behave as specified using only a keyboard and a screen reader.
do: Test site search suggestions using only a keyboard and a screen reader.
dont: Auto-select a suggestion or move focus out of the search box as people type.
finding: The ARIA APG example shows a text input with role combobox and aria-autocomplete=list that opens a listbox of matching suggestions without auto-selecting one, keeps DOM focus in the input, and signals the highlighted option via aria-activedescendant. Arrow keys move through suggestions, Enter accepts one and Escape closes the list or clears the field.
limitation: W3C labels the code illustrative rather than production-ready and warns support varies across browser and assistive-technology combinations, especially on touch devices.
measurement: Keyboard-only task completion for search; screen reader announcement of suggestions; accessibility audit issue count on search field
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: A search box with suggestions should work by keyboard alone: arrow keys move through suggestions, Enter picks one, Escape closes the list, and screen readers announce the highlighted one.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Accessible autocomplete search field markup and keys

application: Audit every icon-only control (nav, wishlist, account, filters) and add a persistent visible text label to any icon outside the home/print/search set; remove hover-only label reveals.
do: Add a visible text label to every icon outside the home, print and search set.
dont: Rely on hover tooltips to explain icons, since they don't appear on touchscreens.
finding: Only a handful of icons (home, print, magnifying-glass search) are broadly understood; symbols like hearts, stars and hamburgers carry inconsistent meanings across sites, and in one test no participant clicked an obscure clock icon used for history. Hover-only labels raise interaction cost and fail on touch screens.
limitation: Evidence is qualitative and anecdotal with no sample sizes or recognition rates; published in 2014, so some icon conventions (e.g., hamburger) may have matured since.
measurement: Icon recognition rate in first-click tests; task success on icon-driven navigation; misclick rate on unlabeled controls
method: Draws on NN/g usability studies and observations (e.g., a site's clock icon, the Combadi site); no formal methodology described
plain: Only a few icons, like home, print and the magnifying glass for search, are widely understood. Others, like hearts or stars, mean different things on different sites, so they need a visible word beside them.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Why Most Icons Need Visible Text Labels

visual.cap: A shopper wants to save an item for later

application: Inventory every modal on the site; remove or convert newsletter and promo modals to nonmodal banners, and ensure no modal interrupts the checkout flow except for irreversible-error warnings.
do: Show promotions in a banner that leaves the page usable.
dont: Open a promotional pop-up in the middle of checkout.
finding: Modals freeze the underlying page, forcing users to break context and take an extra step to dismiss them, so they suit only critical warnings, essential missing input, or stepped workflows. Promotional popups and interruptions inside checkout erode trust, and nonmodal panels are preferable for noncritical content.
limitation: No quantitative data on conversion or abandonment impact; guidance is principle-based and example-driven rather than tested at scale.
measurement: Modal dismissal rate; checkout abandonment at steps with overlays; task completion time with vs without modal
method: Expert guidance with annotated product examples; references a web-usability study in which participants disliked newsletter-signup modals, but that study's method is not described
plain: A pop-up box that freezes the page makes people stop what they were doing just to close it. Keep these for critical warnings or must-have missing info, not promotions.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: When Interruptive Modal Dialogs Earn Their Cost

application: Review forms and product pages at every breakpoint to confirm labels sit beside their fields, headings hug their content, and key actions (e.g., Add to cart, Skip) sit next to the content they affect.
do: Place each action, like Add to cart, right beside the content it affects at every screen size.
dont: Let a responsive layout push a label or button away from the thing it belongs to.
finding: People read elements placed near each other as one group, and this spatial cue can override color or shape similarity. Misplaced controls, such as a Skip link far from the main actions or an Add button buried among unrelated buttons, get overlooked, and responsive reflow can silently break intended groupings.
limitation: Illustrative examples only; no measured effect sizes showing how much spacing changes task success or conversion.
measurement: Form completion rate; time to locate a target action; error rate from mis-associated labels
method: Applies early-20th-century Gestalt perception principles to annotated interface examples; cites NN/g mobile-usability observations; no formal study described
plain: People see things placed close together as belonging together, even more than things that share a colour. A button placed far from what it affects is easily missed.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Spacing as a Signal of Relatedness in UI Layouts

application: For product detail or FAQ pages, test content as plain headings first; keep essential info (price, delivery, returns) out of collapsed sections and avoid nesting accordions.
date: Date not shown (change log entry April 2025)
do: Keep price, delivery and returns visible as plain headings and text.
dont: Hide essential details inside collapsed or nested sections.
finding: GOV.UK advises using accordions only when evidence shows users benefit from an overview and from toggling sections, never for content everyone must read, never nested, and never with disabled sections. A 2021 update fixed buttons being mistaken for links, and users who navigate via element lists may not realise headings are buttons.
limitation: Research findings are summarised without method, sample size, or quantitative outcomes; guidance targets government services rather than commerce.
measurement: Section expansion rate; task success for finding information inside collapsed panels; scroll depth vs content discovery
method: Component guidance informed by team research and an accessibility clinic; participant numbers and method not given
plain: Folding content into expandable sections hides it, and people can miss what's inside. GOV.UK only uses them when testing shows people benefit, never for content everyone needs.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Evidence Bar for Hiding Content in Accordions

application: Test product imagery, logos and text in both appearances (plus Increase Contrast); swap hard-coded hex values for theme tokens and slightly dim white-background product photos in dark mode.
do: Use theme colour tokens that adapt to dark mode and keep text contrast at 4.5:1 or more.
dont: Hard-code white backgrounds and dark text that break when the phone switches to dark mode.
finding: Apple asks apps to follow the system appearance rather than add an app-specific theme toggle, to use adaptive semantic colors instead of hard-coded values, and to keep contrast at 4.5:1 minimum while aiming for 7:1 for custom colors, especially small text. On iOS, brighter elevated backgrounds signal layers sitting above dimmer base backgrounds.
limitation: Platform guidance for Apple OSes, not user research; it does not show that dark mode improves task performance or conversion.
measurement: Contrast ratio of text/background pairs in each theme; share of components using semantic tokens; legibility defects found in dark-mode QA
method: Not stated
plain: When someone's phone is set to dark mode, apps should follow it, using colours that adapt automatically and keep text easy to read in both light and dark.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Apple's Rules for Respecting Dark Appearance

application: Define a small set of text styles (title, headline, body, caption) in your design system, ban light weights for small text, and QA product pages at the largest accessibility text size for truncation and lost hierarchy.
do: Define a small set of text styles and test key pages at the largest text size.
dont: Use thin or light font weights for small text, or let enlarged text get cut off.
finding: Apple recommends conveying hierarchy through weight, size and color with few typefaces, avoiding Ultralight/Thin/Light weights, and respecting platform text sizes (iOS default 17 pt, minimum 11 pt). Hierarchy must hold when users enlarge text, prioritising primary content and minimising truncation at accessibility sizes.
limitation: Prescriptive platform guidance without cited user research; point sizes are Apple-specific and do not translate directly to web CSS pixels.
measurement: Number of distinct type styles in use; truncation defects at largest text size; proportion of text below minimum size
method: Not stated
plain: Use size, weight and colour to show what matters most, and make sure that order still works when people turn up their text size. Avoid very thin fonts for small text.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Building Type Hierarchy That Survives Text Scaling

application: Use a single non-blocking snackbar with an Undo action for reversible events like removing a cart item, anchored above bottom navigation so it does not hide primary controls.
do: Show one brief message with Undo after reversible actions like removing a cart item.
dont: Stack several messages or let one cover the bottom navigation.
finding: Material positions snackbars as brief, non-interrupting messages about a completed or pending process that disappear without user input and may carry an optional action such as undo or retry. Only one shows at a time (a new one replaces the old), they can be anchored above bottom navigation or a FAB, and they are preferred over Android Toasts.
limitation: Developer documentation for Android components; gives no specific timing values or user evidence on how long messages should persist or whether users notice them.
measurement: Undo action usage rate; accidental-removal recovery rate; overlap incidents with bottom navigation or CTAs
method: Not stated
plain: After something like removing an item, show a short message that disappears on its own and offers Undo. Show only one at a time, and keep it clear of the bottom menu.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Material Snackbar Behavior and Placement Rules

application: Reserve toggles for settings that take effect immediately; use checkboxes for consent, yes/no and multi-option choices, default toggles to off, and avoid negatively worded or red-coded toggle labels.
do: Label switches On and Off and use them only for settings that apply instantly.
dont: Use an unlabelled switch for a consent or yes/no question.
finding: Unlabeled gray toggles were read correctly by only 10% of participants versus 95% when on/off labels were added, a significant difference; red 'yes/no' toggles and '1/0' labels also lowered correct state identification. Most participants preferred checkboxes for yes/no answers and for several related options, and expected toggles to apply instantly without a save button.
limitation: Small convenience sample (N=20), only slider-style toggles tested, prototypes rather than live products, and flat-design effects not evaluated.
measurement: Correct identification of toggle state; preference share toggle vs checkbox; settings-change error rate
method: Within-users experiment with 18 Axure prototypes in nine paired cases; remote moderated sessions measuring correct identification of initial state, preferences, and a 13-item Likert questionnaire; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests
plain: Most people couldn't tell whether a grey switch with no label was on or off. Adding On and Off labels fixed that, and people preferred checkboxes for yes/no questions.
sample: 20 participants (12 male, 8 female, aged 18-50), convenience sample from a university and authors' contacts; Norway-based authors

stat.text: of participants read an unlabelled grey toggle correctly, versus 95% with on/off labels (Journal of User Experience study, 20 participants).

strengthWhy: Published study, but observational or correlational.
title: Experiment on Toggle Labels, Defaults and Checkboxes

visual.cap: Someone checks their email settings

application: In usability tests, pair attractiveness or satisfaction ratings with objective task success so a polished visual design does not mask real interaction problems.
do: Measure task success alongside attractiveness ratings in every usability test.
dont: Treat a high 'looks easy to use' rating as proof that the design works.
finding: Perceived ease of use correlated 0.589 with rated beauty, while most structural usability measures correlated weakly with perceived ease of use (familiarity of key pattern was the exception at 0.730). The authors conclude that how usable an interface looks is tied closely to its aesthetics.
limitation: Single static ATM screen, hard-copy stimuli, no actual task performance, no significance tests reported; shows correlation between looks and perceived usability, not that beauty improves real usability.
measurement: Perceived usability rating; aesthetic rating; objective task success rate
method: Two-phase experiment: participants created 26 ATM (cash dispenser) screen layouts, then a separate group rated each hard-copy layout on apparent usability and beauty using 10-point scales; ratings were correlated with seven designer-derived inherent usability measures
plain: In this early study, how easy people expected a screen to be was closely linked to how attractive they found it. Good looks shaped first impressions of usability, but that doesn't prove the screen was easier to use.
sample: 26 layout creators and 252 raters (156 design students, 96 psychology students); country not stated (authors at Hitachi, Tokyo)

stat.text: correlation between rated beauty and expected ease of use (CHI '95 study, 252 raters judging 26 cash-machine screen layouts)

strengthWhy: Published study, but observational or correlational.
title: Origin Study of the Aesthetic-Usability Effect

application: Before adding or keeping a swipe-through intro, test the core task with and without it; if success is unchanged, remove it and invest in clearer UI or in-context help.
do: Test the main task with and without the intro tutorial before keeping it.
dont: Force a swipe-through tutorial before people can use a simple app.
finding: People who skipped the launch tutorial succeeded about as often (94% vs 91%, not significant) and rated the task easier on the 7-point Single Ease Question (5.49 vs 4.92, significant at p=0.047); time on task did not differ significantly. The author reads this as tutorials making simple apps feel more complicated without improving performance.
limitation: Only four simple iOS apps with one tutorial style; does not show results for complex apps, Android, interactive tutorials or long-term retention.
measurement: Task success rate with vs without tutorial; Single Ease Question score; tutorial skip rate
method: Between-subjects remote unmoderated quantitative usability test (Userlytics); participants installed an unfamiliar iOS app, either viewed or skipped its deck-of-cards tutorial, then did a task the tutorial covered
plain: In a test of four simple iPhone apps, people who skipped the swipe-through intro did the task about as well and found it easier than those who watched it.
sample: 70 participants (35 always viewed the tutorial, 35 always skipped); 4 iOS apps; 13 trials (5%) excluded
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Skippers vs readers: do first-launch tutorials help mobile users?

application: Map every first-run step and flag any that is non-interactive, unskippable, asks for setup that could default, or requests a rating/purchase before the user has done anything meaningful.
do: Use sensible defaults and short tips placed next to the feature they explain.
dont: Ask for a rating or purchase before people have done anything in the app.
finding: Apple advises that apps should ideally be learnable by use alone; where onboarding is needed it should be short, hands-on and skippable, with context-specific tips placed near the relevant UI preferred over one long upfront flow. It also recommends deferring nonessential setup in favour of sensible defaults, and waiting until people are engaged before asking for ratings or purchases.
limitation: Platform design guidance without published evidence; does not quantify effects on completion, activation or retention.
measurement: Time from first launch to first core action; onboarding completion vs skip rate; share of users changing default settings
method: Not stated
plain: Ideally people learn an app just by using it. If an intro is needed, keep it short, hands-on and skippable, and wait until people are engaged before asking for ratings or purchases.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Apple's rules for fast, optional, interactive onboarding

application: Scale onboarding to product complexity: skip formal tutorials for simple flows and, for complex tools, deliver instruction at the moment a feature is first needed rather than up front.
do: Teach a complex feature at the moment people first need it.
dont: Add a formal tutorial to a simple flow people can work out alone.
finding: Tutorials only paid off in the complex game: in Foldit, context-sensitive tutorials were linked to 75% more levels completed and 29% more play time than no tutorial, while in the two simpler casual games tutorials showed no significant gain in levels or time. Just-in-time tutorials beat upfront ones in the complex game, and restricting player freedom showed no clear benefit.
limitation: Non-commercial games with unknown player demographics and only text-and-image tutorials; engagement metrics are proxies and may not transfer to productivity apps or websites.
measurement: Feature adoption or tasks completed per new user; active time in first session; return rate within N days
method: Online multivariate experiment randomly assigning new players to eight tutorial conditions varying presence, context-sensitivity, blocking vs nonblocking, and on-demand help; outcomes were levels completed, active play time and return rate
plain: Tutorials only helped in a complex puzzle game, where tips shown at the right moment went with players finishing more levels. In two simpler games, tutorials made no clear difference.
sample: Over 45,000 players across three games (Refraction 13,158; Foldit 9,743; Hello Worlds 22,417); about two weeks of data for two games and two days for the third

stat.text: more levels completed with context-sensitive tutorials than with none in the complex game Foldit (CHI 2012 large-scale A/B test).

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Large-scale A/B test of tutorials across simple and complex games

application: Review your signup or start screen for cost, time-to-complete, required documents, a resume/sign-in route and an action-specific primary button; move eligibility rules into early in-flow questions.
do: State cost, rough time and what to have ready on the start page, with a button that names the action.
dont: Pack complex eligibility rules onto the start page instead of asking them as questions inside the form.
finding: The entry point to a service should tell people what it does and whether it fits their situation, state cost, rough time and what they need to have ready, offer sign-in or resume options and non-digital alternatives, and use a button label that matches the action. Complex eligibility rules belong as questions inside the service rather than on the start page; the page cites a DWP blog post on Carer's Allowance as evidence that embedding the start in a multipart guide helped users, without giving data.
limitation: Pattern guidance for UK government services; the cited research is a summarised blog post with no reported method, sample or metrics.
measurement: Start-to-completion rate; drop-off on first in-service page; share of starters later found ineligible
method: Not stated
plain: The first page of a sign-up or application should say what it's for, who it's for, what it costs, how long it takes and what to have ready, so people can decide before they start.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GOV.UK pattern for the starting point of a service

application: Inspect every data table in the DOM: confirm th elements with correct scope, a caption, id/headers wiring on multi-level tables, and no tables used purely for page layout.
do: Mark header cells as th with the right scope and add a caption.
dont: Make ordinary cells bold so they only look like headers.
finding: The tutorial supports WCAG SC 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A), which requires structure and relationships conveyed visually to be programmatically determinable: header cells should use th and data cells td, ambiguous headers get scope="col" or "row", spanning headers use colgroup/rowgroup scope, and tables whose headers cannot be mapped along one axis need explicit id and headers attributes. A caption naming the table's subject is recommended in most cases.
limitation: Covers markup techniques only; it does not test how real screen reader users perform with each pattern or address interactive grids, sorting or responsive layouts.
measurement: Share of data tables with programmatic headers; share with a caption; screen reader announcement of correct header for sampled cells
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Data tables need their header cells marked as headers, so screen readers can say which column and row each value belongs to. A caption naming the table helps too.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Marking up data table headers for screen readers

application: Check that numeric columns are right-aligned, every table has a descriptive caption, and oversized tables are split rather than crammed onto one screen.
do: Give every table a caption and right-align columns of numbers.
dont: Use a table to lay out page content, or cram a huge dataset onto one screen.
finding: The component is meant for letting people compare information across rows and columns and must not be used to lay out page content. Columns of numbers should be right-aligned so values line up for comparison, a caption should act like a heading for the table, header cells should carry scope so assistive tech can tell row and column headers apart, and large datasets should be broken into several tables or pages where feasible.
limitation: The page reports no user research or statistics on this component, so the guidance reflects design-system convention rather than demonstrated performance gains.
measurement: Proportion of numeric columns right-aligned; proportion of tables with captions; time to compare two numeric values
method: Not stated
plain: Tables are for comparing information across rows and columns. A caption that works like a heading, and numbers lined up on the right, make values quicker to compare.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GOV.UK rules for comparable, captioned tables

visual.cap: A customer compares monthly plan prices
visual.note: Illustration. Plan names and prices are made-up examples.

application: For sortable tables, verify aria-sort updates on each header, sorting uses true numeric/date values, and on phones the table either scrolls with keyboard focus or stacks with visible cell labels.
do: Mark the sorted column with aria-sort and sort dates and numbers by their true values.
dont: Let a wide table spill off a phone screen with no way to scroll it by keyboard.
finding: USWDS offers striped, borderless, scrollable, sticky-header and stacked variants, with stacked tables collapsing into labelled blocks on narrow screens. Sortable headers expose their state through aria-sort, sort on underlying machine values (such as timestamps instead of display dates), and pair with a polite live region; scrollable containers are made keyboard-focusable, and the component is labelled as having passed WCAG 2.1 AA.
limitation: No user research results are given for the variants; the page does not show which mobile pattern performs best for users or measure sort comprehension.
measurement: Correct aria-sort state after sorting; horizontal-scroll or stacked rendering at 320px width; keyboard reachability of scroll container
method: Not stated
plain: Tables that can be sorted should tell screen reader users which way they're sorted, and sort by real values. On small screens they should scroll or stack with labels.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Accessible sortable and responsive tables in USWDS

application: Replace pie, donut and gauge widgets used for comparing values with bar or line charts, and make sure no metric relies on color alone to convey its value or status.
do: Use bar or line charts when people need to compare values on a dashboard.
dont: Show a metric's status or size by colour alone, such as red and green dots.
finding: Drawing on perception research, the article argues that position and length are judged most accurately, so bars, lines and scatterplots suit dashboards, while angle and area (pies, donuts, gauges, treemaps) and 3D effects make quick value comparisons harder. Colour attracts attention but is not read as an ordered scale, so it should not carry magnitude; the article puts colour blindness at up to 4.5% of people overall, roughly 8% of men versus 0.5% of women, varying by ethnicity.
limitation: Does not test dashboards directly; the color-blindness figures are given without a cited source, and the advice may not cover exploratory analytical tools.
measurement: Accuracy of value comparison between chart elements; time to answer a dashboard question; count of charts encoding meaning by color only
method: Synthesis of graphical-perception research, citing Cleveland and McGill's 1985 work
plain: People compare numbers most accurately by length or position, so bars and lines beat pies and gauges on dashboards. Colour grabs attention but isn't read as more or less, and some people can't tell colours apart.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Choosing chart encodings people can read at a glance

application: Audit every toast, 'saved' confirmation, cart counter, result count and inline error to confirm it uses an appropriate live-region role (status, alert or log) and is announced by a screen reader without focus moving.
do: Put toasts, result counts and inline errors in a live region (status or alert role) so they are announced.
dont: Show a 'Saved' message that screen readers never announce, or move focus just to announce it.
finding: WCAG SC 4.1.3 Status Messages (Level AA) requires that messages reporting success, results, waiting, progress or errors, when they appear without a change of context, be exposed through a role or properties so screen readers can convey them without the user's focus shifting. Dialog-based errors, expanding widgets and the search result list itself fall outside this criterion.
limitation: Defines a conformance requirement rather than testing which announcement wording or politeness level users find least disruptive.
measurement: Share of status messages exposed via a live-region role; Screen-reader announcement pass rate in testing; Count of status messages that steal focus unnecessarily
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: When a message like 'Added to bag' or 'Saved' appears, screen reader users need to hear it without being moved away from where they are on the page.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Announcing status updates to assistive tech without moving focus

application: Walk through first-run and each feature entry point to check that no permission dialog fires before the related feature is invoked, that a rationale screen with a decline option precedes sensitive requests, and that denial leaves the rest of the app usable.
do: Explain why you need access in your own screen, with a 'Not now' option, right before the feature uses it.
dont: Fire permission pop-ups the moment the app first opens.
finding: Google advises waiting until a person begins using the feature that needs a permission, explaining the reason beforehand in the app's own UI with a way to decline, and degrading gracefully with specific messaging if access is refused. If a user denies the same permission twice, Android stops showing the system dialog for it, so poorly timed requests can lock a feature out.
limitation: Mentions research on users preferring explained requests but gives no figures, so it does not quantify the grant-rate effect of contextual timing.
measurement: Permission grant rate per request point; Share of requests triggered by a user-initiated feature action; Feature-abandonment rate after denial
method: Not stated
plain: Ask for access to things like location only when someone starts using the feature that needs it, and explain why first. Android stops asking after two refusals, so a badly timed request can lock a feature out.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Asking for Android runtime permissions in context

visual.cap: A shopper wants to find a store nearby

application: Map each notification type the product sends to an interruption level, flag any marketing message using an elevated level, and confirm an in-app notification settings screen with separate marketing opt-in exists.
do: Give each notification type an honest urgency level and keep promotions at the lowest.
dont: Mark a sale alert as time-sensitive to get past someone's Focus mode.
finding: Apple defines four interruption levels (Passive, Active, Time Sensitive, Critical) that determine whether an alert can bypass Focus, scheduled summaries or the silent switch, and asks developers to label urgency honestly to keep trust. Time Sensitive should cover only events happening now or within roughly an hour, promotional pushes require explicit opt-in and must never use that level, and apps need an in-app screen to change notification choices.
limitation: Platform rules and best practice only; it offers no data on how mislabelled urgency affects opt-out or uninstall rates.
measurement: Share of notification types with a justified interruption level; Notification opt-out rate after first Time Sensitive alert; Marketing push opt-in rate
method: Not stated
plain: Apple sorts phone alerts by urgency. Only things happening now or within about an hour should break through Focus mode, and marketing alerts never should, so label urgency honestly.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Matching notification urgency to Apple's interruption levels

tag.text: Broke through Focus for a sale

application: Remove any notification permission request that fires on page load and replace it with a user-initiated opt-in, then track how often visitors dismiss or ignore the prompt versus grant it.
do: Ask for notification permission only after someone taps a 'Get alerts' option.
dont: Fire the browser's notification request as soon as the page loads.
finding: Notification requests were the most common permission prompt in Chrome telemetry (74% of all permission prompts) yet the least granted, at a 10% grant rate on desktop and 21% on Android. The quieter UI produced up to 30% fewer unnecessary actions on prompts while changing grant rates by less than 5%.
limitation: Measures Chrome's browser-level prompt behaviour; it does not test site-level pre-prompt designs or long-term engagement with the notifications that were granted.
measurement: Notification prompt grant rate by platform; Share of prompts dismissed or ignored; Prompts shown per session
method: Two large-scale telemetry studies of real-world Chrome prompt interactions plus an A/B test of a quieter prompt UI shipped in Chrome 80 (February 2020), with adaptive activation and a crowd-sourced block list of interrupting sites
plain: Requests to send notifications were the most common browser permission pop-up in Chrome and the least often accepted. A quieter version cut needless clicks without changing much who said yes.
sample: More than 40 million users, more than 100 million prompts and more than 70 thousand websites

stat.text: of desktop notification requests were granted in Chrome's telemetry (21% on Android), per Google's USENIX Security 2021 study.

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Quieter Chrome prompts cut notification-request disruption at scale
