dont.title: Allow notifications?

application: Audit that the switcher sits top-right/top-left on desktop and above the fold or in the mobile nav, lists languages by their endonym (e.g. Español), and lets language, country and currency be changed separately.
do: Put the language switcher in a top corner, listing names such as 'Español' and 'Deutsch'.
dont: Hide the language choice in the footer or show only small flag icons.
finding: Shoppers abroad struggled when language switchers were tucked into footers or shown only as tiny flag icons; auto-detecting locale from the browser, placing the control in a top corner (or high in the mobile menu), and naming each language in its own script made switching easier. Users also wanted language, shipping country and currency to be set independently, e.g. some Indian shoppers preferred the English site and a Mexican user avoided poor machine translation.
limitation: Qualitative findings with no stated participant count or success-rate data; focused on ecommerce, so it does not show how much switcher placement changes conversion or applies to non-retail services.
measurement: Time to locate language switcher; share of international visitors who change locale; bounce rate of visitors landing on a non-preferred locale
method: Qualitative ecommerce usability studies (China, India, earlier US studies) with observed participant behaviour on live retail sites
plain: Shoppers abroad struggled when the language choice was hidden in the footer or shown only as tiny flags. Put it at the top, name each language in its own words, and let language, country and currency be set separately.
sample: Not stated on page (participants from China, India and Mexico are quoted; counts not given)
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Making language and region switchers findable for global shoppers

visual.cap: A visitor from Spain lands on the site

application: Run an RTL review of every icon and control: confirm directional icons and progress/navigation controls are mirrored, and that logos, media, checkmarks and number strings (phone, card numbers) are not reversed.
do: Mirror the layout, back and next arrows and progress bars in right-to-left languages.
dont: Reverse logos, photos, tick marks or the digits in phone and card numbers.
finding: For Arabic and Hebrew interfaces Apple advises flipping layout, progress controls (sliders, progress bars), back/next navigation and icons that imply reading direction or motion, while leaving photos, logos, universal marks such as checkmarks, real-world objects like clocks, and the digits inside a number unflipped. Multi-line paragraphs should align to their own language rather than the surrounding UI, and Arabic/Hebrew text beside all-caps Latin may need roughly 2 points larger type to look balanced.
limitation: Platform design guidance for Apple OSes with no supporting user data; it does not quantify the usability cost of incorrect mirroring and leaves web-specific implementation (dir attribute, CSS logical properties) out of scope.
measurement: Count of mis-mirrored icons/controls in RTL audit; RTL layout defects per screen; task success with native Arabic/Hebrew testers
method: Not stated
plain: In Arabic and Hebrew, which read right to left, the layout, back and next arrows and progress bars should flip. Photos, logos, tick marks, clocks and the digits in a number should stay as they are.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: What to mirror, and what not to, in right-to-left interfaces

application: Inspect RTL locales for dir="rtl" on the root html element, dir="auto" on inputs and user-generated content blocks, and flag stylesheets that hard-code left/right instead of logical properties.
do: Set dir="rtl" on the page's html element and dir="auto" on form fields.
dont: Hard-code left and right positions in styles for right-to-left pages.
finding: W3C advises declaring right-to-left base direction with dir="rtl" on the html element (alongside lang, which does not set direction by itself) rather than via CSS, so direction survives when styles fail. It recommends dir="auto" for form fields and user-generated or runtime-inserted text, bdi to isolate inserted strings, and CSS logical properties (start/end, margin-inline-start) instead of left/right.
limitation: Technical authoring guidance, not user research; it notes dir="auto" can misjudge mixed-direction text and does not cover visual mirroring decisions for icons or layout.
measurement: Share of RTL pages with dir set on html; count of left/right physical CSS properties in RTL builds; bidi text rendering defects found in QA
method: Not stated
plain: Arabic and Hebrew read right to left. Setting that direction in the page code, not only in the styling, keeps text the right way round even if the styling fails to load.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Setting text direction in markup, not stylesheets, for RTL pages

application: Check every template (including translated locales) sets a correct lang value on the html element that matches the page's dominant language, e.g. lang="cy" on Welsh pages rather than an inherited lang="en".
do: Set the correct lang value on the html element of every template and translated page.
dont: Let translated pages inherit lang="en" from the main template.
finding: WCAG SC 3.1.1 Language of Page (Level A) requires that software can programmatically determine each page's default human language, so screen readers load the right pronunciation rules and browsers render scripts and captions correctly. On multilingual pages the default is the language used most, or the first one used if usage is equal.
limitation: Covers only the page-level default language; it does not require marking language changes within content (that is SC 3.1.2, Level AA) and says nothing about translation quality or locale selection UX.
measurement: Percentage of pages with a valid lang on html; lang/content mismatches per locale; automated audit failures for missing document language
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Each page must state in its code which language it is written in, so screen readers pronounce the words correctly and browsers display the text properly.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Declaring the page's main language for assistive tech

application: Audit each on-site chatbot entry point: confirm it is labeled, placed contextually on complex pages, opens with task-specific starter prompts, and does not duplicate search or filters or lead with promotions.
do: Open the chat with starter questions that fit the page, like sizing or delivery.
dont: Greet people with a vague welcome and lead with promotions.
finding: Embedded retail chatbots were often unnoticed, came with vague welcome messages that hid what they could do, and were slower than search and filters for simple lookups; sales-led answers and recommendations without visible reasoning reduced trust. They helped most with quick product-page questions and complex questions tied to the user's own situation.
limitation: Small qualitative sample of 9 users; shows behavior patterns, not how common these problems are or their effect on conversion.
measurement: Chatbot discovery rate (sessions opening chat / eligible sessions); task completion time via chat vs. search/filters; share of chat answers rated helpful
method: Qualitative moderated usability testing; 60-minute sessions, each participant using 2-3 sites with AI chatbots
plain: Shop chat assistants were often missed, opened with vague greetings, and were slower than search for simple lookups. They helped most with quick product questions or complex personal ones.
sample: 9 participants who had all used at least one general-purpose AI chatbot; 8 site chatbots tested (e.g., Amazon Rufus, Ask Turo, Home Depot Magic Apron)
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Site chatbots fail when users can't see their purpose

visual.cap: A shopper opens chat on a product page
visual.note: Illustration. Wording is a made-up example.

application: Run a heuristic review of any AI feature against the 18 guidelines, scoring each as applied, violated or not applicable, with particular attention to explanations and recovery when the AI is wrong.
do: Show a short reason with each AI suggestion and an easy way to correct it.
dont: Launch an AI feature with no explanation or way to fix wrong output.
finding: The authors distilled 18 design guidelines for AI-infused products, grouped by phase (at first use, during interaction, when the system is wrong, over time). In the practitioner study, 785 guideline examples were logged (313 applications, 277 violations), and the guideline about explaining why the system did something was among the most frequently violated.
limitation: Guidelines are general-purpose and may not fit voice-only or high-risk domains (e.g., surgery, finance); fairness and ethics coverage is limited; evaluators were mostly from one company; it does not measure user outcomes.
measurement: Count of guidelines violated per AI feature; share of AI outputs with an available explanation; user correction/dismissal success rate
method: Four phases: consolidation of candidate guidelines from industry and academic sources; modified heuristic evaluation; user study with practitioners rating AI products; expert review of revised wording
plain: Microsoft researchers wrote 18 rules for AI features, grouped by first use, everyday use, when the AI is wrong, and over time. Explaining why the AI did something was one of the most often broken.
sample: 168 candidate guidelines reduced to 18; 11 team members inspected 13 AI products; 49 HCI practitioners evaluated 20 products across 10 categories; 11 UX/HCI experts in final review. Participants mostly from one large company
strengthWhy: Published study, but observational or correlational.
title: 18 validated guidelines for human-AI interaction

visual.cap: Someone asks an AI assistant for a gift idea
visual.note: Illustration. Wording is a made-up example.

application: For each AI output, check whether confidence or uncertainty is shown in a form tied to a user action (e.g., high/medium/low with guidance, or top alternatives when confidence is low) and avoid bare percentage scores.
do: Show AI confidence as simple levels tied to what the person should do next.
dont: Display a bare percentage score with no guidance on what to do.
finding: The aim is appropriate rather than maximal trust: people should rely on an AI where it performs well and double-check where it may fail, helped by explanations of data use and, where it changes decisions, confidence displays. Categorical levels or several alternative results are usually clearer than raw percentages, which many users misread.
limitation: No publication date or underlying study data on the page; recommendations are not backed by reported methods or effect sizes, so they are expert guidance rather than proven outcomes.
measurement: Over-reliance rate (users accepting incorrect AI outputs); verification rate on low-confidence outputs; user comprehension of confidence display in testing
method: Guidance said to draw on many internal Google user research studies and design explorations (not listed) plus cited academic/industry literature
plain: People should lean on an AI where it does well and double-check where it might be wrong. Simple confidence labels, like high or low, or a few alternatives, are easier to read than raw percentages.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Calibrate trust in AI, don't maximize it

application: Audit AI feature copy (landing pages, onboarding, chatbot intros) for claims that the AI equals or replaces a human professional, and require documented testing evidence before such claims ship.
do: Describe what the AI feature does, backed by your own test results.
dont: Advertise an AI tool as a replacement for a lawyer, doctor or other professional.
finding: The FTC finalized an order against DoNotPay, which had promoted its AI service as a 'robot lawyer'. The order requires $193,000 in monetary relief and notices to people who subscribed in 2021-2023, and bars claims that the service performs like a human lawyer unless backed by sufficient evidence; the Commission approved it 5-0.
limitation: A final FTC order binding DoNotPay only (approved January 2025 after public comment, following a September 2024 complaint); it is not a rule of general applicability and does not define what substantiation would suffice for other AI products.
measurement: Number of AI capability claims in UI copy; share of claims with documented test evidence; frequency of human-equivalence wording
method: Not stated
plain: A US regulator penalised an app that sold its AI as a 'robot lawyer' without proof. Don't claim an AI matches a human professional unless testing backs it up.

stat.text: in monetary relief was ordered by the FTC over DoNotPay's unsupported 'robot lawyer' claims (final order, January 2025).

strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: FTC penalizes unsupported 'robot lawyer' AI claims

application: Audit the site's 404 template: remove error codes, humour and red text, add address-checking advice and a contact or search route, and crawl for broken internal links and unredirected legacy URLs.
do: Use a plain 'Page not found' heading, address-checking tips and a contact route.
dont: Show '404', 'oops' or red warning text with no way forward.
finding: GOV.UK's not-found pattern uses a simple 'Page not found' heading, short steps for checking a typed or pasted address, and a route to contact details, while banning breadcrumbs, technical codes such as 404, jokey wording like 'oops' and red warning text. The team also asks services to test every link and keep old addresses redirecting to live pages.
limitation: The page states that further research is still needed on whether users understand what happened and can fix it themselves; it is government-service guidance, not tested evidence that this layout cuts abandonment.
measurement: 404 hits per 1,000 sessions; exit rate from 404 page; count of broken internal links found by crawl
method: Not stated
plain: When a link leads nowhere, say 'Page not found' in plain words, suggest checking the web address, and show where to get help. Skip error codes, jokes and red warning text.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Plain, blame-free 404 pages that help users recover

visual.cap: Someone follows an out-of-date link

application: Check the 500 template shows saved/not-saved status for in-progress forms, offers an alternative channel or service, and is replaced by a shutter page if an outage lasts beyond a short window.
do: Say whether answers were saved, and give contact details or another way to finish.
dont: Show '500' or 'technical difficulties' with no word on their data.
finding: For unexpected server faults, GOV.UK recommends one shared apology page that tells people to try later, states whether anything they had entered was kept, and offers contact details or another service that completes the task; jargon like '500' and vague 'technical difficulties' phrasing should be avoided. Testing with five users found people wanted to know when the service would return and how else to get their task done, and if the fault persists the team should switch to a planned-closure page.
limitation: Based on a very small test (five users) with several open research questions listed; it does not show that saving answers or the wording measurably improves completion or contact volume.
measurement: Share of 500 views followed by successful retry; support contacts per outage; drop-off rate after server errors in multi-step forms
method: Usability testing of the pattern (as described in research notes)
plain: When the service breaks, the error page should apologise, say whether the person's answers were kept, and offer another way to finish. In a five-user test, people also wanted to know when it would be back.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: 500 error pages that say what happened to users' answers

visual.cap: The service fails halfway through a form

application: Inventory every settings screen: move workflow actions to the main UI, remove Save buttons in favour of instant apply, replace hidden context-dependent options with disabled ones plus a reason, and collapse low-use settings into grouped sections.
do: Apply each setting instantly and grey out unavailable ones with a short reason.
dont: Make people press Save, or hide options without saying why.
finding: Microsoft's WinUI guidance reserves the settings page for infrequently changed preferences (units, notifications, accessibility, theme) plus rarely needed info like version and privacy links, and keeps everyday workflow commands out of it. It asks for smart defaults, changes that take effect immediately without a Save button, unavailable options disabled with an explanation rather than hidden, and a cap of about four to five top-level settings, with the rest grouped into expandable sections.
limitation: Platform guidance for Windows WinUI apps based on design convention; it cites no user research, and the small settings limit may not suit complex web products or account dashboards.
measurement: Number of top-level settings; percentage of settings changed from default; settings-related support tickets
method: Not stated
plain: Settings pages work best for things people rarely change, like theme or notifications. Changes should apply straight away, and options that can't be used should be greyed out with a reason, not hidden.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Lean settings pages with instant-apply controls and smart defaults

visual.cap: Someone switches on dark theme

application: Verify an iOS app exposes a discoverable Delete account action in account settings, with a direct link if a website finishes the process, a clear timeline, a note about retained data, and a warning that Apple-billed subscriptions must be cancelled separately.
do: Put a Delete account option in the app's account settings, with a clear timeline.
dont: Make people email or call support to delete their account.
finding: Under App Review Guideline 5.1.1(v), App Store apps that support account creation must let people begin deleting the whole account and its personal data (including user-generated content) from within the app, usually in account settings; deactivation alone does not satisfy the rule. Confirmation steps such as re-authentication are allowed, but forcing a phone call, email or chat is not except in highly regulated industries, and apps must say how long deletion takes and what data is kept for legal reasons.
limitation: Applies only to apps distributed through Apple's App Store and enforced via App Review, not a law; it does not cover websites, and the page shows no effective date (the copyright footer is the only date).
measurement: Taps from home screen to delete-account action; deletion request completion rate; median time from request to confirmed deletion
method: Not applicable (platform review rule)
plain: Apps on Apple's App Store that let you create an account must also let you start deleting it inside the app, not just switch it off or make you phone or email.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Apple's rule: account deletion must start inside the app

visual.cap: Someone wants to delete their account

application: Audit every autoplaying hero video, carousel, ticker and background loop for a visible, keyboard-reachable pause control that works before the 5-second mark.
do: Add a visible, keyboard-reachable pause button to every autoplaying carousel, ticker and video.
dont: Run an auto-advancing hero slideshow with no way to stop it.
finding: WCAG SC 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A): any motion, blinking or scrolling that begins by itself, lasts over five seconds and sits beside other content needs a user mechanism to pause, stop or hide it; self-starting auto-updating content needs a way to pause, stop, hide or set its update frequency. Essential content and content shown on its own (e.g. a standalone loader) are excepted.
limitation: Covers only visual motion and auto-updates; autoplaying audio falls under SC 1.4.2 and flashing under Guideline 2.3, and Level A conformance does not show the content is free of distraction for all users.
measurement: Share of auto-moving elements with a pause/stop control; seconds of motion before control is available; keyboard operability of pause control (pass/fail)
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Anything that moves, blinks or scrolls by itself for more than five seconds needs a way to pause, stop or hide it, so people who find motion distracting can still read the page.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Letting users halt auto-moving and auto-updating content

visual.cap: A visitor tries to read a rotating sale banner

application: Check that no page autoplays sound beyond 3 seconds, or that a pause/mute control appears early in the page and focus order; prefer starting audio only on user request.
do: Start sound only when people press play, or put a mute button first on the page.
dont: Autoplay a video with sound and rely on the device volume to silence it.
finding: WCAG SC 1.4.2 Audio Control (Level A): when sound plays automatically for longer than 3 seconds, the page must offer a way to pause or stop it, or a volume control independent of the system level. The rationale is that background audio can drown out screen reader speech, and relying on the system volume does not count.
limitation: Only addresses auto-starting audio over 3 seconds; it does not regulate user-initiated media, visual motion, or caption quality, and does not cover conference calls.
measurement: Count of pages with autoplaying audio over 3 seconds; presence and DOM position of a mute/pause control; volume control reachable to zero (pass/fail)
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: If a page starts playing sound by itself for more than three seconds, there must be a way to pause or mute it, because the sound can drown out a screen reader's voice.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Controls for audio that starts playing by itself

visual.cap: A video starts playing with sound

application: Sample each prerecorded video and verify captions exist, are synchronized, name speakers, and describe important sound effects and music rather than dialogue alone.
do: Caption every recorded video, naming speakers and describing meaningful sounds.
dont: Publish product videos with no captions, or with captions that leave out who is speaking.
finding: WCAG SC 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded) (Level A): prerecorded synchronized media must carry captions for its audio, unless the media is itself a clearly labelled alternative to on-page text. Captions should cover dialogue plus speaker identification and meaningful non-speech sounds such as effects and music.
limitation: Applies to prerecorded media only; live captions are SC 1.2.4 and audio description is handled by other 1.2.x criteria, and it sets no numeric accuracy threshold for caption quality.
measurement: Percentage of prerecorded videos with captions; caption accuracy rate from spot checks; share of captions that include speaker IDs and non-speech cues
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Recorded videos need captions so people who can't hear the sound can follow along. Captions should show who is speaking and important sounds like music or effects, not only the words.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Captioning requirements for prerecorded video

application: Audit the site's video player by operating every control via keyboard and screen reader, checking focus visibility and labels, and confirming it can deliver captions and audio description.
do: Choose an existing accessible player and test every control with a keyboard and a screen reader.
dont: Build a custom player with unlabelled icon buttons that only work with a mouse.
finding: WAI advises choosing an existing accessible player over building a custom one, and lists baseline needs: full keyboard operation, visible focus, clearly labelled controls, adequate contrast, and compatibility with screen readers, speech input and zoom. It notes that audio description delivery (text tracks or separate audio files) depends on player support, and names optional extras like adjustable speed, caption styling and interactive transcripts.
limitation: Guidance rather than a conformance requirement; it does not test or rank players, and it explicitly leaves out autoplay and whether captions should be on by default.
measurement: Player controls operable by keyboard (count/total); controls with accessible names; support for captions and audio description tracks (yes/no)
method: Not stated
plain: A video player must work for everyone: every button usable by keyboard, clearly labelled, visible when selected, and able to show captions and audio description. Using a proven accessible player is easier than building one.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: What an accessible media player must support

application: Audit the pricing/plan table: cap visible plans at about five, keep plan names pinned while scrolling, fill every feature cell with consistent values, and add a 'differences only' or collapsible-row option plus a two-plan mobile view.
do: Keep plan names pinned while scrolling and fill every cell with consistent values.
dont: Leave blank cells or describe the same feature differently for each plan.
finding: Comparison tables work best for weighing several attributes across a small, fixed set of options such as pricing tiers or membership levels, ideally five or fewer. The most damaging problem is incomplete or inconsistently worded attribute data, and tables become easier to use with sticky column headers, short scannable cells, plain-language explanations and controls such as showing only the differences.
limitation: Expert guidance based on example sites with no participant data or statistics; the item limits are rules of thumb, and it does not measure conversion or plan-choice accuracy.
measurement: Plan-selection accuracy in task tests; time to identify the cheapest plan meeting stated needs; share of empty or inconsistent table cells
method: Expert review of real comparison tables on retail, software and service websites (no formal study described)
plain: Comparison tables help people weigh a few options, ideally five or fewer, side by side. They fail when cells are blank or worded differently, because people can't tell the plans apart.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Designing plan and product comparison tables

visual.cap: A buyer checks storage across plans
visual.note: Illustration. Plans and values are made-up examples.

application: Review an enterprise or SaaS app for rigid linear wizards, missing undo or preview, and no export path; add step navigation that allows skipping and going back, progressive disclosure for advanced settings, and exports to common tools.
do: Let people skip ahead, go back and undo within long workflows.
dont: Lock expert users into a rigid step-by-step wizard with no undo.
finding: Specialist applications for trained users share common challenges, and the article proposes eight remedies: safe exploration, nudges toward more efficient methods, non-linear workflows, support for tracking work and resuming after interruptions, links to other tools, staged disclosure of advanced options, in-place access to secondary detail, and visual emphasis of key data by stripping out decoration.
limitation: Synthesised guidance without new data or statistics; it does not rank the guidelines or quantify their effect, and domain-specific constraints such as compliance may limit some recommendations.
measurement: Task completion time for expert workflows; error and rework rate after interruptions; adoption rate of shortcuts or efficient methods
method: Guideline synthesis drawing on prior NN/g work on complex applications and established usability concepts
plain: Specialist work tools should let experts explore safely, work in any order, pick up after interruptions and export to other tools, while keeping advanced options tucked away until needed.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Eight design guidelines for complex enterprise applications

application: Audit the subscription journey: a grouped key-terms summary before the pay button, a clearly labelled online cancel route without mandatory feedback forms or repeated retention offers, and trial-conversion reminder emails.
do: Send a reminder before a free or discounted trial converts to full price.
dont: Make online subscribers fill in a feedback form or face repeated offers before cancelling.
finding: Under the DMCC Act 2024 and draft 2026 regulations, traders must present a separate summary of key subscription terms before sign-up, send reminder notices (including before a free or discounted trial converts to full price), and let consumers leave easily, generally online for online sign-ups, with an end-of-contract notice sent within 24 hours when the consumer ends the contract online. Consumers also get a 14-day cooling-off period at the start and again after a free or discounted period ends or an auto-renewal onto a term of 12 months or more.
limitation: Draft guidance: the regulations still need parliamentary approval and final guidance will follow; the rules are set to apply only to contracts entered into on or after 1 January 2027, cover UK consumer (not B2B) contracts, and exclude sectors such as utilities, financial services, Ofcom-regulated telecoms and gambling.
measurement: Number of steps and screens to cancel online; presence and timing of trial-conversion reminders; time to send cancellation confirmation
method: Not applicable (draft government guidance on legislation)
plain: Draft UK rules, planned for contracts from 2027, would make subscription sellers show a terms summary before sign-up, remind people before a trial turns paid, and let them cancel easily online.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: UK subscription contract rules: draft business guidance

visual.cap: A free trial is about to end
visual.note: Illustration; messages are made-up examples.

application: Treat difficult cancellation, unclear auto-renewal terms and unconsented charges as live US enforcement risk: check that trial-to-paid terms are disclosed before billing details and that cancelling online takes no more effort than signing up.
do: Show the renewal price and timing before asking for payment details.
dont: Treat the scrapped click-to-cancel rule as permission to make cancelling hard.
finding: The FTC asked for public comment on whether to update its 1973 Negative Option Rule, including whether to bring back provisions of the vacated 2024 amendments, and on how often consumers are enrolled without informed consent or discouraged from cancelling. It cites more than 100,000 related complaints over five years, with hard cancellation and unlawful retention tactics singled out.
limitation: An advance notice asking for comment, not a rule. The FTC itself describes the 2024 click-to-cancel amendments as vacated, so they are not in force; the original 1973 rule covers only prenotification plans, and subscription enforcement continues under other laws such as ROSCA and Section 5 of the FTC Act.
measurement: Cancellation steps compared with sign-up steps; presence of express consent for recurring charges; disclosure of renewal price and timing before payment entry
method: Not applicable (regulatory announcement of an advance notice of proposed rulemaking)
plain: The US regulator is asking whether to bring back easy-cancel rules after a court scrapped them. Nothing is decided, but hard-to-cancel subscriptions can still be pursued under other laws.
sample: Complaint figure only: over 100,000 negative option complaints to the FTC in the past five years

stat.text: plus subscription-related complaints over five years, cited by the FTC when asking whether to update its rule.

strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: FTC reopens negative option rulemaking after vacatur

application: In each moderated test plan, script neutral prompts only, flag any session segment where the facilitator led the participant, and exclude those segments from findings.
finding: Jakob Nielsen argues that having representative users verbalise their thoughts while doing representative tasks is cheap, robust, flexible across prototype fidelity, and reveals the misconceptions behind usability problems. He cautions that it is unsuited to statistical conclusions, feels unnatural to participants, and is easily distorted by leading facilitator prompts.
limitation: Opinion and experience-based article from a UX consultancy, with no empirical comparison against other methods; it predates current remote and unmoderated testing practice and gives no guidance on quantifying results.
measurement: Number of distinct usability issues found per session; proportion of sessions with facilitator-led segments discarded; issues traced to user misconceptions
method: Expert method guidance based on the author's practitioner experience; no new study data presented
sample: Not stated on page (refers to testing with a handful of users)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Think-aloud testing as the core qualitative usability method

application: Before launching a longitudinal study, set study length from the expected frequency of the target behaviour, over-recruit beyond the saturation target, and schedule a pilot plus a post-study interview.
finding: Diary studies capture behaviour and attitudes in context over days or weeks, which single-session interviews or usability tests cannot. The article advises choosing event-, interval- or signal-based logging, sizing duration to how often the behaviour occurs, over-recruiting for dropouts, piloting, and running a debrief interview at the end.
limitation: Participant ranges and the suggested incentive rate (around $40 per hour for a general US sample) are practitioner guidance, not empirically derived; the article notes dropout, cost, analysis burden and prompt-induced bias as risks it cannot eliminate.
measurement: Participant retention rate across the study; entries logged per participant versus minimum required; themes reaching saturation
method: Practitioner method guidance describing planning, running and analysing remote, asynchronous diary studies
sample: Not stated on page (guidance suggests roughly 5-12 participants for small homogeneous discovery work, 12-30 for large heterogeneous projects, 30-50 for large or academic studies)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Planning diary studies: logging, duration and participant numbers

application: Ask the SEQ after every task in usability tests, compare task scores with the published database average, and add a 'why' follow-up whenever a participant rates below 5.
finding: The SEQ is a one-item 7-point rating of task difficulty asked straight after each task; across the author's database the average sits around 5.3 to 5.6, and ratings correlate only moderately (about r = .5) with task time and completion. In roughly 14% of cases users who failed a task still rated it as very easy.
limitation: Benchmarks come from the publisher's own unpublished dataset without detailed methodology; the SEQ partly reflects inherent task complexity, so low scores do not by themselves prove an interface problem, and it cannot replace completion or time metrics.
measurement: Mean SEQ per task versus benchmark average; task completion rate; time on task
method: Summary of the author's prior research and an aggregated MeasuringU task database
sample: More than 400 tasks and 10,000 users in the benchmark database; period and geography not stated
strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Single Ease Question: post-task difficulty rating and benchmarks

application: Pair every WCAG conformance audit with task-based sessions including assistive technology users whose skill level matches the real audience, and report participant characteristics and study scope alongside findings.
finding: WAI advises running an expert review first to remove obvious barriers, then evaluating with a range of disabled and older users throughout development using realistic tasks and a think-aloud approach with active facilitation. It stresses diagnosing whether a barrier comes from the code, browser, assistive technology, user skill or general design, and focusing measurement on accessibility-related errors.
limitation: User sessions with a few participants cannot be generalised to all people with a given disability and do not establish WCAG conformance; the page gives no specific sample size and is guidance, not a normative standard.
measurement: Accessibility-related errors per task; task success for assistive technology users; satisfaction rating by participant group
method: Not stated
sample: Not stated on page (recommends recruiting a few disabled people and older users suited to the audience)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Evaluating accessibility with disabled and older participants

application: Audit the locator for a plainly labelled link on every page, an explicit 'use my current location' control rather than relying on the browser prompt alone, filterable per-location amenities/hours, and hand-off of directions to familiar mapping apps.
do: Add a 'Use my location' button and hand directions off to familiar map apps.
dont: Rely only on the browser's location pop-up to find nearby stores.
finding: Locator task success climbed from 63% in the first study to 97% in the fourth, yet only 57% of locator tasks were completed easily and users struggled on 40% of attempts, with most trouble in operating the finder itself (too complex or oversimplified). In recent research 80% of people looking for a nearby bank branch started in a search engine or mapping app rather than the bank's own site.
limitation: Qualitative usability findings from a few dozen participants on mainly US sites; does not quantify conversion or store-visit impact, and the detailed 50-guideline report behind it is paid.
measurement: Locator task success rate; share of tasks completed without difficulty; time to get directions to nearest location
method: Four rounds of usability testing in which participants located the nearest branch to their own position or a supplied address and then got directions, sometimes with extra constraints such as opening hours or a drive-through
plain: People could usually find a company's store finder, but using it was often hard. Most people looking for a nearby branch started in a search engine or map app instead of the company's own site.
sample: 46 users across four studies; 28 desktop sites and 28 mobile sites/apps from retailers, banks, tech companies, restaurants and the US Post Office

stat.text: of people looking for a nearby bank branch started in a search engine or map app, not the bank's own site (NN/g research).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Store Locators: Reachable but Still Hard to Use

visual.cap: A shopper looks for the nearest store

do.cap: one tap, or type a place

dont.cap: browser prompt is the only way
dont.title: Allow location access?

application: Review map screens for pin clustering at low zoom, a clear selected-state style, search with category filters, and enough contrast (stroke or shadow) between custom controls and the map surface.
do: Cluster nearby pins and give the selected place a distinct style.
dont: Show dozens of overlapping pins that are hard to tell apart and tap.
finding: Apple advises keeping maps interactive (zoom, pan), offering search plus category filters, giving selected elements distinct styling, and grouping nearby pins into clusters that split apart as the user zooms in; for venue maps it recommends adding detail progressively with zoom and offering a concise floor picker. It also suggests padding of 7 points beside and 10 points above/below the Apple logo and legal link, and notes these are not shown on maps under 200x100 pixels.
limitation: Platform guidance for MapKit-based Apple experiences, not tested evidence; does not show these patterns improve task success, and some items (logo/legal link placement) are licensing requirements rather than usability findings.
measurement: Time to locate a target point of interest; selection/tap errors on dense pin areas; contrast ratio of map controls against map tiles
method: Not stated
plain: On a map, people should be able to zoom, move around and search. Group crowded pins into clusters that split as you zoom in, and make the selected place look different.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Apple HIG Best Practices for In-App Maps

application: Check that every map-based task (e.g. find a site, pick an area) has a non-map route such as a searchable list or address lookup, and that the map itself is fully keyboard operable with visible focus.
do: Offer a searchable list or address lookup alongside every map-based task.
dont: Make picking a spot on the map the only way to complete the task.
finding: Because maps are hard to make fully accessible, the guidance says services should always give users an alternative way to finish the task, and for interactive maps should support mouse and keyboard operation, visible focus, clear pan/zoom controls, adjustable text size and described selectable regions. It also favours the simplest basemap, direct text labels in plain sentence-case language, and warns against both vivid and greyscale basemaps on contrast grounds.
limitation: Design-system advice without cited user research or WCAG mapping; it notes UK public-sector accessibility regulations exempt online maps only where essential navigational information is offered accessibly, so it is not a legal standard in itself and other jurisdictions differ.
measurement: Keyboard-only task completion on map features; availability of a non-map alternative for each map task; label/basemap colour contrast ratios
method: Not stated
plain: Maps are hard for many people to use, especially without a mouse. Always offer another way to finish the same task, such as a searchable list or address lookup, and make the map work by keyboard.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Making Geographic Maps Accessible in Public Services

visual.cap: A visitor looks for their nearest collection site

do.cap: a list route beside the map

dont.cap: the map is the only way
dont.title: Pick a site on the map

visual.note: Illustration. The postcode and site names are made-up examples.

application: Do not rely on explanatory permission copy alone to lift location opt-in; ask in context of a clearly location-dependent feature, avoid ad-related justifications, and offer a manual location entry fallback.
do: Ask for location when someone uses a feature that clearly needs it, and offer manual entry.
dont: Count on explanation text alone to raise location opt-in.
finding: In the randomized experiment with 2,579 US Android users, showing a reason for a location request had no detectable effect on whether people granted access; app type and user demographics drove the decision instead. Reasons did improve perceptions of the platform, but only when they did not mention using the data for advertising.
limitation: Only the abstract is publicly visible on this page; it concerns Android and US users and measures stated grant decisions in an experiment, so it does not prove explanation copy is useless in all contexts or platforms.
measurement: Location permission grant rate by request variant; perceived trust in app/platform; share of users using manual location fallback
method: Survey of Android app developers plus a randomized controlled experiment varying app type, whether a reason for location access was shown, and the reason's content (including monetization)
plain: In a randomised test with US Android users, explaining why an app wanted location didn't change whether people said yes. Reasons improved trust in the platform, but not when they mentioned ads.
publisher: Google Research (Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies)
sample: 323 Android app developers; 2,579 US Android users
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Explaining Location Requests Didn't Change Grant Decisions

visual.cap: An app needs location for its store finder

dont.cap: ad reason at launch, no fallback
dont.title: Allow location?

application: Audit each transactional template: the subject line and preheader must state the specific event and key detail, the main answer must appear before any promotion, and no login or click should be needed to learn order or delivery status.
do: Put the specific event and key detail in the subject line, like 'Order 1234 has shipped'.
dont: Mix promotions into shipping or delivery emails ahead of the order details.
finding: Across 139 diary ratings, order, shipping, delivery and account emails averaged 5.9 on a 7-point scale (7 = best) over six qualities such as subject-line clarity and ease of acting, with individual qualities averaging 5.7 to 6.2. Messages still failed when subject lines or preheaders were uninformative, key details were missing, or ads were mixed into shipping notices, which pushed users toward spam reports.
limitation: Article summarises a 2018 study with no participant count or geography given; ratings are self-reported on emails participants chose to forward, and full method detail sits in a separate report.
measurement: Spam-complaint rate per transactional template; support contacts about order status after a confirmation email; inbox-preview test score for subject line plus preheader clarity
method: In-person usability testing plus a longitudinal diary study in which participants forwarded transactional emails they received and rated each on six characteristics using a 7-point semantic differential scale
plain: People rate order and delivery emails well when the subject line says exactly what happened and key details come first. Vague subjects, missing details or ads inside shipping emails push people to mark them as spam.
sample: 139 diary-study email ratings; participant count, countries and study period not stated on page

stat.text: average rating out of 7 for order, shipping, delivery and account emails (NN/g diary study, 139 ratings)

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Transactional Email Should Be Utility First

visual.cap: A shopper glances at new emails
visual.note: Illustration. Order details are made-up examples.

application: Review every service notification: name the service as sender, use a specific subject line, check the first sentence works as a preview, and confirm links are full visible URLs on the official domain with no tracking redirects or attachments.
do: Open each message with the key fact and end with what the person must do and by when.
dont: Hide links behind tracking redirects or ask for personal details in a text or email.
finding: UK government services should send only transactional messages triggered by a user's own action or subscription messages the user explicitly opted into (always with an unsubscribe route), keep each message to one main point with the key fact in the opening sentence, and say what the user must do, by when, and what happens next. To limit phishing risk, messages should omit sensitive data, never ask for personal details, link only to GOV.UK with URLs written out in full and no redirects, and carry no attachments.
limitation: Guidance for UK government services, not a legal requirement for other organisations; the visible update date is 2017 and the page offers no evidence base, character limits or accessibility guidance for messages.
measurement: Share of messages with a deadline and next step stated; percentage of links using full official-domain URLs without redirects; follow-up contact rate after a transactional message
method: Not stated
plain: Service emails and texts should make one main point, put the key fact first, and say what to do, by when, and what happens next. To avoid looking like scams, they should never ask for personal details.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Writing Government Service Emails and Texts

application: Test each marketing email's unsubscribe flow: it must be visible, finish via a reply or one web page without login or extra data, include an all-messages option, and stop sends within 10 business days.
do: Let people unsubscribe in one step by reply or on one web page.
dont: Ask people to log in or give extra details before they can unsubscribe.
finding: Under the CAN-SPAM Act, every commercial email, including business-to-business, needs accurate header data, a non-misleading subject line, a clear ad disclosure, a valid postal address and a conspicuous opt-out; the opt-out must keep working for at least 30 days after sending, requests must be honoured within 10 business days, and opting out cannot require a fee, extra personal data or more than a reply email or one web page. Messages whose primary purpose is transactional or relationship-based are exempt from most of these rules, but the FTC says promotional content in the subject line or ahead of the transactional content generally makes an email commercial.
limitation: FTC compliance guidance for a US federal law that applies to commercial email; it is not legal advice, does not cover text-message marketing rules or non-US laws, and the stated per-email penalty (up to $53,088) is an inflation-adjusted figure that may change. It sets legal minimums, not evidence of good UX.
measurement: Steps and time required to complete an unsubscribe; days between opt-out request and last marketing send; share of transactional templates whose subject line or opening contains promotion
method: Not applicable (regulatory guidance)
plain: US law says every marketing email needs an honest subject line, a postal address and an easy unsubscribe, honoured within 10 business days, with no fee, login or extra details.

stat.text: is the deadline to honour an email opt-out under the US CAN-SPAM Act, per FTC guidance.

strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: US Commercial Email and Opt-Out Requirements

visual.cap: A subscriber taps Unsubscribe in an email

application: Run each email template through an accessibility check for 4.5:1 text contrast, alt text on images, descriptive links, semantic headings and no layout tables, and replace scanned PDF attachments with accessible or in-body text.
do: Check each email template for 4.5:1 text contrast, alt text on images and descriptive link text.
dont: Send a scanned, image-only PDF or rely on 'click here' links.
finding: US federal email should meet WCAG 2.0 Level AA at minimum, including a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 and never relying on colour alone, with alt text (kept under 250 characters) on every meaningful image, descriptive link text instead of phrases like 'click here' or raw URLs, real heading styles, and simple data-only tables. Attachments must be accessible or their content placed in the email body, since scanned image-only files are unreadable to screen-reader users.
limitation: Written for US federal staff and largely tied to Microsoft Outlook authoring; the 10-11 pt font size and typeface advice are recommendations, as the page notes neither WCAG nor Section 508 sets email font sizes, and it does not address HTML coding for marketing email clients.
measurement: Percentage of images with appropriate alt text; count of text/background pairs below 4.5:1; number of generic or raw-URL links per email
method: Not stated
plain: Emails need the same care as web pages: readable text contrast, descriptions on images, links that say where they go, real headings, and attachments a screen reader can read.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Building Accessible Email Messages

application: Audit every link and button for a non-colour-only clickability cue (underline, outline, fill or shadow), prioritising content-dense pages and novel layouts.
do: Give every button and link a visible cue such as an underline, border or fill.
dont: Style clickable text exactly like the plain text around it.
finding: When clickable elements had weak or missing signifiers, participants needed on average 22% more time and 25% more fixations to locate the target than with strong signifiers (both p < 0.05). Three of the nine page pairs showed no gaze-pattern difference; the penalty shrank on low-density pages where key controls stood out.
limitation: Short single-page find tasks measured findability only; the study did not count wrong clicks or measure discoverability across a full site journey.
measurement: Time to locate target; fixations before locating target; share of users reaching the target link
method: Quantitative desktop eyetracking experiment, between-subjects; each of 9 live web pages was edited into a strong-signifier and a weak-signifier version; participants said when they had found the target
plain: When buttons and links look like plain text, people take longer to find what to click. Clear cues such as underlines, outlines or fills help most on busy pages.
sample: 71 general web users; 9 pages (18 variants) from 6 domains such as ecommerce, hotel, travel and finance

stat.text: more time to find the target when clickable elements had weak or missing signifiers (NN/g eyetracking study, nine page pairs)

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Weak signifiers in flat UIs slow target finding

visual.cap: A shopper looks for how to add an item

application: Treat visual complexity (number of distinct regions, images, text blocks) as a first-impression risk and simplify busy landing pages before adjusting palette.
do: Cut the number of separate blocks, images and text areas on landing pages.
dont: Try to fix a cluttered landing page only by changing its colours.
finding: Image-based models predicted perceived colourfulness (R2 = .78) and visual complexity (R2 = .65), and the appeal model explained 48% of variation in ratings; higher complexity sharply lowered appeal while colourfulness had only a minor effect. Participants older than 45 preferred low-complexity sites more strongly.
limitation: Ratings came from 500ms screenshot exposure by self-selected online volunteers; it predicts first-impression appeal, not task success, trust or conversion.
measurement: Rated visual complexity; rated colourfulness; first-impression appeal score
method: Three online experiments on LabintheWild; participants rated website screenshots shown for 500ms on 9-point scales for colourfulness, complexity and appeal; regression and linear mixed-effects models built from image metrics
plain: After seeing a page for just half a second, people already judge its look, and busy, cluttered pages are liked less. Colour matters far less than complexity, and visitors over 45 prefer simple pages even more.
publisher: Harvard University (CHI 2013 paper, Reinecke et al.)
sample: 548 volunteers (184 colourfulness, 122 complexity, 242 appeal); pool of 450 websites
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Visual complexity drives first-glance website appeal

application: Inventory page images and replace generic stock or look-alike thumbnails with photos that differentiate products or show real people; make enlargements at least double the thumbnail size.
do: Use photos that show real differences between products or real people using them.
dont: Fill product lists with generic stock photos or near-identical thumbnails.
finding: Images carrying task-relevant information attracted close attention while generic or stock-style images were treated as filler. On one Amazon category page, photos received just 18% of viewing time versus 82% for text, with about 0.9 fixations per thumbnail compared with 4.4 per description.
limitation: Based on selected gaze-plot examples from 2010 without a reported sample size or statistical testing; layouts and image conventions have changed since.
measurement: Share of viewing time on images vs text; fixations per image; image enlargement usage
method: Eyetracking study examples presented as individual gaze plots and viewing-time comparisons
plain: People look closely at photos that tell them something, such as how products differ, and skip generic stock images as decoration.

stat.text: of viewing time went to photos (82% to text) on one Amazon category page in NN/g's 2010 eyetracking examples

strengthWhy: Eyetracking study: measures where people look, not sales.
title: Users scrutinise informative photos and skip decorative ones

application: Measure characters per line on desktop body copy and constrain the main content column (e.g. two-thirds of a max-width container) so lines stay under about 75 characters.
do: Limit body text to about 75 characters per line on desktop.
dont: Let paragraphs stretch across the full width of a wide screen.
finding: GOV.UK sets a default maximum page width of 1020px and advises keeping body text to roughly 75 characters per line at most. Main content should sit in a two-thirds column even when no one-third sidebar exists, with layouts designed mobile-first from a single column.
limitation: Presented as design-system guidance without cited research; the 75-character limit is a rule of thumb, and breakpoint values are not given on the page.
measurement: Characters per line in body text; maximum content width in px; layout behaviour at mobile width
method: Not stated
plain: Very long lines of text are tiring to read. GOV.UK keeps main content in a column two-thirds of the page wide and body text to about 75 characters per line.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GOV.UK grid: two-thirds column and capped line length

application: Audit the security settings page: check each passkey shows its provider and a distinguishing label, that cancelled or failed creation gives a clear message with a retry path, and that an email or phone fallback remains when all passkeys are removed.
do: Label each saved passkey by its provider in security settings.
dont: Remove the email or phone fallback once someone has a passkey.
finding: Google advises prompting passkey creation at moments of high security focus (sign-in, security settings, right after recovery or re-authentication), surfacing passkeys through autofill, and always keeping a fallback recovery method. In the management screen it recommends labelling each passkey by its credential provider, numbering ones from the same ecosystem, and using 'create'/'delete' wording because an account can hold several passkeys.
limitation: Vendor guidance with no published data; it does not quantify adoption or conversion gains, and platform dialogs it relies on vary by OS and browser.
measurement: Passkey enrolment rate after prompt; Sign-in success rate by method; Account recovery requests per 1,000 active users
method: Guidance drawing on FIDO Alliance UX guidance and Google's own UX research (no study details given)
plain: A passkey is a way to sign in without a password. Google suggests offering one when people are signing in or checking security, labelling each saved passkey clearly, and always keeping a backup way in.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Where and how to offer passkeys across the account lifecycle

application: On sign-up and change-of-email flows, verify the holding page displays the address entered, offers resend and change-address actions, and that expired or reused links produce an explanatory page rather than a generic error.
do: Show the typed email on the 'check your inbox' page with options to resend or change it.
dont: Leave people on a waiting page with no way to fix a mistyped address.
finding: GOV.UK recommends confirming an email only when key functions such as password reset rely on it, or when a mistyped address could expose sensitive data, and warns that confirmation shows access to the inbox at that moment rather than identity. It sets out blocking versus non-blocking loops, says links should stop working after one use, a time limit, a newer link or an address change, and requires options to resend or correct the address.
limitation: The page reports no research results of its own and links to a community discussion instead; it does not specify an expiry duration or prove one loop type converts better.
measurement: Email confirmation completion rate; Time from sign-up to confirmation; Resend and change-address usage rate
method: Not stated
plain: Only make people confirm their email when something important depends on it, like resetting a password. The waiting page should show the address they typed and let them resend or fix it.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Email confirmation loops: when to block and how links expire

application: Test signed-in areas by idling until timeout: confirm a warning appears before expiry, that a single keypress or button extends the session, and that the extension can be repeated at least ten times.
do: Warn before the session expires and let one button press extend it, more than once if needed.
dont: Sign people out silently with no warning and no way to ask for more time.
finding: SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (Level A) requires that every content-imposed time limit, including session expiry, can be turned off, adjusted to at least ten times the default, or extended after a warning with at least 20 seconds to respond via a simple action, repeatable at least ten times. Exceptions cover real-time events, essential limits and limits over 20 hours; the Understanding doc notes time-based 2FA codes may count as essential.
limitation: The Understanding document is a non-normative explanation of the criterion and does not itself address restoring work lost after a timeout (the page only lists related criteria). WCAG 2.2 is a current W3C Recommendation.
measurement: Timeout warnings shown vs. sessions expired; Share of warnings resulting in extension; Form data lost to expiry incidents
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: If a signed-in session is going to time out, people must be warned and able to extend it with one simple action, so slower users aren't signed out in the middle of a task.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Session timeouts must be extendable under WCAG 2.2.1

application: When adding 2FA, test setup separately from day-to-day sign-in, and offer a fast option such as push or security keys alongside SMS, with step-by-step setup help for hardware tokens.
finding: Participants rated all five 2FA methods (SMS, TOTP, pre-generated codes, push, U2F keys) favourably; per the full paper, median SUS ranged from 75.0 (SMS, U2F) to 88.8 (TOTP) versus 95.0 for a password-only control. U2F keys had the quickest median authentication time at 9.1 seconds, while a few lab participants struggled to set up a hardware token or one-time password.
limitation: Small, campus-recruited, mostly young student sample using a simulated bank site; results may not generalise to older or less technical users, and passkeys were not tested.
measurement: System Usability Scale per method; Median authentication time; 2FA setup completion rate
method: Two-week between-subjects field study with near-daily logins to a simulated banking site, plus a within-subjects lab study of setup
sample: 72 participants (field study), recruited mostly from Brigham Young University campus, largely students aged 20-29; 30 participants (lab setup study)
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Two-week field test of five two-factor methods

application: Audit the delivery address step: confirm a lookup is offered where coverage exists, a manual-entry link is always visible, postcode input is normalised rather than rejected, and every field carries the correct autocomplete token.
do: Offer postcode lookup with a visible 'Enter address manually' link.
dont: Reject a postcode because of lower-case letters or a missing space.
finding: For UK addresses the pattern favours a postcode-based lookup, with a manual route always available for overseas or unmatched addresses; separate inputs suit known address formats, while a single free-text box suits international addresses and pasting. Postcode entry should tolerate any capitalisation, spacing and stray punctuation instead of rejecting it.
limitation: Guidance from a UK public-sector design system with no research data or sample shown on the page; lookup advice is UK-specific and conversion impact for retail checkouts is not demonstrated.
measurement: Address step completion rate; share of users switching to manual entry; postcode validation error rate
method: Not stated
plain: For UK addresses, let people find their address from the postcode, but always offer a way to type it in by hand. Accept postcodes however they're written, in any case or spacing.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Address capture: postcode lookup first, flexible manual fallback

application: Check that the card number accepts spaces and hyphens, field order matches the card face, accepted-card logos react to the detected network, and the security-code hint changes for Amex.
do: Order card fields like the card and switch the security-code hint for American Express.
dont: Reject card numbers typed with spaces, or ask for a 'CVV' without explaining it.
finding: Card fields should sit together on one page and follow the sequence printed on a card, while the number field accepts spaces or dashes in whatever way people normally type them. Detecting the card network from the opening digits lets the form highlight the matching logo and switch the security-code hint, e.g. a 4-digit front code for American Express, without using jargon like CVV.
limitation: Based on a government payment service rather than retail; the page reports no test results, sample sizes or conversion data, and does not cover autofill, wallets or error handling.
measurement: Card number validation error rate; payment step completion rate; security-code field error rate by card type
method: Pattern derived from GOV.UK Pay (live since November 2016); page says the Pay team tests it in quarterly user research
plain: Put card fields together in the same order as the card itself, and accept numbers typed with spaces or dashes. Detecting the card type from its first digits lets the form show the right security-code hint.
sample: Not stated on page (page lists government services using the pattern as of August 2018)
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Card details form: mirror the physical card, adapt the security-code hint

application: Remove Apply buttons from standard checkout fields, place the coupon input behind a disclosure link, auto-apply eligible promotions, and flash or highlight the updated total once a code is accepted.
do: Hide the promo box behind a 'Have a code?' link and highlight the new total once a code works.
dont: Make shoppers press 'Apply' to save ordinary details such as an address or delivery choice.
finding: In testing, people overlooked or misread separate Apply buttons on ordinary checkout inputs, so most fields should save automatically; per Baymard's benchmark, 22% of sites still made users press Apply to save inputs. Promo and gift-card codes are the exception where an Apply button can stay, but the code field should be collapsed behind a link and any change to price, delivery date or availability should be visibly highlighted.
limitation: Participant numbers and benchmark size are not given on the page; it does not quantify abandonment caused by visible coupon fields or Apply buttons.
measurement: Rate of unsaved or lost checkout inputs; coupon field interaction rate versus checkout exits; successful code applications per attempt
method: Repeated rounds of checkout usability testing plus Baymard's UX benchmark of leading US and European ecommerce sites
plain: Most checkout boxes should save what people type automatically; a separate 'Apply' button is easy to miss. Keep 'Apply' only for discount codes, tuck that box behind a link, and highlight the new total.
sample: Benchmark of leading US and European ecommerce sites; participant and site counts not stated on page

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's benchmark still made users press 'Apply' to save checkout inputs.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.

application: Audit the order confirmation page for a visible order number, delivery timeline, support contact, downloadable or emailed receipt, and sensible behaviour when the URL is reopened later.
do: Show the order number, next steps with timing, contact details and a way to keep a receipt.
dont: End on a bare 'Thank you' page that breaks when reopened.
finding: The final page of a transaction should show any reference number prominently, set out what will happen next and roughly when, give contact details and likely next links, and let people keep a record such as a PDF. Because some users bookmark it as proof of purchase, the page should remain reachable or fail gracefully when revisited.
limitation: Public-sector pattern with no study data on the page; it notes that links inside the green panel need a contrast fix and that confirming steps within larger journeys still needs research.
measurement: Post-purchase contact rate about order status; receipt download or email-open rate; return visits to the confirmation URL
method: Not stated
plain: The last page of a purchase works as a receipt: show the order number clearly, say what happens next and when, and how to get help. Some people bookmark it, so it should still open later.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Order confirmation pages that double as a receipt

application: Staff each expert review with at least three independent reviewers, scope it to defined tasks or devices, and log every issue against a named heuristic before a joint severity session.
finding: NN/g recommends that three to five people review the same interface separately, each spending roughly one to two hours, because any single reviewer overlooks some problems; findings stay hidden from colleagues until everyone finishes, then are merged and prioritized together.
limitation: Offers no quantitative evidence of how many issues the method finds; an expert inspection does not replace testing with real users, and a heuristic breach is not automatically a user problem.
measurement: Unique issues found per evaluator; overlap rate between evaluators; share of issues rated high severity
method: Step-by-step practitioner guide: prepare and train evaluators, have each inspect the interface alone against Nielsen's 10 heuristics, then consolidate findings via affinity diagramming
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Running a heuristic evaluation as a team

application: For complex or expert workflows, schedule on-site or screen-shared sessions where participants perform actual tasks, and compare observed steps against what they self-report.
finding: Watching people do real work in their own setting, and questioning them as they go, surfaces habits and workarounds they omit when merely describing a process; in the article's example, observation revealed cross-checking in a second tool and redundant manual saving that interviews had missed.
limitation: Qualitative guidance with no measured outcomes; the article notes it suits complex expert work poorly matched to simple pages, and researcher probing can bias or alter participant behavior.
measurement: Number of undocumented workarounds observed; gap between reported and observed task steps; count of tools or systems used per task
method: Practitioner explainer of the Beyer and Holtzblatt contextual inquiry method: four principles (context, partnership, interpretation, focus) and a four-part session (primer, transition, contextual interview, wrap-up)
sample: Not stated on page (illustrative example involved three insurance data-entry specialists)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Contextual inquiry: observing users where they work

application: Use image-based first-click tests for early navigation checks, but validate any target that depends on hover menus, responsive collapse or other dynamic behavior on a working build.
finding: First-click distributions on screenshots broadly tracked those on live homepages: under lenient region coding the mean absolute gap was 5.1 percentage points, with 4 of 28 regions differing significantly (p < .10). The biggest gaps involved hover menus and responsive layout changes that a static image cannot show.
limitation: Covers only desktop homepages with few dynamic elements, so agreement is likely a best case; it did not test whether first clicks predict task success, and some differences went unexplained.
measurement: First-click success rate per target region; absolute difference between prototype and live click shares; time to first click
method: Online between-subjects study: participants randomly assigned to click on full-page screenshots or on live websites (tracked via browser extension) for five homepage tasks; only the first click analyzed
sample: 130 US online panel participants (68 live, 62 image), fielded February 2023; five homepages (Creative Commons, NASA, Disqus, IKEA, California State)
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Do static-image click tests match live-site first clicks?

application: Where survey space is tight, replace a full SUS with the two UX-Lite items on a 0-100 scale and track it per release against a fixed benchmark.
finding: MeasuringU adapted the two-item UMUX-Lite (ease of use plus usefulness) into the five-point UX-Lite; in the cited 64-person auto insurance study, the five-point version showed alpha of .89 and correlated .87 with SUS, with mean scores not meaningfully different from SUS.
limitation: Equivalence evidence rests largely on one small study in a single domain; internal wording and norm research is not detailed, the article is not peer reviewed, and the publisher sells related tools.
measurement: UX-Lite score (0-100); ease item mean; usefulness item mean
method: Practitioner article summarizing a 2019 Human Factors study by Lewis comparing UMUX-Lite scale formats, plus MeasuringU internal studies of alternative usefulness wordings and normative data collected since 2017
sample: Five-point subset of the Lewis (2019) study: n = 64 rating auto insurance websites; samples for internal wording studies and norms not stated
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: UX-Lite: two-item usability score aligned with SUS

application: Audit every chat entry point to confirm an AI disclosure appears before or at the first message, is visible and announced to screen readers, and is not buried in terms or a tooltip.
do: Show an 'AI assistant' label before or with the chatbot's first reply.
dont: Bury the AI disclosure in the terms or a tooltip.
finding: Chatbots, AI agents and avatars that talk directly with people must make it clear, from the first interaction and in an accessible, distinguishable way, that the user is dealing with AI, unless that is already obvious to an average, well-informed person (an exception the Commission says should be read narrowly). Providers of generative systems must also mark synthetic audio, image, video and text in a machine-readable, detectable format, with listed exemptions.
limitation: Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026, with a grace period to 2 December 2026 only for the marking duty on systems already on the market; it binds providers and deployers in scope of the EU AI Act, and the FAQ explains Commission guidelines rather than being binding law itself or a court interpretation. It says nothing about which disclosure wording or design works best for users.
measurement: Share of chat sessions showing an AI disclosure before the first reply; disclosure detected by screen reader (pass/fail); share of generated media assets carrying machine-readable marking
method: Commission FAQ explaining its Guidelines on Article 50 of the AI Act
plain: In the EU, chatbots and AI assistants must make clear from the first message that you're talking to an AI, unless that's obvious. AI-made images, audio, video and text must also carry a machine-readable mark.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: EU rules on telling people they are talking to an AI
