application: Replace generic 'AI-powered' badges with a short, human-readable note stating what the AI did (drafted, edited, summarised) placed next to the content it applies to.
do: Add a short note next to the content saying what AI did, such as summarised it.
dont: Rely on a vague 'AI-powered' badge, or wait for a platform to label it for you.
finding: Audience reactions to AI disclosure vary with who is reading, what kind of content it is and how much AI did, so no single rule fits; the author notes a penalty is likelier for personal or creative content than for routine notices. Being exposed by a third party (such as a platform label) after the fact hurt trust the most, which the author uses to argue for proactive, specific disclosure.
limitation: PACED is the author's synthesis, not a validated instrument; the underlying studies mostly measured attitudes rather than behaviour and their results conflict, and NN/g reports no pooled effect size.
measurement: Share of AI-assisted content carrying a specific (not generic) disclosure; trust or credibility rating with vs. without disclosure in A/B tests; complaints or feedback mentioning undisclosed AI
method: Synthesis of published studies on AI disclosure, condensed into the PACED framework (Policy, Audience, Context, Expectations, Degree of AI use)
plain: How people react to being told AI was used depends on who they are, the content and how much AI did. Being caught out later by someone else hurts trust most, so say plainly what the AI did.
sample: Not stated on page (draws on several external studies, including a systematic review of 47 news studies)
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Deciding when and how to disclose AI involvement

application: For each AI feature, map the likely failure types and confirm every failure screen offers a concrete next step (rephrase, manual route, human contact) plus a feedback control.
do: Give every AI error screen a next step and a quick way to send feedback.
dont: Show a dead-end 'Something went wrong' when the AI can't answer.
finding: The chapter sorts AI mistakes into user, system and context errors plus 'failstates' where no answer can be given, and traces them to sources such as prediction, input, relevance and background errors. It advises explaining limits specifically, offering alternatives, gathering feedback at the point of failure and handing control back to the user with enough context to carry on.
limitation: Guidance only: it presents no study data, the Google research it relies on is unpublished, and the page shows no publication or update date.
measurement: Share of AI failure states offering at least one alternative path; feedback submission rate on rejected outputs; task completion rate after an AI error
method: Design guidance chapter of the People + AI Guidebook; says it draws on Google user research studies (not listed) and cited literature
plain: When an AI feature can't help or gets something wrong, it should say so plainly and offer a next step, like rephrasing, doing it by hand or reaching a person.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Designing recovery paths when AI gets it wrong

application: Test every chatbot flow for a clearly labelled, always-available route to a human agent, and check that dispute or complaint wording is recognised and escalated rather than looped.
do: Show a 'Talk to a person' option in every chatbot conversation.
dont: Loop people through the same canned reply when the bot doesn't understand.
finding: The CFPB describes customers stuck in repetitive, unhelpful chatbot exchanges with no route to a person, receiving inaccurate answers, or having disputes go unrecognised, sometimes leading to fees. It reports that all of the ten largest US commercial banks used chatbots and, citing a secondary source, that roughly 37% of the US population (about 98 million people) used a bank chatbot in 2022.
limitation: An issue spotlight, not a rule: the report states it creates no new obligations or legal interpretations, and covers US consumer finance only. Its usage figures and the frustration survey it cites are secondary sources, and it predates the CFPB's 2025 policy shifts, so its current enforcement weight is uncertain.
measurement: Number of turns before a human-handoff option appears; share of sessions ending in repeated fallback responses; dispute-intent recognition rate
method: Issue spotlight drawing on CFPB consumer complaints, a market review and secondary research and industry sources
plain: Bank customers get stuck in loops with chatbots that repeat themselves, give wrong answers or miss complaints, with no way to reach a person. Always offer a clear route to a human.
sample: Not stated on page (complaint examples quoted; no total complaint count given)

stat.text: of the US population (about 98 million people) used a bank chatbot in 2022, per a secondary source cited by the CFPB.

strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: US regulator's review of bank chatbot doom loops

application: Audit the sign-up screen: confirm users can complete most of the task before registering, that 'Create an account' and 'Sign in' are clearly distinct paths, and that no CAPTCHA or repeated field is present.
do: Let people finish one-off tasks without an account, and keep 'Create account' clearly separate from 'Sign in'.
dont: Put an account wall or a puzzle test in front of a one-off task.
finding: GDS advises offering accounts only where people return repeatedly to view or change their data, since registration is a drop-out point; one-off transactions can use an emailed or texted reference number instead. Where accounts exist, the sign-up step should be clearly separated from sign-in, labelled with 'create' wording, kept free of distractions and duplicate entry, and should avoid CAPTCHAs that test cognition.
limitation: Guidance pattern without published study data on the page; drop-out claims are asserted rather than quantified, and it is written for UK public services rather than commercial SaaS.
measurement: Sign-up start-to-completion rate; share of users entering the sign-in path by mistake when intending to register; abandonment at the account-creation step
method: Not stated
plain: Only ask people to create an account if they will come back to view or change things. For one-off tasks, a reference number sent by email or text does the job without a sign-up step.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: When a service should (and should not) require an account

application: Check the password-creation and session flows: passphrases of 64+ characters and paste are accepted, no character-mix rules, rejection messages say why, and a warning appears before an idle session expires.
do: Accept long passphrases and pasting, and warn people before an idle session times out.
dont: Force regular password changes or demand mixes of symbols and numbers.
finding: This informative section of SP 800-63B (800-63-4 revision) asks services to cut authentication friction by offering a choice of authenticators, allowing long passphrases with any characters and paste/autofill, dropping composition rules and forced periodic changes, and explaining rejections clearly. It also covers lockout and loss: give self-service recovery paths and alternative methods, warn users before an inactivity timeout (two minutes is the example), and provide an accessible log-off.
limitation: The customer-experience section is labelled informative, not normative; binding requirements sit in other sections of SP 800-63B, and the guidelines formally apply to US federal agencies, so private SaaS adopts them voluntarily.
measurement: Password creation error rate; account lockout and recovery-request volume; sessions lost to timeout without warning
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Let people use long passphrases, paste and password managers, drop forced password changes and symbol rules, and warn them before an idle session signs them out.
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: NIST customer-experience rules for authenticators and sessions

application: On the SaaS pricing page, confirm every plan shows a price, range or 'from' figure, and that enterprise tiers give a representative example instead of only a 'Contact sales' button.
do: Show a price, range or 'from' figure for every plan, including enterprise.
dont: Replace prices with only a 'Contact sales' button.
finding: In NN/g's studies with business buyers, price was the information people most wanted, and participants who could not find it grew frustrated and moved to competitor sites, which then had a better chance of being shortlisted. The author recommends at least approximate figures such as ranges, 'starting at' prices or typical scenarios, rather than relying on complex configurators that only highly engaged prospects used.
limitation: Qualitative findings with no participant counts or metrics; dated 2013 and centred on B2B website research, so it does not show the effect of price display on conversion for modern self-serve SaaS.
measurement: Pricing page exit rate; demo or trial requests per pricing-page visit; usage rate of any pricing calculator
method: Qualitative observations drawn from multiple usability studies with business customers; study design not detailed
plain: Business buyers most wanted to see prices. When they couldn't find any, they got frustrated and moved on to competitors, who were then more likely to make the shortlist.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Hidden B2B pricing loses shortlist places

application: Check that account settings offer a secure self-service export in an open format (CSV/JSON) covering user-provided and activity data, with clear labelling of what is included.
finding: The ICO explains that, under UK GDPR, people can get data they provided (including observed activity data, but not inferred profiles) in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format such as CSV, JSON or XML, normally free and within one month. Organisations may meet the right with an automated tool that lets users extract their own data, provided it is secure and the output is usable by the individual.
limitation: Applies only where processing is automated and based on consent or contract, and only in UK law; the page states the guidance is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 became law on 19 June 2025, so details may change.
measurement: Time from export request to file delivery; share of export requests handled self-service vs via support; format and completeness of exported data
method: Not applicable (standard)
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: UK rules for self-service personal data export

application: Before changing a search engine or ranking, build a judged query set and run a live A/B test tracking clickthrough, refinement and search-page exits together.
do: Test a new search engine or ranking live against the current one before switching everyone over.
dont: Judge a search change by one number alone, such as clicks on results.
finding: When GOV.UK swapped its long-running custom search engine for an LLM-based semantic engine, the live A/B test showed results-page clickthrough up 14%, searches needing refinement down 11% and exits from the search page down 8%. The team treated these shifts together as evidence people were reaching what they needed with less effort.
limitation: Relative changes only, with no sample size, duration or significance reported; one government site, and it does not separate engine quality from interface effects.
measurement: Search results clickthrough rate (and position of clicked result); Query refinement rate; Exit rate from search results page
method: Prototype comparison using judgement lists and internal relevance ratings, then a live A/B test of new vs old engine ramped to half of analytics-consenting users
plain: GOV.UK tested a new search engine against the old one with real visitors. With the new one, more people clicked a result, fewer had to rephrase their search and fewer left from the results page.
sample: Not stated on page (A/B test sample size and duration not given; users who consented to analytics tracking on GOV.UK)

stat.text: rise in results-page clickthrough in GOV.UK's live A/B test of a new semantic search engine (relative change).

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: GOV.UK A/B test of a semantic site search engine

application: Audit autocomplete by running every top suggestion and removing any that return zero or irrelevant results; check that typed versus suggested text is styled differently.
do: Show suggestions that all lead to relevant results, with the typed part styled differently from the suggested part.
dont: Suggest searches that return zero or unrelated results.
finding: Participants picked a suggested query in roughly 23% of the cases where suggestions were shown (31 of 136, margin of error about 7%), yet the list still helped by revealing what the site carries and how terms are spelled. Suggestions must lead to relevant results, distinguish typed from suggested text visually, and present scope as a separate indented element.
limitation: Ecommerce-only sample with undisclosed methodology; selection rate does not measure downstream task success, and no guidance on number of suggestions or keyboard behaviour.
measurement: Suggestion selection rate; Zero-result rate for suggested queries; Search task success after suggestion use
method: Usability study of ecommerce websites with observed participant sessions (full methodology not described)
plain: As people typed in a shop's search box, they picked one of the suggested searches roughly 23% of the time. Even unused, the list showed what the shop sells and how words are spelled.
sample: 136 instances where suggestions appeared in an ecommerce usability study; participant count and geography not stated on page

stat.text: of the times suggestions appeared, participants picked one (31 of 136 cases, NN/g ecommerce usability study).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Designing query suggestions that help even when unused

application: Export 3 to 6 months of search logs, test the top 100 queries by hand, and fix zero-result terms with synonyms, best bets or redirects.
finding: The article lays out a repeatable log review: take a three-to-six-month window, examine the most frequent queries, rebuild sessions to spot repeated reformulations, and look closely at zero-result and very long queries. One illustrative case showed 11,750 searches for heating pads in a month against only 13 purchases, signalling a findability problem.
limitation: Examples are anecdotal cases rather than measured outcomes; it does not show how much fixing log issues improves conversion or success.
measurement: Zero-result query rate; Reformulation rate within session; Search-to-conversion rate for top queries
method: Practitioner guidance with illustrative client examples; not a formal study
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Step-by-step method for mining site search logs

application: When auditing enterprise search, analyse full queries and term pairs rather than single-word frequency lists, and refresh best bets yearly as top queries change.
do: Analyse whole search phrases and refresh promoted results every year.
dont: Rely only on single-word frequency counts to decide what to fix in search.
finding: Intranet searchers mostly used one-word queries, and frequency lists of single terms overlapped only about half with lists of full queries, so term counts alone can mislead. Only around one in eight top-100 queries stayed in the top 100 across all three years, meaning some needs persist while many shift.
limitation: Single organisation with unequal sampling periods and data now dated; qualitative review covered only the most frequent terms.
measurement: Average terms per query; Share of single-term queries; Year-over-year persistence of top queries
method: Transaction log analysis of a corporate intranet search engine, counting single terms, term pairs, triplets and full queries, with Zipf rank-frequency comparison
plain: Staff searching a company intranet mostly typed single words. Counting single words gave a different picture from counting whole searches, and most top searches changed from year to year.
sample: 128,000+ search activities from 23,000+ users at a Swedish manufacturing group (80,000+ employees); about four weeks in 2000 and one week each in 2002 and 2004

stat.text: top-100 intranet queries stayed in the top 100 across all three years studied (128,000+ searches at a Swedish manufacturing group, 2000–2004).

strengthWhy: Published study, but observational or correlational.
title: Intranet query logs: terms vs full queries over time

application: Compare header, footer and side menus on 5–10 templates of one site and flag any where shared links appear in a different sequence.
do: Keep header, footer and side menu links in the same order on every page.
dont: Reshuffle the menu order on some templates, such as checkout or a separately built section.
finding: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation (Level AA) requires navigation blocks repeated across a set of pages to keep the same relative order on each page unless the user changes it. Inserting or removing items, such as an expanded submenu, does not break the order.
limitation: Covers relative order only, not identical visual layout; pages with a different purpose or author (e.g. a separately built checkout or subdomain) may fall outside the 'set'. Understanding docs are informative, not normative.
measurement: Templates with reordered nav items; time to locate a repeated link; repeat-visit task success
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Menus that appear on many pages should keep their links in the same order everywhere, so people can find things by habit.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Keeping repeated navigation in the same order across pages

visual.cap: A visitor moves from one page to the next

application: Check that contact links, chat launchers and FAQ links appear at the same point in the DOM order on every page that includes them.
do: Put contact, chat and FAQ links in the same spot on every page that has them.
dont: Move the help link around from page to page, so it's in the footer on one and the header on another.
finding: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help (Level A) says that when pages in a set repeat help options (human contact details, a contact form or chat, a self-help page, or a chatbot), those options must sit in the same order relative to other page content. Order is judged in the serialized source, not just visual position.
limitation: Does not require any help to be offered, does not cover PDFs or contextual help like form hints, and lets pages omit help entirely; it only governs placement where help is repeated.
measurement: Pages with inconsistent help placement; help-link findability; contact-centre contacts per task
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: If a site shows help options like a phone number, chat or FAQ on many pages, they must appear in the same place each time so people can find help when stuck.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Putting help and contact options in a predictable spot

application: Test every dropdown with keyboard only and with a slightly unsteady mouse path; flag submenus that close instantly or lack a current-page marker.
do: Test every drop-down menu with only a keyboard, and with a slightly shaky mouse path.
dont: Build fly-out menus that snap shut the moment the pointer drifts off them.
finding: WAI's menus tutorial advises marking up menus so their code reflects the site structure, labelling each menu, making states such as the current page easy to spot, and building fly-out submenus that work by mouse and keyboard and do not snap shut as soon as the pointer drifts away.
limitation: An overview linking to detailed subpages; it is implementation guidance, not usability research, and does not quantify which menu designs perform best.
measurement: Keyboard operability of menus; accidental submenu closures; current-location identification rate
method: Not stated
plain: Menus should be built so their code matches the site's structure, each menu has a name, and drop-down menus work with a keyboard and don't vanish when the mouse wobbles.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: W3C tutorial on structuring and labelling accessible menus

application: Check that the current section is exposed programmatically (aria-current) and visually, and that the mobile menu toggle is hidden from screen readers when not shown.
date: Date not shown (change history to August 2026)
do: Mark the current section both visually and in the code so screen reader users hear it.
dont: Leave a hidden mobile menu readable by screen readers when it isn't shown on screen.
finding: GOV.UK's service navigation component shows the service name and top-level links beneath the header, marks the active link with aria-current, and collapses links behind a Menu toggle on small screens. The page warns that custom content added to its slots may change in future releases and should be retested.
limitation: Component documentation; it gives no research findings itself (it points to the navigate-a-service pattern) and sets no maximum number of links.
measurement: Current-section identification; mobile menu open rate; navigation task success
method: Not stated
plain: GOV.UK's service navigation shows the main links under the header, marks the page you're on, and folds links behind a 'Menu' button on small screens.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: GOV.UK service navigation bar: current page and mobile menu

application: Press and slide your finger off each button, swipe card and drag target; flag controls that act on touch-down with no way to cancel.
do: Trigger actions when the finger lifts. If something is dragged and dropped in the wrong place, snap it back.
dont: Fire an action the instant the screen is touched, with no way to cancel or undo. (WCAG 2.5.2, Level A.)
finding: WCAG SC 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation (Level A) requires single-pointer functions to avoid triggering on the down-event, or to complete on release with a way to abort or undo, or to reverse on release, unless down-event activation is essential (e.g. an on-screen piano or keyboard emulation).
limitation: Applies only to pointer handling in web content, not the browser or assistive technology; it does not address target size or gesture complexity.
measurement: Controls activating on down-event; accidental activation reports; undo usage
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: Buttons should act when you lift your finger, not the moment you touch the screen. That way, if you press the wrong one, you can slide away and nothing happens.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Pointer actions should fire on release, not on press

visual.cap: How a button should behave

dont.cap: No way to take it back
dont.title: Item deleted

application: Inventory shake-to-undo, tilt-to-scroll and similar features; confirm each has an equivalent button and a setting (or OS setting respected) to turn motion off.
do: Give every shake or tilt feature an on-screen button and a setting to turn motion off.
dont: Make 'shake to undo' the only way to undo. (WCAG 2.5.4, Level A.)
finding: WCAG SC 2.5.4 Motion Actuation (Level A) requires anything triggered by moving the device or gesturing at it to also work through ordinary on-screen controls, and lets users disable motion response to avoid accidental triggers, except where motion runs through an accessibility-supported interface or is essential.
limitation: Does not cover touchscreen gestures, typing or mouse movement, and allows exceptions when motion is essential to the activity.
measurement: Motion features lacking UI alternative; motion-disable setting present; accidental-trigger complaints
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: If shaking or tilting the phone does something, there must also be a normal button for it, and a way to switch the motion off so it doesn't trigger by accident.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: Shake and tilt features need buttons and an off switch

visual.cap: Someone who can't shake their phone wants to undo

application: Measure computed tap-area size and gaps for icons, links and close buttons on mobile templates; pad anything under 48px or closer than 8px to a neighbour.
do: Add padding around small icons (close, menu, heart) so the tap area reaches about 48px. Keep about 8px between neighbours.
dont: Let a 16px icon be the whole tap area, or pack small links tightly together.
finding: web.dev recommends interactive elements of roughly 48×48 device-independent pixels on a properly configured mobile viewport (it equates this to about 9mm), spaced about 8px apart, and suggests padding small icons and using the any-pointer: coarse media query to enlarge targets on touch devices.
limitation: Guidance, not a study; the 9mm finger-pad comparison is unsourced and the page dates from 2020. The 48px figure is stricter than WCAG 2.5.8's 24px minimum.
measurement: Share of targets under 48px; mis-tap rate; tap-to-correct ratio
method: Not stated
plain: Anything people tap should be roughly 48px square, with a small gap between neighbours, so a finger hits the thing it meant to.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Sizing and spacing touch targets around 48px

visual.cap: Shown at actual size on your screen
visual.note: The dark square is the icon. The pale area around it is what you can actually tap. Padding grows the tap area without changing how the icon looks.

application: Use 44×44 CSS px as a stretch target for primary actions on touch-heavy flows, logging any small targets that rely on one of the four exceptions.
do: Aim for 44 × 44 px on main buttons in touch-heavy flows.
dont: Treat the AAA size as a legal must-have; most requirements use the AA 24px minimum.
finding: WCAG SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA, requires pointer targets to be at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels unless an equivalent larger control exists on the page, the target is inline in text, the size is set by the user agent, or the presentation is essential.
limitation: AAA criteria are rarely required by law or policy; most conformance targets use AA, where SC 2.5.8 sets a smaller 24px minimum.
measurement: Primary targets under 44px; exception usage count; mis-tap rate
method: Not applicable (standard)
plain: The strictest WCAG level asks for tap targets of at least 44 by 44 pixels, with a few exceptions such as links inside a sentence. Most rules only require the smaller Level AA minimum.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: The AAA 44px target size and its four exceptions

visual.cap: Shown at actual size on your screen
visual.note: The 24px figure comes from the separate AA rule (SC 2.5.8).

application: Audit pages for stacked or decorative banners; merge them into one, move task-relevant notes into the page body, and use error summaries for validation.
do: Merge several messages into one banner, or show only the most important. Put task-related notes in the page itself.
dont: Use banners for form errors, stack several at once, or use them in a step-by-step application.
finding: GOV.UK reserves notification banners for news not tied to the page's task (outages, deadlines, the result of a previous action), advises at most one per page placed just above the h1, and rules them out for validation errors and linear transactions. It notes users often miss banners and flags that this needs more research.
limitation: Pattern guidance; the page states that how often users miss banners, and whether dismissal helps, has not yet been researched.
measurement: Banners per page; banner content recall; error-summary vs banner misuse count
method: Not stated
plain: Use a banner only for things that aren't part of what the person is doing on the page, like a service outage or a deadline. Show one at most, just above the main heading.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Using one notification banner for messages outside the task

application: Map each system message to its type and urgency; replace auto-dismissing toasts used for errors with inline validation or a persistent message.
do: Show errors next to the field, or in a message that stays until it's dealt with.
dont: Report a failed payment in a pop-up message that fades after a few seconds.
finding: NN/g distinguishes passive contextual indicators, input-linked validation errors that users must resolve, and notifications about system events, which can be passive or demand action. It warns that passive messages such as fading toasts are easy to miss and unsuitable for errors or critical information.
limitation: Guidance article without a reported study; it does not quantify miss rates for each message type.
measurement: Errors shown via toast; message noticed rate; repeat error rate after message
method: Author's analysis of real-world product examples; no formal study described
plain: Some messages sit quietly in place, some flag a mistake people must fix, and some report events. Messages that fade on their own are easy to miss, so never use them for errors.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Choosing between indicators, validations and notifications

application: Pull field TTFB at the 75th percentile, then check redirect chains, cache headers and Server-Timing breakdowns on slow templates.
do: Check for chains of redirects, pages that could be cached, and whether a CDN serves visitors from nearby.
dont: Judge speed on this number alone. A good start doesn't guarantee the page loads or responds quickly.
finding: web.dev treats Time to First Byte as the groundwork for later metrics like FCP and LCP, giving a rough guide of 0.8s or less as good and over 1.8s as poor. It recommends CDNs, caching, removing redirects (with HSTS), streaming markup, service workers and 103 Early Hints.
limitation: TTFB is not a Core Web Vital and the thresholds are presented as a rough guide; a good TTFB does not guarantee good LCP or interactivity.
measurement: 75th-percentile TTFB; redirect count per navigation; CDN cache hit rate
method: Not stated
plain: Time to First Byte (TTFB) is how long a site takes to start sending the page after someone clicks. Until it does, they stare at a blank screen.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Cutting server response time before anything renders

visual.cap: Same tap, two servers
visual.note: An illustration built on Google's marks: 0.8 seconds or less counts as good, over 1.8 seconds as poor. Google calls these a rough guide, not a hard rule.

application: Run Chrome DevTools' back-forward cache test on key listing and product pages; remove unload handlers and avoid no-store on non-sensitive pages.
do: Run Chrome's back/forward cache test on your listing and product pages. It names what's blocking it.
dont: Use the old "unload" event, or tell browsers never to store pages that aren't sensitive.
finding: The back/forward cache restores a paused snapshot of a page so returning feels instant. Citing Chrome usage data, web.dev says roughly 1 in 10 desktop and 1 in 5 mobile navigations are back or forward; unload listeners, Cache-Control: no-store and open connections can make pages ineligible.
limitation: Usage share comes from Chrome data only; eligibility rules vary by browser, and no-store may still be needed for sensitive content.
measurement: bfcache hit rate; back-navigation load time; pages failing bfcache test
method: Not stated (usage figures attributed to Chrome usage data)
plain: Browsers can keep the last page frozen in memory so pressing Back brings it straight back, in the same spot. Some common code quietly switches this off, and Back becomes a slow full reload.

stat.text: mobile page visits are Back or Forward (1 in 10 on desktop), according to Chrome data.

strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Making Back and Forward instant with the bfcache

application: Pick a fixed set of attributes per product type for list tiles, check every tile in a category shows them (or says 'not available'), and style brand, name and specs differently.
do: Show the same key details on every product tile in a list, each in its own style.
dont: Let supplier-written blurbs decide what each tile shows, so details appear on some items and not others.
finding: Shoppers tend to dismiss a listed product when it lacks an attribute that neighbouring items show, so inconsistent tiles can make a range look thinner than it is. In Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark, 64% of sites did not show the same attributes consistently across list items and 40% did not visually separate elements such as brand, title and specs.
limitation: Benchmark sample size and scoring are not given on the page, and the evidence for abandonment is qualitative; it does not cover price, ratings, swatches or badges.
measurement: Share of tiles missing a key attribute; list-to-product click-through; filter use per session
method: Large-scale qualitative usability testing of product lists plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: If some products in a list show a detail (like screen size) and others don't, people skip the ones without it. Run-together text also makes every tile slow to read.
sample: Not stated on page (benchmark size and participant counts not given in the article)

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark didn't show the same details consistently across product tiles.

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Consistent, distinct details on product list tiles

application: On each top-level category, check that subcategory tiles with clear names and images appear before promotions, that there is a 'View all' route to the full list, and that there are no more than one or two such layers for a mid-size catalogue.
do: Lead a category page with named subcategory tiles and a 'View all' link.
dont: Fill the category page with sales banners so shoppers can't see how to narrow down.
finding: Intermediary category pages (subcategory tiles, guides and related content before any product list) help undecided or new-to-category shoppers and were leaned on more heavily on mobile, while roughly as many participants wanted to skip straight to products. Baymard's benchmark found 13% of sites offer none; it advises 1–2 layers for most sites, subcategories with clear titles and thumbnails first, and a 'View all' link.
limitation: No participant counts or effect sizes are given; the right number of layers depends on catalogue size, and small catalogues may not need these pages at all.
measurement: Subcategory tile click-through; 'View all' usage; exits from category landing pages
method: Large-scale usability testing (desktop and mobile) from Baymard's Premium research, plus its e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: A category page that shows clear subcategories helps people who aren't sure what they want yet. People who already know can jump to everything with a 'View all' link.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Category landing pages that lead with subcategories

visual.cap: A shopper taps 'Computers' in the menu

application: Count how many products a category list shows before pagination or a 'Load more' button on desktop and mobile, and compare against the ranges for that product type.
do: Load a full batch of products suited to the device, then offer a 'Load more' button.
dont: Split a category into many tiny pages that people must click through one by one.
finding: Baymard found the ideal default number of products varies by more than ten times across product type and device, recommending roughly 50–150 per load on desktop (more for visual products like apparel, fewer for spec-driven ones) and 15–30 on mobile, with lower numbers for search results. Its benchmark found 52% of desktop sites' product lists fell outside these ranges.
limitation: Sample sizes and test protocols aren't disclosed, the ranges are from 2020, and the comparison of 'Load more' with other methods is only cited here, not shown.
measurement: Products viewed per list session; 'Load more' or next-page clicks; scroll depth on mobile lists
method: Large-scale usability testing combined with Baymard's UX benchmarking
plain: If a list shows too few products at a time, people spend their visit clicking 'next page'. Too many, especially on a phone, and the list becomes an endless scroll.

stat.text: of desktop sites in Baymard's benchmark showed too few or too many products per list load.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: How many products a list should load at once

visual.cap: A shopper browses lamps
visual.note: Illustration of the idea, not a recommended count.

application: On listing pages for visual products, check each tile offers at least two extra images in the list, that arrows or dots signal them, and that the default image clearly shows what the item is.
do: Offer at least three images per product tile, with visible dots or arrows showing there are more.
dont: Hide extra images behind a hover with no sign they exist, especially on mobile.
finding: Baymard found one or two images per list item often left people unable to judge visual products, so some dismissed suitable items or had to open product pages. It now recommends at least three thumbnails per item (default plus two more), reachable by hover or swipe, with a visible cue that more exist (always visible on mobile); apparel may need 5–15.
limitation: Qualitative recommendation without reported participant counts or measured effects; mainly tested on visually driven product types, and the article's wording on '2+' versus '2 additional' thumbnails is inconsistent.
measurement: Thumbnails available per tile; list-to-product click-through; product page bounce back to list
method: Multiple rounds of large-scale qualitative usability testing, including furniture and home decor and apparel and accessories sites
plain: With only one photo on each product in a list, shoppers often can't tell if an item suits them. Letting them flick through a few more pictures right in the list saves trips back and forth.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Several thumbnails per product in listings

application: On mobile category pages for apparel or furnishings, check each tile shows all colour swatches (or a clearly scrollable row) rather than a count of hidden colours.
do: Show every colour as a swatch on the product tile, using a clearly scrollable row if there are many.
dont: Replace extra colours with a '+7 more' count that people skim past.
finding: For visual products, Baymard found people missed colours shown only as '+7'-style counts or 'more colours' text, assumed visible swatches were the full range, or had to open product pages one by one. Its benchmark found 57% of sites don't make all colour variations available in the product list; a horizontally scrolling swatch row performed well when it was clearly scrollable.
limitation: The benchmark sample isn't stated and it's unclear whether the 57% covers mobile only; behavioural findings are qualitative.
measurement: Share of tiles showing all colours; swatch taps in lists; product page visits per purchase
method: Mobile usability testing from Baymard's Premium research plus its e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: When a product list shows only a few colours and a '+7' note, people miss the hidden ones or assume they don't exist. Showing every colour on the tile lets them spot what they want.

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark don't show all colour variations in the product list.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Show every colour swatch on mobile list items

application: Audit a sample of product tiles for name, distinguishable photo, option indicators and price, then check whether ratings, sale/new badges and stock are shown where they matter.
do: Put the name, a clear photo, option swatches and the price on every product tile.
dont: Make shoppers open each product just to find its price or available colours.
finding: NN/g says listings should at minimum carry a concise name with meaningful characteristics, a photo big enough to tell items apart, signs of other colours or options, and price; ratings, badges (popular, new, on sale), availability, quick views and alternate images help too. Where category and listing pages merge, subcategories shown apart from filters, usually above the list, worked best.
limitation: Qualitative summary of a 2018 report with no task metrics; examples are illustrative, and it does not address grid versus list views or items per page.
measurement: Tiles meeting the four minimum elements; list-to-product click-through; pogo-sticking between list and product pages
method: NN/g ecommerce usability research summarised from a longer report (69 guidelines)
plain: Each product in a list should show at least a clear name, a good-sized photo, signs of other colours or options, and the price. Ratings and labels like 'new' or 'on sale' help people decide what to open.
sample: 49 ecommerce sites; participant numbers, countries and years not stated on page
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: What a product listing needs to show

visual.cap: A shopper scans a list of jackets on a phone
visual.note: Illustration. Product names and prices are made-up examples.

application: Check that every product tile in category, search and recommendation lists shows the rating count next to the star average.
do: Show the number of ratings beside the stars on every product tile.
dont: Show a star average on its own with no review count.
finding: Without a visible rating count, participants often distrusted star averages, and items rated between 4 and 4.5 were hard to compare from the list. In the latest survey nearly twice as many respondents picked a 4.5-star item with 57 ratings over a 5-star item with 4 ratings; sites omitting counts in list items fell from 25% (2015) to 5% (2022).
limitation: Survey choices are stated preferences between two mock items, not observed purchases; test participant numbers are not given and the effect on click-through or sales is not measured.
measurement: List-to-product click-through on rated items; share of tiles showing a rating count; sort-by-rating usage
method: Multiple rounds of large-scale usability testing, Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark (tracked since 2015), and five surveys in which respondents chose between two otherwise identical list items, with answer order randomized
plain: A star score means little unless people can see how many reviews it is based on. Shoppers trusted a slightly lower score from many reviews over a perfect score from a handful.
sample: 5 surveys with 5,170+ respondents in total; usability-test participant counts and benchmark site count not stated on page
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Rating counts beside stars in product lists

application: Add a visible label or border (with a view-cart link) to list tiles for products already in the cart, and style visited products differently.
do: Mark tiles for items already in the cart with a label and a 'View cart' link.
dont: Leave in-cart items looking identical to every other tile in the list.
finding: Of 50 large US sites benchmarked, 96% did not mark list items that were already in the shopper's cart. In testing, people who went back to a list to find accessories or to compare often struggled to re-find the product they had added, because tiles looked alike and search results could reorder.
limitation: 2016 research on 50 US sites with no participant counts; Baymard frames it as an enhancement to add once core usability is solid, and reports no effect on sales.
measurement: Time to re-find an added item in tests; accessory add rate after a first add-to-cart; returns from cart to product list
method: Large-scale usability testing of product lists and category navigation, plus a product-list benchmark of large US sites
plain: After adding something to the cart, people often go back to the list for accessories or to compare. If nothing marks the item they chose, it blends in and is hard to find again.
sample: Benchmark of 50 of the largest US ecommerce sites; usability-test participant count not stated on page

application: Make the whole tile one link to the product page with a single shared hover state, and group secondary actions such as review links or add-to-cart lower in the tile.
do: Make the whole product tile open the product page, and highlight it all together on hover.
dont: Mix several links, tooltips and plain text in one tile with no sign of which does what.
finding: At 76% of the 50 benchmarked sites, list tiles made it unclear which parts could be clicked and where each would lead. Test participants clicked static text, and when aiming for the product page sometimes set off tooltips, expanding content or offer pages instead.
limitation: 2016 benchmark of 50 US sites with no participant counts or error rates; hover cues do not exist on touch screens, so mobile tiles need other signals.
measurement: Clicks on non-interactive tile text; unintended tooltip or offer opens; list-to-product click-through
method: Large-scale usability testing of how users navigate product listing pages, plus a benchmark of major US sites
plain: If different parts of a product tile go to different places, or some look clickable but are not, people tap the wrong thing. One big tap area that opens the product avoids that.
sample: Benchmark of 50 major US ecommerce sites; participant count not stated on page

stat.text: of 50 major US ecommerce sites had list tiles where it was unclear what could be clicked (Baymard benchmark, 2016).

application: Before a speed audit, note the client's platform baseline and treat a result below it as a site-specific problem (theme, apps, images, hosting) rather than an unavoidable platform cost.
do: Compare a store's Core Web Vitals with its own platform's baseline before diagnosing.
dont: Assume a slow store is fine just because it runs on a popular platform.
finding: About 19% of analysed sites were detected as ecommerce (19.9% desktop, 19.2% mobile). On mobile, 76% of Shopify origins had good Core Web Vitals versus 35% of WooCommerce and 35% of Magento origins; on desktop the Shopify and WooCommerce figures were 76% and 33%.
limitation: Platform pass rates are correlational: they mix hosting, themes, apps and site size, so they do not show that switching platform would make a given store faster; only origins with enough Chrome traffic are included.
measurement: Origin Core Web Vitals pass rate (mobile); p75 LCP; p75 INP
method: Ecommerce platform detection on the HTTP Archive crawl (home page plus one inner page, desktop and mobile), joined to Chrome UX Report field data; an origin counts as good when it meets the LCP, INP and CLS thresholds
plain: Across hundreds of thousands of real online shops, the platform mattered: 76% of Shopify shops passed Google's Core Web Vitals on phones, versus 35% of WooCommerce shops.
sample: 16.2M websites (12.2M desktop, 15.4M mobile), July 2025 crawl with CrUX field data from June 2025; e.g. 567,932 Shopify and 995,782 WooCommerce mobile origins

stat.text: of WooCommerce shops had good Core Web Vitals on mobile, versus 76% of Shopify shops (Web Almanac 2025, 16.2M-site July 2025 crawl).

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Core Web Vitals pass rates by ecommerce platform

application: On home, category and product templates, check the LCP image carries no loading="lazy" or data-src swap, and give it fetchpriority="high".
do: Load the main above-the-fold image straight away, with high priority.
dont: Apply lazy loading to the hero image or the first row of product images.
finding: About 16-17% of pages lazy-load the image that becomes their Largest Contentful Paint element, roughly unchanged since 2024. Native loading="lazy" on the LCP image rose to 10.4% of mobile pages, while script-based approaches such as data-src fell to 5.9%.
limitation: Shows how common the anti-pattern is, not how much LCP each affected site loses; the lab-detected LCP element can differ from what real users see.
measurement: Templates with a lazy-loaded LCP image; p75 LCP (mobile); LCP resource load delay
method: Lab analysis of pages in the HTTP Archive crawl, reported alongside Chrome UX Report field data for Core Web Vitals
plain: On about 16-17% of websites, the biggest image at the top of the page is set to load late on purpose, so the main picture appears later than it needs to.
publisher: HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025 (Jariyal, Rasam, Humaira & Grogg)
sample: 16.2M websites (12.2M desktop, 15.4M mobile), July 2025 crawl; CrUX field data from June 2025

stat.text: of pages lazy-load their Largest Contentful Paint image (Web Almanac 2025, 16.2M-site July 2025 crawl).

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: How often sites lazy-load their main image

application: Where BNPL is offered, test it as a clearly explained payment option at checkout and track rejections, defaults and returns alongside conversion.
do: Test pay-later as a clearly explained checkout option and track defaults and returns, not just sales.
dont: Judge a pay-later rollout on conversion alone.
finding: Showing a buy-now-pay-later option raised the share of visits ending in a purchase by 9 percentage points (about 13%) and revenue per customer by roughly 18-21%, mostly from extra conversions. Effects were largest for customers with low credit scores, and about 13% of BNPL applications were rejected.
limitation: One German furniture retailer, a small control group and three weeks of 2022 data; it does not test how prominently BNPL is shown, and the gains came mostly from lower-credit-score customers, which raises affordability questions.
measurement: Visit-to-purchase conversion; revenue per visitor; BNPL rejection and default rate
method: Randomized controlled trial run by the retailer (not pre-registered): customers were assigned by digits of their customer ID to see or not see a buy-now-pay-later option at checkout; intent-to-treat estimates
plain: In a real shop's controlled test, showing a pay-later option at checkout led more visitors to buy and raised revenue. The biggest change came from customers with weaker credit, which raises affordability questions.
publisher: NBER Working Paper 33152 (Berg, Burg, Keil & Puri); published in Journal of Financial Economics vol. 171, 2025
sample: 75,072 customers (74,128 shown BNPL, 948 control) at one German online furniture retailer; about three weeks in February-March 2022

stat.text: rise in visit-to-purchase conversion when BNPL was shown (75,072-customer randomized test, German furniture retailer, 2022).

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Field experiment: offering pay-later at checkout

application: For UK checkouts and product pages offering BNPL, confirm the lender's key product information (payment schedule, amounts, risks) is shown before the shopper commits, and that the shop's own pay-later messaging stays consistent with it.
do: Show the repayment schedule and that pay-later is credit before the shopper chooses it.
dont: Hide the repayment details behind a link the shopper has to hunt for.
finding: From 15 July 2026, interest-free deferred payment credit (previously unregulated BNPL) in the UK falls under FCA rules: lenders need authorisation, must assess creditworthiness proportionately even for loans of £50 or less, and must give key product information, such as the credit amount and the number, frequency and amount of payments, before the agreement. Merchants that only broker these agreements stay exempt from authorisation.
limitation: The rules bind lenders, not merchants, and do not prescribe checkout layout, default selection or prominence; agreements made before 15 July 2026 stay unregulated. Not legal advice.
measurement: Key product information shown before agreement (pass/fail); BNPL selection rate; BNPL-related complaints
method: Not applicable (regulatory policy statement and final rules)
plain: Since 15 July 2026, UK pay-later loans count as regulated credit. Lenders must check people can afford them and show the repayment details before signing; shops that simply offer them do not need their own licence.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: UK rules for pay-later lenders from July 2026

application: In any category with varied pack sizes or volumes, show a smaller unit price (per item, kg, litre or serving) under the total price on every list tile.
do: Show a smaller price per unit under the total price on every multi-pack tile.
dont: Show only pack prices for items sold in different sizes, leaving shoppers to divide.
finding: 86% of sites in Baymard's benchmark do not show a price per unit for products sold in different quantities or volumes. In testing, people did the sums in their heads, made calculation errors, compared only a few items, and sometimes rejected good-value products or abandoned the purchase.
limitation: No participant or site counts are given and abandonment is not quantified; unit prices can still mislead when doses or strengths differ between products.
measurement: Share of multi-quantity tiles showing a unit price; add-to-cart rate in multi-pack categories; list-to-product click-through in multi-pack categories
method: Multiple rounds of large-scale usability testing of product lists and filtering, plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: When packs come in different sizes, shoppers cannot tell which is better value without doing sums. Showing the price per item or per kilo on each tile saves them the maths and the mistakes.
sample: Not stated on page (participant numbers and benchmark size not given)

stat.text: of sites in Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark do not show a unit price for items sold in different quantities.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Unit prices on multi-pack products in lists

application: Where a free-shipping threshold exists, track orders, returns and margin together, and review return rates on items added just to reach the threshold.
do: Track orders, returns and margin together whenever you set or change a free-delivery threshold.
dont: Assume a free-delivery threshold will automatically make every basket bigger.
finding: For customers whose shipping fees fell under the new €20 free-shipping threshold, daily sales rose about 45% and order count about 44%, with no significant change in average order value. Return probability rose slightly overall, while 'filler' items added to reach the threshold (2.49% of purchases) were returned less often than regular items.
limitation: Working paper, not peer reviewed; one unnamed retailer and a before-and-after policy switch rather than a randomized test. The paper's own period description and some return statements are inconsistent, and the fee cut is mixed with the threshold, so it does not isolate threshold messaging such as progress bars.
measurement: Orders per visitor; return rate for items added to reach the threshold; average order value
method: Natural experiment using company data: in November 2017 an online retailer replaced category-based fixed shipping fees with one €2.95 fee and free shipping over €20; daily time-series regressions for sales, orders and order value, plus logit models for product returns
plain: When a big European shop switched to free delivery above a set spend, customers whose delivery got cheaper ordered much more often, but each basket did not get bigger. Returns rose slightly.
publisher: University of Groningen (SOM working paper 2021012-MARK; Hirche, Gijsenberg & Bijmolt)
sample: 26.21M orders, 83.79M items and 3.81M customers at one unnamed major European online retailer, July 2017 to June 2019

stat.text: rise in daily sales for customers whose fees fell after a switch to free shipping over €20 (26.21M orders at one European retailer, 2017–2019).

strengthWhy: Natural or quasi-experiment; not randomised.
title: Threshold free shipping: more orders, not bigger baskets

application: Check each product page and the cart show free-shipping status and any threshold near the buy button, with the remaining amount updated to the current cart.
do: Show free-delivery terms next to the buy button and say how much more the shopper needs to spend.
dont: Rely on a site-wide banner alone, or hide the threshold behind an asterisk.
finding: 32% of benchmarked sites state free shipping only in a site-wide banner or header, which test participants often overlooked; on one tested site 27% of participants missed or struggled to find the free-shipping information. Baymard advises placing it near the buy section, stating any threshold beside it, and telling shoppers how much more they need to spend.
limitation: Participant and benchmark counts are not given, the core research dates from 2017, and it does not measure whether a 'spend X more' message changes basket size or conversion.
measurement: Product-to-cart rate; share of testers who notice free-shipping terms; cart value distribution near the threshold
method: Product page usability testing (sessions on sites such as Crutchfield, Sears and Home Depot) plus Baymard's product page benchmark; abandonment figure from a separate checkout survey
plain: Many shops mention free delivery only in a strip across the top of the page, which people skim past. Put it next to the buy button, say what qualifies, and show how much more is needed.
sample: Not stated on page (participant counts and benchmark size not given)

stat.text: of e-commerce sites in Baymard's benchmark show free shipping only in a site-wide banner or header.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Free-shipping terms beside the buy button, not only in a banner

application: Measure saved-payment or express checkout adoption by customer cohort and compare repeat-purchase frequency against matched non-users before crediting it with uplift.
do: Let returning customers save payment and delivery details so they can buy in one step.
dont: Credit express checkout with extra sales without comparing similar customers who don't use it.
finding: In the 15 months after adopting one-click buying, matched customers' monthly purchases rose about 28.5%, orders placed about 43% and items bought about 36% compared with before, with no significant change in store purchases or returns. Estimated effects were positive for every customer but varied widely.
limitation: Customers chose to adopt, so unmeasured differences may remain despite matching; one retailer in Asia. It tests stored one-click buying, not wallet buttons such as Apple Pay or where they are placed.
measurement: Orders per customer per month; spend per customer; share of customers using saved or express payment
method: Quasi-experiment: customers who signed up for one-click buying were matched to similar non-adopters on propensity scores (rolling entry matching), then monthly spending, orders and items were compared before and after adoption; causal forests for differences between customers
plain: At one Asian retailer, customers who switched on one-click buying went on to order more often and spend more than similar customers who didn't. They weren't just moving purchases out of the shops.
publisher: Cornell University (Unal dissertation chapter 'Fewer Clicks, More Purchases'; published in Management Science, 2023, with Park)
sample: 977 adopters (806 matched pairs) drawn against about 17,200 non-adopters at one anonymised Asian retailer with online and offline channels; January 2016 to November 2018

stat.text: more orders per month from customers after adopting one-click buying (806 matched pairs at one Asian retailer, 2016–2018).

strengthWhy: Natural or quasi-experiment; not randomised.
title: One-click buying and later customer spending

application: Check the payment step offers at least one wallet or third-party method common in the target market, and that selecting it changes the primary button label.
do: Offer at least one popular wallet, and change the main button to 'Continue to PayPal' when it is picked.
dont: Hide payment choices in a dropdown or keep a 'Place order' label that misleads wallet users.
finding: In Baymard's 2023 survey, 11% of US shoppers had abandoned a checkout in the past three months because their preferred payment option was not offered, and 6% because their card was declined. It recommends at least one third-party option such as PayPal or Apple Pay, radio buttons or tabs instead of dropdowns, and relabelling the main button (for example 'Continue to PayPal') when one is chosen.
limitation: Survey reasons are self-reported; the article's '21% of sites' figure is defined inconsistently, and it does not cover express-checkout buttons on product or cart pages or their placement.
measurement: Payment-step abandonment; share of orders by payment method; recovery rate after card declines
method: Checkout usability testing on desktop and mobile, Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark, and a 2023 quantitative survey of US online shoppers on abandonment reasons
plain: Some shoppers only want to pay with a service like PayPal or Apple Pay, and others need a backup when their card is declined. Offer at least one, and make the main button say where it leads.
sample: Survey of 2,219 US online shoppers (2023); usability-test participant and benchmark site counts for this finding not stated

stat.text: of US online shoppers abandoned a checkout in the past three months because their preferred payment option was missing (Baymard survey of 2,219 shoppers, 2023).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.

application: Review cart and added-to-cart suggestions for a sample of baskets, removing unrelated items and ranking compatible accessories first with a reason label.
do: Show a few compatible add-ons, like the right battery, with a short reason label.
dont: Fill the basket with generic 'customers also bought' items or offers that don't fit the order.
finding: 52% of benchmarked desktop sites show cart or 'Added to cart' cross-sells that are irrelevant or based only on what other customers bought. In testing, even one unrelated suggestion made people distrust all of them, so Baymard advises fewer, labelled, compatible suggestions and offers matched to the order.
limitation: No participant or site counts are given and it does not measure attach rate or revenue; 2021 research.
measurement: Cross-sell click-through in cart; attach rate; cart-to-checkout rate
method: Large-scale checkout usability testing plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark
plain: Suggestions in the basket only help when they fit what is already in it. One unrelated item made testers ignore the rest, so show fewer, say why, and put must-have accessories first.
sample: Not stated on page (desktop benchmark size and participant counts not given)

stat.text: of desktop sites in Baymard's benchmark show cart cross-sells that are irrelevant or based only on other customers' purchases.

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.

application: List every pop-up and its trigger; remove any that fire on arrival or mid-task, and switch email capture to a non-modal prompt after meaningful engagement.
do: Ask for an email after someone has engaged, in a small box they can ignore.
dont: Throw a full-screen sign-up box at people the moment the page loads.
finding: Anna Kaley lists ten problematic pop-up patterns, including prompts shown before people have seen any content, email requests before any interaction, feedback requests in the middle of a task, and several pop-ups stacked at once. She advises waiting until the prompt is relevant, using smaller non-modal overlays, and offering something concrete in exchange for an email address.
limitation: Qualitative guidance with no measured sign-up or bounce data; it does not cover exit-intent timing, discount size or dismissal-button design.
measurement: Bounce rate on first page; email sign-up rate per session; pop-up dismissal rate
method: Expert guidance drawing on NN/g user research, one recent usability study and the author's log of pop-ups met over several weeks
plain: Pop-ups that appear before people have read anything, or in the middle of a task, mostly get closed straight away. Wait until the person has seen something useful, then ask in a smaller box with a real reason.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Timing pop-ups and email sign-up prompts

application: Tab through key templates and confirm every link, button and field shows a clearly visible focus style wherever the default outline has been removed.
do: Replace any removed outline with a clear, high-contrast focus style for keyboard users.
dont: Set the outline to none without adding another visible focus style.
finding: About 67% of pages explicitly remove the browser's default focus outline, which the chapter reports as up 14% from 2024 (it does not say whether points or relative), while only about a quarter of pages use :focus-visible (25% desktop, 24% mobile) to style focus for keyboard users.
limitation: Detects CSS that removes outlines, not whether a custom replacement focus style exists, so it overstates true failures; covers home and secondary pages only.
measurement: Controls with no visible focus indicator; templates removing the outline without a replacement; keyboard-only task completion
method: Automated analysis of CSS and Lighthouse audits on home and secondary pages in the HTTP Archive crawl
plain: When someone moves through a page with the Tab key, an outline shows where they are. About two in three pages switch that outline off, and only about a quarter use the newer way to show it to keyboard users.
sample: HTTP Archive 2025 crawl; the chapter says about 17 million sites are crawled each month (home and secondary pages); crawl month and page count not stated in the chapter

application: List every third-party script on key templates with its owner and purpose, and remove or defer any without a current business owner.
do: Keep a list of every outside script, who owns it and why, and remove the ones nobody needs.
dont: Let marketing tags pile up on checkout pages without anyone reviewing them.
finding: At least 90% of pages load one or more third parties. The median page makes 79 third-party requests on mobile and 83 on desktop, rising to 106 and 129 among the top 1,000 sites, with ad, analytics and CDN providers the most common categories.
limitation: Counts requests, not their performance cost; the chapter gives no blocking-time data, and this edition counts providers rather than domains, so some year-on-year comparisons are not like for like.
measurement: Third-party requests per page; third-party script bytes; p75 INP
method: Analysis of third-party requests in the HTTP Archive crawl; a third party is an entity other than the site owner whose resources appear on at least five unique pages
plain: Most web pages pull in code from other companies, such as ads and analytics. The typical mobile page makes 79 requests to these outside services before you count the site's own files.
sample: HTTP Archive 2025 crawl (crawl month not stated in the chapter); medians reported for all sites and for the top 1,000 sites, desktop and mobile

stat.text: third-party requests on the median mobile page (Web Almanac 2025 Third Parties chapter, HTTP Archive crawl).

title: How many third-party requests a typical page makes

application: On the signed-in order page, check for an expected delivery date, a status bar that includes pre-shipment stages, the carrier name, a linked tracking number, shipping history and a contents summary.
do: Show the expected delivery date, progress stages, courier and a clickable tracking number on the order page.
dont: Send shoppers to a courier site with no link back to their order.
finding: Half of respondents in Baymard's survey named order tracking as the most important account or self-service feature, yet 67% of test sites did not consistently give all key tracking details and 25% did not reliably show an expected delivery date. Participants mostly tracked orders to learn the arrival day, and were disoriented when sent to carrier pages with no route back to their order.
limitation: Sample sizes are not given, the percentages describe the sites used in testing rather than a stated benchmark, and the article does not measure effects on support contacts or repeat purchases.
measurement: 'Where is my order' contacts per order; Order-page visits that end on a carrier site; Share of orders showing an expected delivery date
method: Qualitative usability testing from Baymard's Accounts & Self-Service research, observing participants tracking orders on test sites, plus a quantitative survey for the importance figure
plain: After buying, people check their order mainly to find out when it will arrive. Show the delivery date, progress, courier and a working tracking link on your own site, not only on the courier's.
sample: Not stated on page (participant, test-site and survey counts not given)

application: Walk through starting a return while signed in: check for an online flow on your own site, an emailed label people can save, in-store returns shown beside postal ones, and an immediate status update with refund timing.
do: Let people start a return online, email them the label, and show 'Return pending' with the refund timeline.
dont: Make a pre-printed label the only way to return, with no status update afterwards.
finding: 54% of the 42 benchmarked sites had substantial UX problems in their returns flow, 30% offered no online return feature at all, and 55% did not update the order status once a return began. In Baymard's survey, 11% of users said an unsatisfactory returns policy alone made them abandon at least one order in the past quarter.
limitation: 2019 research with no survey sample size given; the 'up to 20%' customer-loss framing is the author's, exchanges are barely covered, and repeat-purchase effects are not measured.
measurement: Returns-related support contacts; Online return-flow completion rate; Repeat purchase rate after a return
method: Quantitative survey of online shoppers about returns, usability testing of accounts and self-service (including remote in-home sessions), and a benchmark rating complete returns flows
plain: Many big shops make returns awkward: no way to start one online, labels that must be printed on the spot, and no status update afterwards. Unsure customers end up calling support.
sample: Benchmark: 660 manually assigned ratings of the returns flows of the 42 largest ecommerce sites worldwide; survey and test participant counts not stated

stat.text: of the 42 largest ecommerce sites had substantial UX problems in their returns flow (Baymard benchmark, 2019).

application: Add an item on each product template and check that the cart badge updates and that a lasting confirmation lists the chosen options with View cart and Checkout actions.
do: Update the cart count and keep a confirmation showing the item, size and price until it is closed.
dont: Flash a brief 'Added' message that disappears before people can read it.
finding: Many sites left shoppers unsure whether an item had gone into the cart, or whether the right size and options were added; confirmation overlays that disappeared too quickly led some participants to add the same item twice and find duplicates at checkout. Page Laubheimer recommends a cart-count badge (ideally with the subtotal) plus a confirmation that stays until dismissed and shows the image, name, price, quantity and chosen options.
limitation: No participant counts or error rates are given, and the article neither compares cart drawers with full cart pages nor measures conversion.
measurement: Duplicate cart lines removed at checkout; Add-to-cart to checkout rate; Cart icon clicks after adding
method: Usability testing of ecommerce sites (a new round of testing plus earlier ecommerce research)
plain: When someone taps 'Add to bag', they need clear proof it worked and that the right size went in. Messages that flashed and vanished led testers to add items twice.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.

application: At the delivery step, check that shipping, store pickup and local delivery appear together with cost and timing, that 'pickup' and 'ship to store' are distinguished, and that the pickup store can be changed.
do: List shipping, store pickup and local delivery together, each with its cost and timing.
dont: Offer store pickup only on the product page, so it is missing at the delivery step.
finding: Half of benchmarked sites that offer several fulfilment methods leave some of them out of the selector where shoppers choose delivery. Testers who wanted store pickup or local delivery had to backtrack to the cart or product page, and some concluded the option was unavailable and abandoned.
limitation: No sample sizes are given; it does not measure how many orders shift to pickup or the conversion effect, and the survey figures it cites concern costs and speed in general rather than pickup.
measurement: Checkout exits at the delivery step; Share of orders using store pickup; Returns to the cart from checkout
method: Multiple rounds of qualitative checkout usability testing plus Baymard's e-commerce UX benchmark; abandonment figures from a separate quantitative survey
plain: If a shop offers store pickup but the delivery step lists only postal options, shoppers assume pickup isn't possible. Show every option side by side, with its cost and timing.

application: List every primary button on home and landing pages, rewrite generic labels to name the next step, and check that pricing and fees appear before any form or quiz.
do: Label main buttons with the next step, such as 'See plans and prices'.
dont: Use 'Get started' to send newcomers into a quiz or sign-up before they understand the offer.
finding: Aurora Harley and Kim Flaherty found a generic 'Get Started' button attracted people whatever their goal, then routed them into quizzes, surveys or account creation before they understood the offer; on one meal-delivery site, 6 of 8 users asked to learn about the service clicked it. They advise labels that state what happens next and showing key facts such as pricing before asking for details.
limitation: Examples are drawn from several studies without overall counts; it does not compare label variants statistically or measure conversion.
measurement: Drop-off on the first screen after the main button; First-click accuracy on landing-page tasks; Share of visitors seeing pricing before sign-up
method: Examples from NN/g usability studies of ecommerce and service sites, including an eyetracking study; no single study design reported
plain: A button that just says 'Get started' looks right for any goal, so people click it and land in quizzes or sign-up forms before learning what's on offer. Say what the button actually does.
sample: Not stated overall; in one example task 8 users were asked to learn about a meal-delivery service

stat.text: users asked to learn about a meal-delivery service clicked 'Get Started' instead (NN/g usability study example).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Vague 'Get started' buttons pull people off course

application: Audit sign-up, subscription and checkout flows for hidden terms, obstruction, trick wording and preselected options first, since these moved choices most, and remove fake countdown timers.
do: Show the full cost and a plain 'No thanks' option as clearly as 'Yes'.
dont: Hide costs, block the way out, or add a fake countdown to push sign-ups.
finding: Acceptance of the plan rose from 11.3% with a neutral interface to 25.8% with mild and 41.9% with aggressive dark patterns, and the price level made no significant difference. Tested one by one, hidden information roughly doubled acceptance (14.8% to 30.1%), while a scarcity message with a one-minute countdown timer had no significant effect.
limitation: A simulated sign-up for a fictitious service in an online panel, not live purchases; only one countdown-timer design was tested, so it does not show scarcity cues never work. Mild patterns produced little backlash, so complaint data alone may not reveal them.
measurement: Complaints mentioning unexpected charges; Opt-in rate under a neutral design versus the current one; Cancellations within the first billing cycle
method: Two online experiments (the first pre-registered): participants were told they were enrolled in a fictitious paid identity-theft protection plan and saw a neutral, mild or aggressive dark-pattern interface (study 1); a factorial design then isolated individual patterns such as hidden information, social proof, scarcity, confirmshaming, defaults and obstruction (study 2)
plain: In a large online experiment, tricky designs more than tripled how many people signed up for a paid plan. Hiding key terms worked strongly, while a countdown timer made no real difference.
publisher: Journal of Legal Analysis (Oxford University Press; Luguri & Strahilevitz)
sample: Study 1: 1,963 participants; Study 2: 3,777 participants; both census-weighted samples of American adults recruited online

stat.text: accepted a paid plan when shown aggressive dark patterns, versus 11.3% with a neutral design (Luguri & Strahilevitz, 1,963-person US experiment).
