application: Compare a client's key mobile templates with these medians, starting with image bytes and unused JavaScript on category and product pages.
do: Set a size budget for each page type and trim images and unused code first.
dont: Add heavy images, video or scripts without checking what the page already weighs.
finding: The median mobile page transfers 2,164 KB (2,412 KB on desktop) across 72 requests, with images the largest component at 911 KB on mobile. The median mobile page carries 646 KB of compressed JavaScript, and Lighthouse finds a median of 251 KB of unused JavaScript (measured uncompressed).
limitation: Medians across all crawled pages, not ecommerce specifically; bytes are not the same as speed, and the chapter is internally inconsistent on mobile home-page weight, so home-page figures are left out here.
measurement: p75 LCP (mobile); Total transfer size per template (mobile); Unused JavaScript bytes per page
method: Analysis of bytes transferred and requests per page in the HTTP Archive crawl (home and inner pages, desktop and mobile); JavaScript sizes are compressed, while unused-JavaScript figures come from Lighthouse and are uncompressed
plain: The typical web page on a phone now downloads just over 2 MB before it's complete, mostly images, and carries a sizeable chunk of code it never uses.
sample: HTTP Archive 2025 crawl of millions of sites (count not given in this chapter; other 2025 chapters cite 16.2M sites); trend data runs to July 2025

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: How heavy a typical web page is in 2025

application: Run a cookie scan of key templates, list every third-party cookie with its owner and purpose, and confirm none are set before the visitor has answered the consent banner.
do: Keep a list of every outside company setting cookies, and block them until the visitor agrees.
dont: Let ad and analytics tags set cookies before the cookie banner has been answered.
finding: Of cookies set across the top million sites, 59% on desktop and 60% on mobile were third-party, rising to 78% among the top 1,000 sites on desktop. DoubleClick set cookies on more than a third of sites, and the median cookie was set to expire after 364 days (desktop).
limitation: Counts what a crawler sees without logging in or consenting; shares are of cookies rather than sites, and it says nothing about whether consent was valid or how visitors feel about tracking.
measurement: Third-party cookies set before consent; Third-party cookie-setting domains per page; Cookie expiry length
method: Analysis of cookies set during the HTTP Archive crawl of the top one million sites by Chrome UX Report rank, on desktop and mobile; shares are of cookies, not of sites
plain: Most cookies placed by popular websites come from other companies, such as ad and analytics firms, and the typical cookie is set to last about a year.

application: Use the national online share as context when sizing a client's channel mix, and compare their own year-on-year online growth with the 12.2% national figure before claiming outperformance.
do: Compare a client's online growth with the national figure before calling it strong or weak.
dont: Quote this national share as proof that any single store's site is performing well or badly.
finding: US retail e-commerce sales were an estimated $340.2 billion in Q2 2026 (seasonally adjusted), 17.1% of total retail sales. That was up 3.8% (±0.4%) on Q1 2026 and 12.2% (±0.9%) on Q2 2025, while total retail grew 2.9% on the quarter.
limitation: A national aggregate across all retail categories, not adjusted for inflation; it says nothing about conversion or UX. The page notes these figures will be revised in the Q3 2026 release due 19 November 2026.
measurement: Online share of client revenue; Year-on-year online revenue growth; Online vs total sales growth gap
method: Quarterly estimate from the Census Bureau's retail trade surveys; seasonally adjusted but not adjusted for price changes; percentages carry stated margins of error
plain: About one in every six dollars Americans spent in shops in spring 2026 was spent online, and online spending grew much faster than shopping overall.

application: Audit where low-stock messages appear; limit them to genuinely low stock, and A/B test removing them on high-traffic items rather than assuming they lift sales.
do: Show stock warnings only when stock is truly low, and test whether they help.
dont: Add 'only a few left' labels everywhere on the assumption that urgency always sells.
finding: When the retailer showed a message that five or fewer units were left, average daily sales of those items fell by 17.60%. A 1% price cut raised average daily sales by about 3%, so discounts did far more than scarcity messages to move stock.
limitation: One retailer and product range, non-randomised before/after design; it measures sales, not customer trust or returns, and may not generalise to fashion or flash-sale contexts.
measurement: Daily units sold per SKU; Conversion rate on products showing low-stock messages; Add-to-cart rate
method: Econometric analysis of price and sales data from one online retailer, comparing sales before and after it began showing a low-stock message, across several restocking cycles
plain: One shop found that telling people only a few were left made those items sell less per day, not more. A small price cut did much more to shift stock.
publisher: Journal of Operations Management (Park, Rabinovich, Tang & Yin)
sample: Durable consumer-goods SKUs at one US online retailer; message shown when stock fell below 6 units (SSRN version: 199 items, Aug 2014–Jan 2016)

stat.text: drop in average daily sales after low-stock messages appeared (one US online retailer, Journal of Operations Management, 2020).

strengthWhy: Natural or quasi-experiment; not randomised.
title: Low-stock messages lowered daily sales at one retailer

application: Before removing or redesigning a 'you may also like' module, measure repeat visits and long-run revenue per visitor, not just same-session sales.
do: Judge recommendation changes on repeat visits and spending over weeks, not one session.
dont: Remove a recommendation strip because it shows no same-day sales lift.
finding: Recommendations shifted purchases toward recommended items and away from others, so short-run total sales did not necessarily rise. But switching recommendations off lowered long-run sales because shoppers became less loyal; returning visitors who lost them once were more likely to defect.
limitation: Abstract only on this page: no effect sizes, sample or product category; one retailer and one recommender type, so results may differ elsewhere.
measurement: Return-visit rate; Long-run revenue per visitor; Recommended-item click-through
method: Randomised field experiment switching an item-based collaborative-filtering recommender on or off for visitors to an online retailer
plain: In a real shop test, product suggestions didn't always raise sales on the day. But people who lost them came back less often, so the shop sold less over time.
publisher: MIS Quarterly (Sun, Chen, Zheng, Su & Zhang)
sample: Not stated on page (one online retailer; abstract gives no visitor counts)
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Field experiment: switching off recommendations cost loyalty

application: Score the homepage against the five principles: logo link home, a plain tagline, concrete product examples, specific link labels, and no autoplaying media or non-required pop-ups.
do: Show real products and a one-line tagline that says what you sell.
dont: Fill the homepage with seasonal promos, autoplay video and labels like 'Learn more'.
finding: NN/g distils homepage design into five principles: make the homepage easy to return to, say who you are and what you offer, show real examples of content rather than vague category labels, use specific labels and a clear hierarchy for top tasks, and keep it simple with little motion and no needless pop-ups.
limitation: Guidance with no new study or data; it does not rank the principles or measure their effect on sales.
measurement: Homepage bounce rate; Click-through to category or product pages; First-click success on top tasks
method: Expert guidance applying NN/g's earlier 113 homepage guidelines, illustrated with annotated real homepages
plain: A homepage should quickly tell visitors what the shop sells by showing real examples, point clearly to the main tasks, and avoid distracting motion or pop-ups.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.

limitation: Benchmark size and participant numbers not given; it does not measure revenue impact, and gift cards themselves are not covered in detail.

application: On listings with sets, bundles or multipacks, check that each tile states contents and quantities in the title, subtitle or a consistent attribute line.
do: Write the contents on the tile, like 'Table + 4 chairs'.
dont: Label bundles only 'Dining set' and leave shoppers to count items in the photo.
finding: Test participants often could not tell what a set or bundle contained or how many of each item, so they counted items in photos, bounced between list and product pages, or bought separate items instead. Baymard recommends listing contents and quantities in the list item itself.
limitation: Qualitative findings from furniture and home-decor testing, with no sample size or prevalence figure; effect on sales is not measured.
measurement: List-to-product-page bounce-backs on bundle items; Bundle add-to-cart rate; Bundle return rate
method: Large-scale usability testing of furniture and home-decor sites, with participants browsing product lists, plus Baymard's UX benchmark
plain: When a listing says 'dining set' without saying what's in it, shoppers have to count chairs in the photo or open every product. Spell out the contents and numbers on the tile.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.

application: Review the pricing table: explain each feature in plain words (tooltip or link), avoid hiding rows behind 'View more', and group the roughly 40 features into scannable sections.
do: Add a short plain-English explanation to every feature in the plan table.
dont: Hide half the features behind 'View more' or list them in unexplained jargon.
finding: Nearly every benchmarked SaaS site has a pricing page with a plan comparison table, and 44% performed mediocre or worse on its usability. Common problems were dense text, unexplained feature jargon (20% of sites) and features hidden behind 'View more' (25%); plan tables average around 40 features.
limitation: No site counts per figure or participant numbers; it does not measure sign-up or upgrade impact.
measurement: Pricing page to sign-up rate; Plan-selection time in testing; Feature tooltip open rate
method: Large-scale usability testing of SaaS websites plus Baymard's SaaS UX benchmark
plain: Software price pages usually compare plans in a big table. People struggle when features use insider terms with no explanation or are hidden behind 'View more'.

application: Before swapping pagination for infinite scroll on category or search pages, run it as an A/B test tracking items viewed, item clicks and purchases from listings, and test its assumptions (more items, faster loading) separately.
do: Test infinite scroll against numbered pages before rolling it out to listing pages.
dont: Assume that loading more products at once will lead to more purchases.
finding: When Etsy added infinite scroll to search results, the test group saw and clicked fewer items, saved fewer favourites and bought fewer items from search than the control group; total purchases held steady because people shifted away from search. Follow-up tests found more results per page barely changed item-page visits and did not lift purchases, and slowing search down did not measurably change purchases.
limitation: One marketplace's search results, an older experiment reported without percentages, sample size or dates; the author says too many changes were bundled to isolate the cause and that infinite scroll may suit other sites.
measurement: Listing-to-item click rate; Purchases from search and listing pages; Items viewed per listing session
method: Live controlled experiment on Etsy search results (infinite scroll vs the paged control), followed by experiments varying results per page and adding artificial delay, as described by an Etsy engineer
plain: Etsy tried endless scrolling on its search results, expecting people to browse more. In the test, people actually clicked and bought fewer items from search, so the team removed it.
sample: Not stated on page (Etsy search users; experiment size, duration and dates not given)
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Etsy's infinite scroll test: fewer purchases from search

application: Run a first-click test on your settings or account pages using the most common tasks; put the most-searched settings in a prominent group and give collapsible sections descriptive, clickable titles.
do: Group the most-used settings at the top under descriptive, clickable section titles.
dont: Bury common settings inside collapsed sections with vague labels.
finding: After GitLab moved the most-used settings into a prominent section, made expandable section labels more descriptive and made section titles clickable, correct first clicks rose from 34% to 97% and from 49% to 92% on two of three tasks (the third stayed at 77–78%). Confidence and ease ratings improved overall, but time to click got longer on two tasks.
limitation: Static designs, self-selected community participants, unequal group sizes and no significance tests; one product's group settings only; time to answer worsened on two tasks without explanation.
measurement: First-click success rate; Time to first click; Post-task confidence rating
method: Two remote first-click tests on static designs (original vs redesigned group settings page), three findability tasks each, followed by 1–5 ease and confidence ratings
plain: GitLab reorganised its settings page so the most-used options sat up front under clearer headings. In a click test, far more people found the right setting on their first try in two of three tasks.
sample: 389 participants (original) and 266 (redesign), self-selected via Twitter and GitLab's research mailing list; test dates not stated

stat.text: of participants clicked the right place for one settings task after GitLab's redesign, up from 34% (first-click tests with 389 and 266 people).

application: Audit your app's notification types: keep alerts about messages or events that involve the person, and cut, bundle or make optional generic and promotional pushes.
do: Send alerts only about things that directly involve the person, like a reply or an order update.
dont: Send frequent generic promotional pushes and expect people to open them.
finding: The median person received 56 notifications a day, mostly from messaging apps. Individual and group messages led to the app being opened before removal 63.67% and 65.81% of the time, versus 26.55% for social, 16.19% for other (non-social) apps and 15.47% for email; non-social notifications were often removed quickly.
limitation: Android users in one country in 2016; 'opened the app' misses replies made from the notification itself or another device, and a removal can mean dismissed or timed out. It does not test notification wording or timing.
measurement: Notification open rate by type; Notification opt-out rate; Notifications sent per user per day
method: In-the-wild logging study: a custom Android app recorded when each notification was posted and removed, and whether its app was opened first
plain: People get dozens of phone alerts a day. They open the app for most personal messages, but most other alerts, like app updates or email, are cleared without the app being opened.
publisher: Telefonica Research & University of Macedonia (MobileHCI '18, ACM)
sample: 278 Android users in Spain (recruited to match national age and gender split), about 26.6 days each on average, April–July 2016; 794,525 notifications

stat.text: notifications a day for the median person, logged across 278 Android users in Spain (794,525 notifications, 2016).

strengthWhy: Published study, but observational or correlational.

application: Move the notification permission request out of first launch to after a key moment (e.g. first order), precede it with a screen explaining what alerts contain, and add notification preferences to in-app settings.
do: Ask for notification permission after a useful moment, explaining what the alerts will contain.
dont: Show the system notification prompt on first launch with no explanation.
finding: In NN/g's usability studies people usually turned down notification requests straight away. NN/g advises asking only after people have experienced the app's value, saying what the alerts will contain, sending fewer and combining bursts, keeping alerts personally relevant, and offering notification preferences inside the app's own settings.
limitation: Qualitative guidance from 2018 with no participant numbers; it does not measure opt-in rates, and current operating systems handle permission prompts and grouping differently.
measurement: Notification permission opt-in rate; Notification opt-out rate; Push open rate
method: Expert guidance informed by NN/g usability studies and critiques of named apps
plain: Phones let an app ask 'Allow notifications?' and people tend to say no if it's asked the moment the app opens. Ask once they've seen why it's useful, and say what you'll send.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.

application: In dashboards and admin tables, check that column headers and the first column stay visible while scrolling, active filters are flagged, and editing doesn't open a modal that hides other rows.
do: Freeze the header row and a readable first column when a table is bigger than the screen.
dont: Open an editing pop-up that covers the rows people need to check.
finding: Large data tables should support four jobs: finding records, comparing data, viewing or editing one row, and acting on records. Guidelines include a human-readable first column (not an auto ID), freezing the header row and first column on big tables, striping or hover highlighting, easy column hiding and reordering with visible indicators, and editing in non-modal panels rather than pop-ups that cover nearby rows.
limitation: No statistics or participant numbers; aimed at complex workplace tables, not ecommerce comparison tables.
measurement: Time to find a record; Task success comparing values; Editing errors
method: Expert guidance drawing on usability-testing observations of workplace data tables
plain: Big tables in admin tools must help people find, compare and change rows. Start each row with a readable name, keep column titles in view while scrolling, and edit beside the table rather than over it.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Data tables that let people find, compare and edit

application: Audit the confirmation page: order summary, delivery date and email note first, then test one post-purchase extra such as password-only account creation or an add-to-order cross-sell.
do: Show the order summary, delivery date and email note first, then one optional extra like account creation.
dont: Push the order details aside for promotions, or pre-tick a newsletter box.
finding: The order confirmation page is often a dead end, yet it can carry extras that would clutter checkout: relevant cross-sells added to the existing order, an opt-in (never pre-ticked) newsletter sign-up, account creation needing only a password, product guides, app promotion and one-tap surveys. These should sit below the core content: order summary, expected delivery date and a note that a confirmation email was sent.
limitation: No statistics, participant counts or measured impact; examples are named sites, and Baymard advises testing which additions suit each industry.
measurement: Post-purchase account creation rate; Newsletter opt-in rate on confirmation page; Add-to-order rate
method: Large-scale usability testing and Baymard's benchmark case studies (details not given on the page)
plain: After paying, people land on a 'thank you' page and usually leave. Confirm the order clearly first; then it's a calm moment to offer an account that needs just a password, or a relevant add-on.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.

application: On large category pages, add 2–3 category-specific filter buttons above the products (a scrollable row on mobile), make them apply a real filter with match counts, and keep them in the main filter panel too.
do: Show two or three category-relevant filter buttons above the product list, with match counts.
dont: Hide every filter behind a single 'Filter' button on mobile.
finding: In testing, most people's first move on a product list was to look for filters. Showing a few industry-relevant filters above the list (as well as in the usual filter panel) helps people narrow long lists faster, especially on mobile where filters are otherwise hidden; 61% of benchmarked sites show no filters above the product list.
limitation: No participant or site counts; it does not measure conversion, and promoted filters don't fix a weak category structure.
measurement: Filter use rate on listing pages; Listing-to-product click rate; Time to first product click
method: Large-scale usability testing (including travel accommodation and European sites) plus Baymard's ecommerce UX benchmark
plain: On a long product list, people look for a way to narrow it before anything else. Put a few useful filters right above the products, so phone shoppers don't have to open a hidden filter menu.
sample: Not stated on page (participant counts and benchmark size for this figure not given)

application: In AI chat features, replace generic starter prompts with task-specific examples for new users and add a few follow-up suggestions under each answer, placed where people will notice them.
do: Show suggested follow-up questions right under each answer, based on the conversation so far.
dont: Show everyone the same generic starter prompts, far from the input box.
finding: Prompt suggestions help people past an empty chat box, cut typing and show what an AI tool can do, but users ignore them when they're badly placed or unhelpful. NN/g separates use-case examples (for new users), autocomplete (for speed) and follow-up questions after an answer, which currently seem most useful because they fit the conversation.
limitation: No participant numbers or usage data; based on one study described only briefly, and it does not measure whether suggestions improve task outcomes.
measurement: Prompt suggestion click rate; Messages per session; Sessions abandoned at the empty prompt
method: Expert guidance informed by an NN/g study of generative AI tools (study details not given)
plain: An empty chat box leaves new users unsure what to ask an AI assistant. Specific example prompts, and suggested follow-up questions after each answer, help, but people skip vague or badly placed ones.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Prompt suggestions that help people use AI chat

application: Audit any auto-advancing video, carousel or next-episode countdown and test a version that waits for an explicit tap to continue.
do: Ask people to tap to start the next video, or let them easily turn autoplay off.
dont: Start the next video automatically with no clear way to switch that off.
finding: Compared with the control group and their own six-month baseline, people who turned autoplay off watched about 21 minutes less per day and had sessions about 17.6 minutes shorter; gaps between sessions did not change. About half planned to switch autoplay back on afterwards.
limitation: Small US-only sample over under three weeks; playback logs don't show attention, and the effect on satisfaction or long-term retention was not tested. The linked page is the preprint version.
measurement: Average session length; daily watch time; share of next plays started by a tap
method: Controlled field experiment: treatment group turned autoplay off, control kept it on; viewing logs from Netflix data requests compared with each person's six-month baseline, plus pre/post surveys; June–August 2023
plain: When people turned off the feature that starts the next episode by itself, they watched about 21 minutes less per day. Their viewing sessions got shorter because each new episode needed a real choice.
publisher: University of Chicago (Schaffner, Chetty et al.), ACM CSCW
sample: 76 US Netflix users recruited via Prolific (38 per group), 10–17 days each

application: Review what happens when nobody acts after warnings, consent screens and countdowns, and make the safer or user-protective outcome the default.
do: Make the protective choice happen by default when someone doesn't respond to a warning.
dont: Let warned content play automatically after a short countdown.
finding: After a simple warning, just under one in four participants skipped potentially harmful clips. When the clip started on its own after a five-second pause with no action, only 16% skipped, while auto-skipping after the same pause raised skipping to 48%.
limitation: A mock platform where people knew they were being studied; it tests one warning flow, not commercial outcomes, and Ofcom calls its explanation of the differences not conclusive.
measurement: Share of warned clips skipped; share of outcomes left to the default; warning recall
method: Randomised online experiment on a mock video-sharing platform; six clips in random order, warning before each potentially harmful clip, with baseline, autoskip and autoplay conditions triggered by a five-second pause with no action
plain: Whatever happens when nobody taps decides what most people end up doing. On a test video site, many more people skipped a warned clip when skipping was automatic than when it played automatically.
sample: 2,800 adults (country of panel not stated in the blog)

stat.text: of participants skipped a warned clip when it autoplayed, versus 48% when it auto-skipped (Ofcom experiment, 2,800 adults).

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.

application: When adding an express or wallet payment option, offer it beside the standard checkout and A/B test completion rather than routing every buyer into it.
do: Offer express payment as an extra button beside the normal checkout, then test completion.
dont: Push every shopper into a new payment screen they have never seen.
finding: Sending buyers to the browser's Payment Request sheet instead of the regular checkout lowered checkout completion by an average 7% (standard error ±1%), and about 60% of buyers left the sheet without touching the shipping details. Shopify put the drop largely down to buyers being unfamiliar with the sheet.

method: Randomised 50/50 A/B test: eligible buyers clicking checkout in the cart went either to the regular checkout or to the browser's Payment Request sheet; Chrome only
plain: When one shop platform swapped its normal checkout for an unfamiliar browser payment screen, fewer shoppers finished buying, and most left that screen without filling anything in.
sample: 30 merchants, about 5% of their traffic, over two months in 2018; peak around 15,000 payment-sheet opens per week

stat.text: of buyers left the browser payment sheet without entering shipping details (Shopify test, 30 merchants, 2018).

application: Before quoting CrUX or PageSpeed field data in an audit, check what share of the site's traffic comes from iPhones, in-app browsers and non-Chrome browsers; if large, add your own real-user monitoring.
do: Compare your traffic mix with who CrUX covers, and add your own speed tracking if many visitors are missing.
dont: Treat a site's CrUX score as the experience of every visitor.
finding: The Chrome UX Report (CrUX) only includes visits from Chrome users who share usage statistics and sync history without a passphrase, on desktop or Android; Chrome on iOS, Android WebView apps and other Chromium browsers such as Edge are excluded. Pages must be publicly indexable and above an undisclosed popularity threshold, and query strings are stripped so URL variants are grouped.
limitation: Chrome does not publish the share of users who meet the criteria or the popularity threshold; this page does not state the collection window or the Core Web Vitals thresholds.
measurement: Share of sessions from browsers CrUX excludes; share of sessions covered by field speed data; gap between CrUX and own real-user LCP
method: Real-user field data from eligible Chrome users, aggregated into histograms with small random noise added
plain: Google's public speed data, the Chrome UX Report, only counts some visitors: Chrome users on computers and Android phones who share usage statistics. iPhone visitors and in-app browsers are missing, so scores may not match your audience.
sample: Chrome users who enable usage statistics and sync history without a passphrase, on Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, Linux and Android; origins and pages above an undisclosed visitor threshold
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Who is missing from Chrome's public speed data

application: Check that every gift card and e-gift page states expiry and any fees before payment, and that e-gift emails or cards carry the required disclosures.
date: Current regulation; applies to cards sold from 2010-08-22
do: Show the gift card's expiry and any fee terms on the product page, before payment.
dont: Hide expiry dates or inactivity fees in terms that appear only after purchase.
finding: Under US Regulation E (12 CFR 1005.20), gift card funds must last at least five years from issue or the last load; dormancy, inactivity or service fees are allowed only after 12 months with no activity, at most one per month, and must be stated on the card. Fee and expiry terms must be disclosed before purchase, including online sales and emailed gift codes.
limitation: US federal rule only (shown as the current regulation); state laws can be stricter and other countries differ, and loyalty, promotional and some other cards are excluded from most rules. It sets fee, expiry and disclosure terms, not page design. Not legal advice.
measurement: Gift card pages showing expiry and fee terms before payment; gift card support contacts about expiry or fees; e-gift messages carrying required disclosures
method: Not applicable (regulation)
plain: In the US, money on a gift card must stay usable for at least five years, and any fee for not using it has to be shown to the buyer before they pay.
strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: US gift card rules: five-year funds and upfront fee terms

application: Audit sign-up and checkout forms for required last-name fields, first/last labels, length caps and character rules that reject apostrophes, hyphens or non-Latin letters.
do: Use one 'Full name' field that accepts spaces, hyphens, apostrophes and non-Latin letters.
dont: Make 'Last name' required or reject names that contain apostrophes or hyphens.
finding: W3C's internationalisation guidance favours a single full-name field where possible, not requiring a family name because many people have only one name, and avoiding 'first/last name' labels because many people write their family name first. It also advises accepting spaces, hyphens and apostrophes, keeping the case people type, not capping name length, and asking separately what to call someone.
limitation: Expert guidance with no user-testing data and no date on the page; separate fields may still be needed for legal, payment or postal systems.
measurement: Name field validation error rate; junk entries such as '.' in name fields; form completion rate
method: Not stated
plain: Forms built around 'first name, last name' break for many people: some write their family name first, and some have only one name. One 'Full name' box fits almost everyone.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Name fields that work for names around the world

application: Run each form through a browser translation tool and list any label, hint or instruction that stays untranslated, especially text held only in aria-label.
do: Write every label, hint and instruction as visible text and set the page language.
dont: Put instructions people need only in hidden aria-label text.
finding: web.dev advises keeping all form text visible in the page's HTML so translation tools can handle it, and avoiding aria-label since a lot of translation tools skip it. It also recommends setting lang and dir on the html element, linking translated versions with hreflang alternates, and using CSS logical properties so spacing stays correct in right-to-left layouts.
limitation: 2021 implementation guidance with no test data; translation tool behaviour varies and may have changed, and the page does not cover postal codes or phone numbers.
measurement: Form strings held only in aria-label; pages with lang set; form completion rate in translated sessions
method: Not stated
plain: Many visitors use their browser's translate button. Words tucked away in hidden labels are often left untranslated, so keep form wording as visible text on the page and declare the page's language.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Making forms work with browser translation

application: Audit product, homepage and help videos for autoplay with sound, missing length on the thumbnail, missing captions or transcript, and dead-end endings.
do: Show the video's length on the thumbnail and wait for a tap before playing.
dont: Autoplay video with sound as soon as the page opens.
finding: Video or audio should not start without the person's consent; autoplaying media confuses and distracts, and people's first reaction is often to mute or pause. People need to play, pause, replay, mute and change the volume, see a video's length before committing, get captions and a transcript, and find related links at the end rather than a dead end.
limitation: 2014 qualitative guidance with no participant numbers or measures; it does not test muted looping product clips or modern streaming players.
measurement: Video start rate from a tap; video completion rate; share of plays paused or muted straight away
method: Observations from NN/g usability testing; no study design or participant count stated
plain: Videos that start by themselves surprise people, and their first move is often to hunt for pause or mute. Show how long a video is, let people control it, and add captions.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Video players people can control

application: Pick a high-traffic landing template, ship server-rendered critical HTML and properly sized hero images to half of traffic, and compare field LCP and conversion against the current version.
do: Test speed fixes like resized hero images against the current page with real traffic.
dont: Judge a speed fix only by lab scores without measuring what real visitors do.
finding: Vodafone's optimised landing page reached LCP in 5.7s versus 8.3s for the original (31% better); the optimised version saw 8% more total sales, a 15% higher lead-to-visit rate and an 11% higher cart-to-visit rate.
limitation: One landing page from one company, with no significance, duration or absolute figures reported; it does not say which change drove the gain, and another load metric (DOMContentLoaded) got slower.
measurement: LCP (field, 75th percentile); lead-to-visit rate; cart-to-visit rate
method: A/B test of two landing-page versions that looked and worked the same; version A got Web Vitals optimisations (server-side rendering, less render-blocking JavaScript, resized and optimised images); LCP measured on real sessions
plain: Vodafone made one landing page show its main content faster, while keeping it looking the same, and tested it against the old one. The faster version showed its main content in 5.7 seconds instead of 8.3 and sold more.
sample: Paid-media traffic split 50/50; about 100K clicks and 34K visits per day to each version; test length not stated

stat.text: more total sales on Vodafone's faster landing page in a 50/50 A/B test (about 34K visits a day per version).

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Vodafone A/B test: faster main content, more sales

visual.note: Illustration. Times are the measured LCP values from the case study; page content is a made-up example.

application: Remove any notification permission request that fires on page load; offer an in-page 'Get alerts' control and only call the browser prompt after someone chooses it.
do: Let visitors choose alerts from a button on the page before the browser asks.
dont: Fire the browser's notification request the moment someone lands.
finding: Notification requests made up 74% of all permission prompts in Chrome yet had the lowest grant rate, 12% on desktop and 23% on Android, with most people blocking or ignoring them. A quieter prompt cut unnecessary prompt actions by up to 30% while grant rates fell by under 5%.
limitation: Google researchers evaluating Chrome's own prompt; it measures browser-level prompts across all sites, not how a specific site's timing or pre-prompt changes opt-in, and covers Chrome only.
measurement: Notification permission grant rate; prompt block/ignore rate; push subscribers per 1,000 visitors
method: Two large-scale studies: analysis of Chrome telemetry on how people respond to notification permission prompts, then an A/B test of a quieter prompt design and its activation logic
plain: When a website asks 'Allow notifications?', most people block or ignore it. In Chrome these requests are the most common permission pop-up and the least accepted.
publisher: USENIX Security Symposium 2021 (Bilogrevic et al., Google)
sample: More than 300M Chrome users across both studies; the A/B test covered 40M+ users, 100M+ prompts and 70K+ websites

stat.text: of desktop notification permission prompts were granted (23% on Android), in Chrome data from over 300M users (USENIX Security 2021).

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Chrome data: people mostly refuse website notification requests

application: Crawl key templates (home, category, product, content) and flag any page with no h1 or an empty one, then check the h1 text names what the page is about.
do: Give every page one main heading that names what it is about.
dont: Leave the main heading empty or style plain text to look like one.
finding: An h1 heading was present on 71% of desktop and 70% of mobile pages, but a non-empty h1 appeared on only 66% of pages on both; h2 was the most used heading level, at 72% of desktop and 71% of mobile pages.
limitation: Counts whether heading tags exist, not whether the text is meaningful or the heading order is logical; it does not link headings to search ranking or task success.
measurement: Templates with a non-empty, descriptive h1; screen reader heading-navigation success; pages with skipped heading levels
method: Automated analysis of page markup in the HTTP Archive crawl (with Lighthouse and CrUX data elsewhere in the chapter)
plain: A page's main heading tells readers, and people using a screen reader, what the page is about. Across millions of sites crawled in 2025, only 66% of pages had a main heading with text in it.
sample: HTTP Archive 2025 crawl: 16.2M websites (15.4M mobile, 12.2M desktop), July 2025 crawl unless a chapter says otherwise; heading figures not split by home or secondary page

stat.text: of pages had a non-empty h1 main heading (Web Almanac 2025 SEO chapter, HTTP Archive crawl of 16.2M websites).

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: A third of pages lack a filled-in main heading

application: Report each key template's field LCP, INP and CLS at the 75th percentile against these thresholds, separately for mobile and desktop.
do: Judge speed by the 75th-percentile visit from real users on each device.
dont: Report only the average or a single fast lab test as proof of speed.
finding: A page counts as good when at least 75% of its visits have LCP of 2.5s or less, INP of 200ms or less and CLS of 0.1 or less; poor starts above 4s, 500ms and 0.25. Each good threshold had to match perception research and be reached by at least 10% of origins in CrUX.
limitation: The cut-offs are Google's judgement calls balancing quality and achievability; CLS had no prior research behind it, and passing them does not show any effect on conversion.
measurement: Share of templates passing all three at p75; LCP p75; INP p75
method: Thresholds chosen against published research on response-time perception plus Chrome UX Report (CrUX) data on how many origins could reach them; assessed at the 75th percentile of page views; CLS set from internal testing
plain: Google's speed pass marks judge the slower visits too: a page passes only if three in four visits are quick enough. The limits were set from research on what feels fast and what real sites could manage.
sample: CrUX origin data from April 2020 (LCP, CLS) and May 2022 (INP); origin counts not stated
strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: How Google set the Core Web Vitals pass marks

application: List every first-run tour and popover; replace launch-time card decks with tips shown when a feature is first used, add a place to re-open help, and drop tips for standard icons.
do: Show a short tip next to a feature the first time someone uses it.
dont: Make people swipe through a welcome tour before they can start.
finding: Upfront walkthroughs such as card decks at launch interrupt people who want to start, are often skipped, and are hard to remember out of context. NN/g favours help triggered by what the person is doing, easy to dismiss and find again, and skipped entirely for familiar controls; walkthroughs can suit truly novel interactions, ideally hands-on.
limitation: Opinion piece with no participant counts or measured outcomes; it does not compare retention or activation, and contextual help depends on reading intent correctly.
measurement: Tour skip rate; first core action completion in first session; help re-open rate
method: Expert opinion article drawing on the author's experience and earlier NN/g research; no study method stated
plain: Welcome tours that show several cards before you start get skipped and forgotten. Short tips that appear when you reach a feature work better, as long as they're easy to close and find again.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Contextual tips beat upfront app tours

visual.note: Illustration. Wording is a made-up example.

application: On each template, count buttons styled as primary; keep one for the main next step, restyle the rest as secondary or links, and rewrite vague labels to name the action.
do: Style only the main next step as the primary button and label it with the action.
dont: Give three buttons the same bold style with vague labels like Submit or OK.
finding: GOV.UK uses its main (primary) button style for the single main action on a page and advises against more than one, because several main buttons weaken each other; too many secondary buttons make the next step unclear. Labels should be sentence case and say what happens, and GOV.UK reports its green start buttons improved click-through.
limitation: Built for government services, with no published data on the one-primary rule; the click-through claim for green start buttons gives no figures or method.
measurement: Primary buttons per template; first-click success on the main action; form step completion rate
method: Design-system guidance; mentions GOV.UK testing of start-button colour without giving a method
plain: When a page has one button that clearly stands out and says what it does, people know what to press next. Several equally bold buttons make each one weaker.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: One main button per page

visual.cap: A shopper finishes entering an address

application: Load list, product and search pages on a phone and remove or shrink any app-install banner that covers controls, reappears after closing, or shows outside the home page or order confirmation.
do: Promote the app on the order confirmation page or in emails instead.
dont: Show an install-app banner over product lists, product pages or filters.
finding: 53% of mobile sites in Baymard's testing showed an 'Install App' ad while people browsed. These ads covered key controls such as add-to-cart and filter buttons, came back after being dismissed, and shrank the visible page; some participants never closed them and missed what was underneath.
limitation: 2019 research with no participant or site counts and no conversion data; it does not show how much app installs are worth against lost web sales.
measurement: Install-banner dismissal rate; mobile add-to-cart rate on pages with the banner; mobile exit rate on list and product pages
method: Large-scale mobile ecommerce usability testing with recorded sessions
plain: Banners asking shoppers to install the shop's app often covered buttons like Add to cart and kept coming back. Some testers never closed them and missed what was underneath.
sample: Not stated on page (share of tested sites given; participant and site counts not given)

stat.text: of mobile sites in Baymard's usability testing showed an 'Install App' ad while people browsed (2019).

strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: 'Install our app' banners that hide the shop

application: Check the header, footer and mobile menu for a country or region selector that shows the full country name with currency code and symbol, sits beside the language selector, and opens as a light popover.
do: List each country by full name with its currency code and symbol.
dont: Offer bare country codes or flags with no currency shown.
finding: Shopify's theme guidance places the country selector at the top of the sub-footer and near account or cart links, always beside any language selector, and treats it as a utility link in mobile menus. Each option shows the full country name with currency code and symbol, for example United Kingdom (GBP £), in a popover rather than a modal.
limitation: Platform theme guidance with no research basis or date given; it says nothing about flags, automatic location detection or redirects.
measurement: Visitors who change country before checkout; currency-related support contacts; checkout abandonment among international visitors
method: Not stated
plain: Shoppers abroad need to know which country's shop they're in and which currency they'll pay in. Showing the full country name with its currency avoids surprises.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Show the currency in the country selector

visual.cap: A shopper abroad picks where to shop

application: Check that the cart drawer links to a full cart page listing every item with image, chosen size and colour, price, editable quantity and a Remove option, and that the cart persists between visits.
do: Link the cart drawer to a full cart page where every item can be compared, edited and removed.
dont: Rely on a narrow drawer that shows two items and jumps straight to payment.
finding: Many shoppers use the cart as a holding area while they decide, so it should help them compare and edit rather than just collect items. NN/g advises a dedicated full cart page within checkout, because mini carts and overlays show only a few items at a time and skip the review-and-edit step.
limitation: Guidance from 2014 based on qualitative testing; it gives no participant numbers and does not measure whether drawers or full cart pages convert better.
measurement: Full cart page visits after add-to-cart; cart edits (quantity, remove) per session; cart-to-checkout rate
method: Observations from NN/g ecommerce usability testing with real users shopping on websites
plain: Many shoppers treat the basket like a fitting room, deciding what to keep. A small pop-out basket shows only a couple of items, so give them a full basket page to compare and edit.
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Keep a full cart page, not only a mini cart

application: On product, cart and checkout templates, check the Apple Pay button is at least as large as other payment buttons, appears without scrolling, sits right of or above Add to Cart, and that a missing size or colour is flagged when it is tapped.
do: Show the Apple Pay button at full size, above or to the right of Add to basket.
dont: Shrink the Apple Pay button or tuck it below the fold under other options.
finding: Apple asks for the Apple Pay button to be no smaller than other payment buttons and visible without scrolling; beside an Add to Cart button it goes on the right, and in a stacked layout it goes above. It also suggests offering it on product pages for single-item purchases, collecting options such as size and colour first, and not requiring account creation before purchase.
limitation: Platform owner's design rules with no research data or conversion evidence; it covers only Apple Pay, not Google Pay, PayPal or Shop Pay. Where a site uses Apple's APIs to detect an active Wallet card, Apple requires Apple Pay to be the primary payment option.
measurement: Express payment button clicks on product pages; express checkout completion rate; share of mobile orders paid by wallet
method: Not stated
plain: If a shopper's phone can pay with Apple Pay, the button should be easy to spot: as big as the other buttons, visible without scrolling, and beside or above Add to basket.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Where to put the Apple Pay button

application: Review site-search suggestion ranking: put the most likely query first, keep suggestions stable as people finish each word, and check suggestion click share by position in search analytics.
do: Rank the most likely full search first in the suggestion list.
dont: Order suggestions alphabetically or put promoted terms above better matches.
finding: In Bing's logs, the second autocomplete suggestion drew under 40% of the engagement the top suggestion got, though the authors note this mixes relevance with position bias. Engagement peaked at word boundaries, with about 38% of uses coming right after a word's last character was typed.
limitation: Web search engine data, not a shop's site search; results are relative ratios rather than absolute rates, position bias cannot be separated from relevance, and it shows nothing about sales.
measurement: Suggestion click share by position; share of searches using a suggestion; search exit rate
method: Query-log analysis of Bing searches; engagement counted when a user submitted a query offered by query auto-completion, reported as relative ratios
plain: When people type in a search box, they mostly pick the first suggestion, often just after finishing a word. So the best guess has to come first.
publisher: SIGIR 2014, ACM (Mitra, Shokouhi, Radlinski & Hofmann, Microsoft)
sample: About 1.6 million queries sampled from Bing's log, first week of February 2014; user count not reported

stat.text: Under 40%: how much engagement the second autocomplete suggestion got compared with the first, in about 1.6 million Bing queries (Mitra et al., SIGIR 2014).

strengthWhy: Published study, but observational or correlational.
title: Bing logs: the top autocomplete suggestion gets most picks

application: Inventory every third-party tracking domain on key templates with a tag audit, remove unused tags, and confirm none fire before consent where consent is required.
do: List every third-party tracker your pages load and remove the ones nobody uses.
dont: Add marketing tags without checking whether they fire before visitors give consent.
finding: The crawl found at least one third-party tracker on 75% of desktop and 74% of mobile pages. Only advertising, adult advertising, site analytics and social media domains counted as trackers, and figures count unique domains rather than requests.
limitation: Measures whether tracker domains are present, from a US-based crawler, so region-specific consent behaviour may be missed; it says nothing about whether the tracking was lawful or how visitors reacted.
measurement: Third-party tracking domains per template; tags firing before consent; third-party script weight per page
method: Automated crawl by HTTP Archive; third-party domains matched to WhoTracks.Me categories, counting only advertising, pornvertising, site analytics and social media domains as trackers
plain: Most web pages quietly load code from advertising, analytics or social media companies that follow visitors. Knowing exactly what your own pages load is the first step to keeping shoppers' trust.
publisher: HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025 (Habib, Tiwari & Demir)
sample: 16.2M websites (15.4M mobile, 12.2M desktop), July 2025 HTTP Archive crawl from a US-based crawler; the chapter does not say whether inner pages were included

stat.text: of desktop pages had at least one third-party tracker (HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025, 16.2M websites, July 2025 crawl).

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Three in four web pages load a third-party tracker

application: Check each page's @font-face rules: use swap or optional for body and heading text, keep block only for icon fonts, and test on a slow connection for invisible text.
do: Show text in a backup font straight away while the custom font loads.
dont: Use the hide-until-loaded setting for headlines and body text.
finding: About half of pages use font-display: swap (49.6% desktop, 50.1% mobile), which shows fallback text immediately, while about a quarter use block (24.7% and 24.9%), which briefly hides glyphs while the font loads; the chapter attributes roughly 70% of block usage to icon fonts. Only about 0.4–0.5% use optional.
limitation: Counts which settings pages declare, not how long text was actually hidden or how visitors reacted; it shows no effect on reading, bounce or sales.
measurement: Time to first visible text on a throttled connection; share of text fonts using block; CLS caused by font swaps
method: Automated crawl by HTTP Archive measuring web font requests and the CSS font-display values pages declare
plain: Websites tell the browser what to do while a custom font downloads: show a backup font straight away, or hide the words for a moment. About a quarter of pages choose to hide them, mostly for icons.
sample: 16.2M websites (15.4M mobile, 12.2M desktop), July 2025 HTTP Archive crawl from a US-based crawler

stat.text: of desktop pages use font-display: block, which briefly hides text while fonts load (Web Almanac 2025, 16.2M websites, July 2025 crawl).

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Half of pages show text at once while fonts load

application: On home and landing pages, check the first screen on common phone and desktop sizes holds the main message and primary action, and that no tall empty banner creates a false floor that looks like the end of the page.
do: Put the main message and main button on the first screen, with a visible hint of what follows.
dont: Open with a tall empty banner that makes the page look finished.
finding: In NN/g's eyetracking data, the 100 pixels just above the fold were viewed 102% more than the 100 pixels just below it; Google's ad data showed ads just above the fold were 66% more visible. People do scroll, but only when what they see first suggests there is more worth seeing.
limitation: A 2015 study of desktop-era pages; the two figures measure different things (where people looked versus whether an ad was on screen), and it does not show that moving content above the fold raises sales.
measurement: Share of visitors reaching each scroll depth; primary CTA clicks; click share of first-screen elements
method: Eyetracking heatmap of fixations across many non-search web pages, compared with Google's study of display-ad viewability
plain: People look much more at what they see before scrolling. They will scroll, but only if the first screen hints that something useful sits below.
sample: 57,453 eyetracking fixations; Google ad study size not stated on page

stat.text: more viewing for the 100 pixels just above the fold than for those just below it (NN/g eyetracking, 57,453 fixations).

strengthWhy: Eyetracking study: measures where people look, not sales.
title: Content just above the fold gets far more looks

visual.cap: A visitor lands on a shop's home page
visual.note: Illustration. Product and button text are made-up examples.

application: Check that every language offered in the selector has full equivalent pages, that the selector appears in the same place on every template, and that the page and each language link carry the correct lang attribute.
do: List only languages with complete translated pages, in the same place on every page.
dont: Offer a language that sends people back to English pages after one click.
finding: USWDS recommends a language selector only when equivalent translated content exists, using a two-language variant for two languages and a dropdown for three or more, and advises against it when translations are limited or incomplete. Each page should declare its language, and links to other languages should mark their own language in the code.
limitation: Based on accessibility testing, not user research; it does not say how to name languages, whether to use flags, or where visitors expect to find the selector.
measurement: Language switches per session; bounce after switching language; pages missing a lang attribute
method: Accessibility testing by the USWDS team against WCAG 2.1 AA (12 tests: 10 passes, 2 passes with exceptions)
plain: A language switch is a promise. Only offer a language if the site is really available in it, and keep the switch in the same spot on every page.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Offer a language only where translations are complete

application: Plan qualitative usability rounds of about five users per user group, fix what they reveal and retest; use larger samples when the goal is a metric such as success rate or time on task.
do: Run small rounds of about five users, fix what you find, then retest.
dont: Use five-user tests to report percentages such as success rates.
finding: In Nielsen and Landauer's model, where a typical single user reveals about 31% of usability problems, five users uncover roughly 85%. The article recommends several small rounds of 3 to 5 users with redesign in between rather than one big study, and points to larger samples for quantitative metrics (20 users) and card sorting (15).
limitation: Applies to finding problems in qualitative tests, not to measuring rates; the 31% figure is a typical value from older projects, not a constant, and the article does not say how many projects it draws on.
measurement: Usability problems found per round; problems repeating across rounds; task success after redesign
method: Based on Nielsen and Landauer's 1993 mathematical model of how usability problems are found, fitted to data from many projects
plain: A handful of test users finds most of the obvious problems. It's better to test with five, fix, and test again than to spend the whole budget on one big session.
sample: Number of projects not stated on page

stat.text: of usability problems found by five users in Nielsen and Landauer's model, where one user finds about 31%.

strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: Test with about five users, then test again

application: Rank speed fixes on product and listing pages by how much they speed up the content people see first, and measure speed changes with A/B tests rather than assuming their value.
do: Speed up the main content people see first before tuning anything lower down the page.
dont: Spend speed effort on late-loading extras while the main content still lags.
finding: In a Bing experiment that deliberately slowed pages, every 100 ms of speed-up was worth 0.6% of revenue. Delaying only the right-pane content that loads after the page by 250 ms had no detectable effect across almost 20 million users, so the speed of the main, first-seen content mattered most.
limitation: Search results pages at Bing; the authors stress that results vary by site, so the 0.6% figure is Bing's and does not show the same return for a retail shop.
measurement: Revenue per user; Largest Contentful Paint (LCP); clickthrough rate
method: Online controlled experiments (A/B tests) with random, persistent user assignment; the slowdown test delayed Bing pages by 100 ms for one 10% of users and 250 ms for another 10% over two weeks
plain: When Bing deliberately slowed its pages for some visitors, it earned less from them. Slowing content that appears later made no difference, so the part people see first is what must be fast.
sample: Bing users: two 10% slices of traffic in the slowdown test; almost 20 million users in the right-pane delay test; paper draws on experiments at Amazon, Booking.com, LinkedIn and Microsoft

stat.text: of revenue per 100 ms of speed-up in Bing's controlled slowdown experiments (Kohavi et al., KDD 2014).

strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Bing slowdown tests: speed above the fold pays

visual.cap: Two visitors open the same product page
visual.note: Illustration. 100 ms and 250 ms are the delays Bing tested; real page loads take longer.

application: Compare home and landing page layouts with the conventions of the category and remove clutter from the first screen before testing a novel layout.
do: Keep the first screen uncluttered and follow the layout people expect for your kind of site.
dont: Crowd the first screen with competing graphics or an unconventional layout.
finding: Screenshots with low visual complexity and a layout typical for that kind of site received the highest beauty ratings. Both factors already changed ratings at 17 ms of exposure, and typicality mattered most when complexity was low.
limitation: Beauty ratings of static screenshots in a lab, not usability, trust or sales on live sites; company websites only.
measurement: First-impression rating (5-second test); landing page bounce rate; competing elements on the first screen
method: Two lab experiments in which participants rated the beauty of briefly shown website screenshots varying in visual complexity and prototypicality (how typical the layout looks for its kind of site)
plain: In a split second, people already preferred sites that looked simple and were laid out the way they expected. Busy or unusual layouts made a worse first impression.
publisher: Google and University of Basel (Tuch et al.), International Journal of Human-Computer Studies
sample: Study 1: 59 participants, 119 company-website screenshots shown for 50, 500 or 1000 ms; Study 2: 82 participants, 80 screenshots shown for 17, 33 or 50 ms

stat.text: of viewing was enough for complexity and typicality to change beauty ratings, in two lab studies with 59 and 82 participants (Tuch et al., 2012).

strengthWhy: Published study, but observational or correlational.
title: Simple, familiar layouts win the first glance

application: On site search results, keep one consistent layout, make the first screen of results the most relevant, and add special result blocks only where they suit the content.
do: Keep the results layout the same for every query and put the best matches on the first page.
dont: Change the results layout from query to query or leave strong matches on later pages.
finding: Across 471 queries, people jumped around results pages rather than reading down the list, drawn by prominent features, which were looked at in 74% of cases when present. The first result got 28% of clicks, compared with 51% in a 2006 study, and people clicked past page one in only 2% of queries.
limitation: Web search engines, not shop site search; percentages pool earlier studies, and the 2006 comparison comes from a different study.
measurement: Click position on search results; search exit rate; clicks beyond the first results page
method: Meta-analysis of usability-testing and eyetracking sessions run 2017–2019 (NN/g Search Meta-Analysis Project)
plain: People don't read search results in order. Eye-catching boxes pull their eyes around the page, and they almost never go beyond the first page.
sample: 471 queries; participant count not stated on page

stat.text: of queries led to a click past the first results page, in NN/g's analysis of 471 queries from 2017–2019 studies.

strengthWhy: Eyetracking study: measures where people look, not sales.
title: Search results are scanned like pinball, not top to bottom

application: Audit how pay-later appears on product and checkout pages: the instalment schedule, late-fee terms and lender name should be visible before the shopper commits, not only inside a pop-up.
do: Show the instalment amounts, payment dates and late-fee terms beside the pay-later offer.
dont: Advertise only 'pay later' and hide the schedule and fees inside a pop-up.
finding: Loans from the five lenders rose from 16.8 million in 2019 to 180 million in 2021, and 10.5% of borrowers were charged at least one late fee in 2021. The report describes pay-later offers on product pages as a visual cue linking to a pop-up with details, and names overextension and data harvesting among consumer risks.
limitation: US data from five lenders up to 2021; a market study, not a test of how product-page messaging changes behaviour, and not itself a rule. See BD-277 for UK rules.
measurement: Pay-later share of orders; clicks on pay-later terms; shoppers able to state what they will owe
method: Market-monitoring orders issued in December 2021 requiring five pay-later lenders to supply loan data, combined with public sources and submissions
plain: Pay-later loans grew very fast in the US, and 10.5% of borrowers were charged a late fee in 2021. Shops usually show the offer as a small badge that opens a pop-up with the terms.
sample: Five lenders (Affirm, Afterpay, Klarna, PayPal, Zip); loan data 2019–2021; US

stat.text: of borrowers with five large US pay-later lenders were charged at least one late fee in 2021 (CFPB loan data).

strengthWhy: A standard or rule: says what's required, not what it changes.
title: US regulator data on pay-later growth and late fees

application: Below the hero, check that the homepage shows the main product types and links straight to popular categories and subcategories; replace fast-rotating carousels with static featured-category sections.
do: Show popular categories and subcategories as links right under the hero.
dont: Rely on a rotating promo carousel as the main way into the range.
finding: In Baymard's late-2020 benchmark, 62% of sites did not help visitors reach a well-defined category scope from the homepage, and testers who landed in the wrong scope often wrongly concluded the shop lacked what they needed. 36% of sites used a carousel, and nearly 75% of those implemented it poorly.
limitation: Late-2020 benchmark scored against Baymard's own guidelines; the page gives the sample as 60 sites in one place and 80 in another, and Baymard notes a newer article exists. Does not measure sales.
measurement: Homepage clicks into category pages; homepage exit rate; share of product types shown on the homepage
method: Manual UX benchmark scoring of homepage elements against 17 homepage guidelines, based on Baymard's usability testing
plain: Most big shops' homepages didn't lead people clearly into categories. Shoppers who ended up in the wrong section often decided the shop didn't sell what they wanted.
sample: 60 top-grossing US and European ecommerce sites, late 2020 (one section says 80); 10,900+ homepage and category elements reviewed

stat.text: of top-grossing US and European shops didn't help visitors reach a clear category from the homepage (Baymard benchmark, late 2020).

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Homepages that show the range and route into categories

application: When auditing a site, compare its CrUX Core Web Vitals result with its platform's typical rate to judge whether a failure comes from the theme and add-ons or the platform itself.
do: Benchmark a site's real-user speed against others on the same platform before blaming the platform.
dont: Assume a slow result is unavoidable because of the platform without checking themes and add-ons.
finding: The share of mobile sites with good Core Web Vitals differed widely by platform in 2025: 85% for Duda, 79% for TYPO3, 74% for Wix (up from 55% in 2024) and 45% for WordPress. Over 54% of observed websites used a CMS.
limitation: Platform averages mix very different sites, so they do not show that switching platform makes a site faster; mobile only, and the chapter does not spell out the thresholds or whether 'good' means passing all three metrics.
measurement: Core Web Vitals pass (mobile, CrUX); share of page loads with good LCP; share with good INP
method: HTTP Archive crawl with CMS detection; real-user Core Web Vitals from the Chrome UX Report (CrUX)
plain: How fast real visitors find a site depends a lot on what it's built with. On phones, 45% of WordPress sites had good Core Web Vitals, against 85% of Duda sites.
sample: 16.2M websites (15.4M mobile), July 2025 crawl; CrUX July 2025 dataset

stat.text: of WordPress sites had good mobile Core Web Vitals, versus 85% for Duda (Web Almanac 2025, 16.2M-site July 2025 crawl).

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Core Web Vitals pass rates by website builder

application: Use unmoderated tests for quick checks of live checkout or search tasks, pilot the tasks before launch, and screen participants on behaviour rather than demographics alone.
do: Pilot every task first and make each one specific, realistic and clear about when to stop.
dont: Use unmoderated tests on rough early prototypes or tasks that rely on imagination.
finding: In unmoderated tests, software gives instructions and records sessions with no researcher present, so dozens or hundreds of people can take part and results can arrive within hours. NN/g says they suit live sites, working prototypes and simple tasks, and need precise tasks and a pilot because participants cannot ask for clarification.
limitation: Expert method guidance, not a comparison of results between moderated and unmoderated tests; gives no recommended sample size.
measurement: Task success rate; time on task; share of sessions excluded as invalid
method: Not stated
plain: In an unmoderated test, people do tasks alone while software records them. It's fast and reaches many people, but if a task is worded badly nobody is there to explain it.
strengthWhy: Expert advice or a summary of others' research.
title: When to run usability tests without a moderator

application: Review every order, shipping and pickup notification: lead with its purpose, name the items, send it when the event happens, and keep marketing out of SMS.
do: Lead each order alert with its purpose and name the item it's about.
dont: Send a delivery text with only a long order number, or after the parcel has arrived.
finding: People wanted order texts and push alerts to be short, timely and to identify the order: messages giving only an order number left them unsure what they referred to, and a delivery text arriving after the parcel frustrated them. SMS suited urgent or critical updates, push suited non-urgent ones, and promotions were unwelcome in either.
limitation: Qualitative diary findings with no stated participant count; does not measure open rates or effects on repeat purchases.
measurement: Where-is-my-order contacts; notification opt-out rate; SMS and push click rate
method: Two longitudinal diary studies in which participants logged the transactional emails and notifications they received
plain: People want order updates that say what the message is about and which items it covers, sent at the right moment. A text with only an order number leaves them guessing.
sample: Participants in four countries; number not stated on page
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Order texts and push alerts that say which order
