application: On product pages, test showing accepted payment methods (including express and pay-later options) as visible logos near the buy button instead of inside a collapsed accordion.
do: Show accepted payment methods as logos in an open area near the add-to-cart button.
dont: Hide the list of payment options behind a collapsed 'Payment' accordion.
finding: In the field test, only the version showing payment-method logos in a section that was already open raised add-to-cart compared with the retailer's collapsed text list. In the online studies, visible payment options raised stated purchase likelihood (3.53 vs 2.62 on a 7-point scale for a $360 item), but not when participants were under heavy cognitive load.
limitation: One retailer over one week, with add-to-cart rather than purchase as the field outcome (the retailer reported only r = .21 between them); the paper's field-model figures don't fully reconcile, so rely on direction, not size. It tests payment options in general, not pay-later specifically, and the online outcomes are self-reported intentions.
measurement: Add-to-cart rate on product pages; Product page to checkout progression; Payment-section expand rate
method: One-week field experiment on a fashion retailer's product pages (2×2: payment methods as text vs logos, section collapsed vs open by default), plus three online experiments with Prolific participants
plain: Shoppers were a little more willing to buy when the ways to pay were shown openly on the product page as logos, rather than tucked inside a closed section. Overloaded, distracted shoppers didn't respond the same way.
publisher: Journal of Retailing (Elsevier); Lefkeli, Gurdamar-Okutur & Villarroel Ordenes
sample: Field: 4,497 product-and-device observations, 16–22 January 2024; online studies: N = 201, 284 and 363
strengthWhy: Controlled experiment (A/B or randomised) with a stated sample.
title: Show payment options openly on the product page

application: Audit product, cart and checkout pages for express-pay buttons that are smaller or placed lower than card buttons, and check required options are captured before the wallet sheet opens.
do: Size the wallet button to match neighbouring payment buttons and add it to product pages.
dont: Let the wallet payment sheet open before size, quantity and delivery choices are made.
finding: Google asks merchants to give the Google Pay button at least the same size and prominence as other payment buttons, with 8 dp of clear space around it, and to offer it on product detail pages too so a single item can be bought quickly. All other required choices (size, quantity, shipping, promo code) should be collected before the button is enabled, with live feedback if something is missing.
limitation: Brand and integration rules written by the payment provider, not user research; it shows no conversion effect, and other wallets (Apple Pay, PayPal, Shop Pay) set their own rules.
measurement: Express-pay share of orders; Express-pay button click rate on product pages; Wallet payment errors from missing options
method: Not stated
plain: If a site offers Google Pay, its button should be as big and easy to spot as the other ways to pay. It can sit on the product page too, so one item can be bought in a few taps.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Give Google Pay equal billing and a product-page spot

application: In speed audits, check whether the store's HTML and images are served from a CDN and compare server response time (TTFB) for visitors far from the origin server.
do: Serve the store's pages and images through a CDN and check TTFB from distant regions.
dont: Assume the site is fast because it loads quickly from an office near the server.
finding: On mobile, 35% of HTML (main document) requests were served through a CDN in 2025, up from 33% in 2024, and CDN use drops with popularity: 71% among the top 1,000 sites versus 35% across the top 10 million. Median connection set-up was faster through CDNs, e.g. mobile DNS lookups took 176 ms versus 217 ms from origin servers.
limitation: Detection misses some CDN set-ups (such as Anycast or direct address records), measurements come from one location, and the chapter doesn't say exactly what its rank-band figures count. Using a CDN says nothing about whether it is configured well for a given site.
measurement: TTFB at the 75th percentile (field data); Share of requests served from a CDN; LCP at the 75th percentile
method: Automated crawl with simulated Chrome connections; CDNs detected mainly from DNS CNAME records and HTTP headers; sites grouped by Chrome UX Report popularity rank
plain: A CDN keeps copies of a site on servers close to visitors so pages arrive faster. Most of the very popular sites use one, but only about a third of main page requests on mobile go through one.
sample: 16.2M websites (15.4M mobile), July 2025 crawl (Almanac default; the chapter doesn't restate the month); single geographic vantage point

stat.text: of mobile HTML requests were served through a CDN (HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025, about 15.4M mobile sites, July 2025 crawl)

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: CDN use falls sharply outside the most popular sites

application: Check that every page, including checkout, account and image or script URLs, loads over HTTPS with no mixed-content warnings, and that HSTS is set.
do: Serve every page, image and script over HTTPS and switch on HSTS.
dont: Leave old http:// image or script links that trigger mixed-content warnings at checkout.
finding: In 2025, 97.3% of mobile and 97.5% of desktop home pages loaded over HTTPS, and over 98.8% of mobile requests did. Extra protections lag: HSTS, which tells browsers to always use the secure connection, was on 36% of mobile pages, and a Content Security Policy on 21.9% of pages.
limitation: Counts what the crawler saw on home and some secondary pages, not checkout or signed-in areas; HTTPS shows the connection is encrypted, not that the business is trustworthy. The chapter gives the Content Security Policy growth rate inconsistently (about 18% vs close to 20% relative).
measurement: Share of pages and assets served over HTTPS; Mixed-content warnings per page; HSTS header present (yes/no)
method: Automated crawl analysing TLS connections and HTTP security headers on home and secondary pages, mobile and desktop profiles
plain: Almost every website now uses a secure, encrypted connection (HTTPS), so a site without one is now the rare exception. Extra safeguards that work behind the scenes are still much less common.
sample: 16.2M websites (15.4M mobile, 12.2M desktop), July 2025 crawl (Almanac default; the chapter doesn't restate the month)

stat.text: of mobile home pages loaded over HTTPS (HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025, about 15.4M mobile sites, July 2025 crawl)

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Nearly every home page now uses HTTPS

application: Open the account area and confirm the dashboard links directly to orders, tracking, returns, saved cards, addresses and personal details, with full order history one tap away.
do: Link every self-service task, from order history to saved cards, from the account dashboard.
dont: Show only recent orders with no route to full history, saved cards or addresses.
finding: Baymard rated 73% of desktop and 66% of mobile sites mediocre or worse for accounts and self-service, and 78% of sites didn't link to every account feature from the account dashboard. Where a dashboard was offered, 52% of usability-test participants used it.
limitation: Free summary of a paywalled study; benchmark scores are expert judgements of large retailers, the page gives no participant numbers and it doesn't show effects on repeat purchases or support contacts.
measurement: Task success for 'find a past order'; Dashboard link click-through; Account-related support contacts
method: Manual UX benchmark scoring of leading ecommerce sites, plus a quantitative survey and qualitative usability testing
plain: Customers sign in to get a job done: track an order, update a card, check past purchases. When the account homepage doesn't link to every task, they have to hunt through menus to find it.
sample: 5,400+ UX scores across 150+ benchmarked sites; survey of 1,026 US online shoppers; usability-test participant count not stated

stat.text: of benchmarked sites didn't link to every account feature from the dashboard (Baymard benchmark of 150+ ecommerce sites)

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Account dashboards that link to every self-service task

application: Review email send frequency and add a preference centre that lets subscribers choose fewer emails or fewer topics instead of only unsubscribing.
do: Offer a 'send me fewer emails' option on the unsubscribe page and in email settings.
dont: Send several promotional emails a day from the same shop with no way to slow them down.
finding: Asked why they had unsubscribed from a store's newsletter, 48% said that retailer emailed too often, 46% said they get too many newsletters overall, and 44% had lost interest in the content.
limitation: Self-reported reasons from US shoppers only; the free article doesn't say whether several reasons could be chosen and covers 3 of 20+ insights, with the rest paywalled. It doesn't show what send frequency is right.
measurement: Unsubscribe rate per send; Share choosing 'fewer emails' instead of unsubscribing; Email click-through rate
method: Online survey of US online shoppers
plain: When people stop a shop's newsletter, the most common reason they give is that the shop emails too often, closely followed by having too many newsletters overall and losing interest.

stat.text: of shoppers who unsubscribed said that retailer emailed too often (Baymard survey of 1,083 US online shoppers, 2026)

strengthWhy: Survey: what people say, not what they do.
title: Why shoppers unsubscribe from store newsletters

application: For multi-step onboarding or B2B set-up flows, check a task list is justified, that incomplete tasks stand out from completed ones, and that the task name, not the status, is the link.
date: Date not shown (component added December 2023, updated August 2024)
do: Mark unfinished tasks with a coloured status tag and make the task name the link.
dont: Style every status the same in capital letters, or make the status label look like a button.
finding: A task list suits long, complex services that people may finish over several sessions or in their own order; each task shows a short status, with tasks still needing action in a coloured tag and completed ones in plain text. Research found users clicked statuses thinking they were buttons and found uppercase statuses hard to read, so the task name and whole row became the link and statuses moved to sentence case.
limitation: No sample sizes or measured results are given, and GOV.UK lists open questions (whether whole-row links cause accidental clicks, whether status contrast and wording work). Not suited to flows that must be completed in a fixed order.
measurement: Application completion rate; Completion of saved applications on return visits; Misclicks on status labels
method: Not stated (page summarises findings from government teams' user research)
plain: For long applications people finish over several visits, a checklist of tasks shows what's done and what's left. Unfinished tasks should stand out, and you tap the task's name, not its status label.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Task lists for long applications finished over several visits

application: Walk through the app or site as a new visitor and note every point where sign-in is demanded; check that browsing, search and the basket work without an account.
do: Let new visitors browse and fill a basket, asking them to sign in only at purchase.
dont: Show a sign-up wall before people can see a single product.
finding: Apple advises requiring an account only when core features need one and delaying sign-in as long as possible, because people often abandon apps that demand it before anything useful happens; a shopping app, for example, can allow free browsing and ask only at purchase. Sign-in views should briefly explain why an account is needed, and sign-in buttons should name the method used, such as Face ID.
limitation: Platform guidance for Apple apps with no cited data; it states the abandonment risk but gives no figures, and its account-deletion rules are separate App Store requirements.
measurement: First-session drop-off at sign-in walls; Share of new visitors reaching a product page; Sign-in completion rate
method: Not stated
plain: Asking people to sign up before they've seen anything useful makes many give up. Let them look around first and ask only when an account is really needed, such as at purchase, with a short reason why.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Let people look around before asking them to sign in

application: Show the full price including mandatory fees on listing and product pages, and track drop-off at the checkout review step instead of treating late-added fees as free revenue.
do: Show the total price, including every mandatory fee, from the first price a shopper sees.
dont: Add mandatory booking or service fees for the first time on the checkout review page.
finding: When StubHub showed prices without its roughly 15% buyer fee and revealed the fee only later in checkout, users were about 14% more likely to buy over the test and spent almost 21% more, partly by choosing pricier seats. More people clicked into ticket details under hidden fees, but a much smaller share completed the purchase once the full price appeared at review.
limitation: One US ticket marketplace in 2015; the paper's dates and headline revenue figure (about 20–21%) differ slightly between sections. It shows drip pricing raised the seller's short-term revenue, not that it serves customers. Mandatory fees revealed late are now restricted: the US FTC fees rule covers live-event tickets and short-term lodging, and UK DMCC Act rules (from 6 April 2025) prohibit drip pricing.
measurement: Purchase rate; Drop-off between basket review and payment; Complaints or refunds mentioning fees
method: Randomised controlled experiment on StubHub: browsers (by cookie) split about 50/50 between fee-inclusive prices from the first listing and base prices with the fee (about 15% plus delivery) added later in checkout; plus a smaller 2012 event-level experiment
plain: In a large live test, a ticket site that added its fees only at checkout sold more, but many shoppers dropped out once they saw the real total. US ticket rules and UK law now require mandatory fees upfront.
publisher: NBER Working Paper 25186 (Blake, Moshary, Sweeney & Tadelis); published in Marketing Science, 2021
sample: Several million US StubHub users (exact count not given), August 2015 (the paper gives slightly different start and end dates); users affected by two assignment glitches excluded

stat.text: higher purchase rate when fees were hidden until checkout (StubHub randomised test, several million users, 2015) — a short-term gain that UK and US rules now restrict

strengthWhy: Randomised experiment with millions of users, but one ticket site, 2015.
title: Hiding ticket fees until checkout: a live A/B test

dont.cap: fees appear at the last step

application: When testing email or SMS frequency, track unsubscribes and longer-term revenue per subscriber alongside the week's sales, and consider a lower cadence for subscribers at risk of opting out.
do: Measure unsubscribes and long-term revenue per subscriber whenever you test email frequency.
dont: Judge an email cadence only by the sales it brings in that week.
finding: Sending coupon emails every other day instead of daily cut the chance of unsubscribing by 59.2% in relative terms, but during the test week daily revenue per customer fell 7.6% and the daily chance of purchase fell 4.8%. The authors' historical data link unsubscribing to much lower later spending, so they argue the cadence should balance both.
limitation: One retailer, one week and coupon emails only; the unsubscribe drop is large in relative terms but starts from a very small base, and the revenue loss was not significant in one robustness check. The paper shows no date or venue, and its abstract and body give slightly different revenue figures (5–10%). The long-run benefits come from modelling, not the experiment.
measurement: Unsubscribe rate per send; Revenue per subscriber over 90 days; Purchase rate per subscriber
method: Randomised field experiment: customers were assigned to daily coupon promotional emails (control) or one email every two days (treatment); plus a historical analysis of 2024 customer data and model simulations
plain: A retailer that emailed coupons every other day instead of every day lost far fewer subscribers, but sold a little less that week. Daily emails win short-term sales while wearing out the list.
publisher: Columbia Business School and others (Baek, Chen, Ma & Mitrofanov); paper hosted by Will Ma
sample: 603,153 customers of one unnamed major North American online retailer, 25–31 October 2024; historical analysis of about 200,000 customers in 2024

stat.text: relative drop in unsubscribes when coupon emails went from daily to every other day (randomised test, 603,153 customers, one retailer, October 2024)

strengthWhy: Randomised field experiment, 603,153 customers, but one retailer for one week.
title: Halving promo emails: fewer unsubscribes, smaller short-term sales

application: Never trigger the browser's notification permission on page load; ask only after an in-page offer the shopper chooses (such as a back-in-stock alert), then check how often visitors see Chrome's quiet version.
do: Ask for notifications only after a shopper taps an in-page offer such as a back-in-stock alert.
dont: Fire the browser's notification permission prompt as soon as the page loads.
finding: Chrome's prediction model chose the quiet (collapsed) prompt for 43% of website notification requests and 24% of location requests, and people ignored quiet prompts 99% of the time they were shown. In the surveys, 51% of respondents had not noticed the quiet prompt, while 84% rated quieting at least moderately helpful.
limitation: Observational telemetry without a randomised control in this paper, desktop Chrome only, and written by Google staff about Google's own feature; some summary figures differ slightly between abstract and tables. It shows unwanted prompts get suppressed, not how much a well-timed in-context ask recovers.
measurement: Notification opt-in rate per prompt shown; Share of permission prompts shown after a user action; Push subscriber growth
method: Analysis of desktop Chrome telemetry from opted-in users after launch of a machine-learning system that decides when to show a quieter permission prompt, plus six in-product surveys
plain: When a site asks to send notifications as soon as someone arrives, Chrome often shrinks the request to a small icon. Almost nobody acts on that hidden version, and half of people never notice it.
publisher: NDSS Symposium 2024 (Harbach, Bilogrevic et al., Google)
sample: More than 20 million prompt requests (over 10 million per permission type), desktop Chrome, June 2023; surveys: 13,109 retained responses from 156 countries, March 2023

stat.text: of website notification requests were shown in Chrome's quiet form (NDSS 2024, over 20 million desktop prompt requests, June 2023)

strengthWhy: Large real-world telemetry dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Chrome quietly hides many notification requests

application: In AI and search visibility audits, check robots.txt rules for AI crawlers and whether key product, delivery and returns facts are available as plain text; treat llms.txt as optional, since few sites use it.
do: Check robots.txt rules for AI crawlers and keep key delivery, returns and product facts in plain text.
dont: Treat adding an llms.txt file as a proven way to win traffic from AI assistants.
finding: In the July 2025 crawl, valid llms.txt files (a proposed plain-text guide to a site for AI tools) were found on 2.13% of desktop and 2.1% of mobile pages. Citing the Almanac's SEO chapter, it reports that robots.txt mentions of OpenAI's GPTBot crawler rose to about 4.5% of sites (2.6% in 2024), and 20.9% among the top 1,000 sites.
limitation: The chapter doesn't define what counts as a valid llms.txt, and having the file says nothing about whether AI tools read it or send traffic; the GPTBot figures come from a different chapter. It is a single crawl snapshot, mostly of home pages.
measurement: Presence of llms.txt and AI-crawler rules in robots.txt; Referral sessions from AI assistants; Share of key policy facts available as plain text
method: Automated crawl of home pages; files and code detected by pattern matching, not by checking whether anything is used at runtime
plain: An llms.txt file is a proposed way to tell AI tools what a site contains. In mid-2025 only about 2% of sites had a valid one, so it is far from standard practice.
publisher: HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025 (Generative AI chapter; Liebel, Vekaria & Pagel)
sample: 16.2M websites (12.2M desktop, 15.4M mobile), July 2025 crawl; robots.txt analysis covers about 12.9M sites

application: On mobile product pages, test a share button that opens the native share menu (with a copy-link fallback) for shoppers who want to send an item to someone.
do: Add a Share button on mobile product pages that opens the phone's own share menu.
dont: Leave shoppers to copy the web address by hand to send a product to someone.
finding: The Web Share API, which opens the device's own share menu, was detected on 6.6% of mobile sites in 2025 (6.0% in 2024), and the async Clipboard API on 11.2% of mobile sites (10.0% in 2024). The chapter describes Web Share as roughly flat and Clipboard as growing steadily.
limitation: Detection scans source code, so minified code can hide real use and matched code may never run; it shows presence only, not whether share buttons help shoppers or sales.
measurement: Share button taps per product view; Sessions from shared links; Share completion rate
method: Automated crawl of desktop and mobile pages; 86 regular expressions based on Project Fugu API data scan page source for API calls
plain: Phones have a built-in share menu that sends a link to any app a person uses. Only 6.6% of mobile sites use it, so sharing a product is often harder than it needs to be.
publisher: HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025 (Capabilities chapter; Silvente Fuentes)

application: Audit every countdown, 'limited time' and low-stock message: confirm each is true, tied to a real end date or stock level, and doesn't reset on reload or a new visit.
do: Tie every countdown or 'last chance' message to a real end date that never resets.
dont: Show a countdown timer that starts again when the page is reloaded.
finding: Under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, falsely claiming a product is available only for a limited time to push an immediate decision is one of the Schedule 20 banned practices; the CMA's example is a countdown offer that restarts. Other pressure messages, such as a recent-sales pop-up when stock is plentiful, are not banned outright but can be misleading, and fake or undisclosed-incentive reviews are banned.
limitation: UK consumer law guidance, applying to commercial practices from 6 April 2025; it doesn't measure how urgency messages affect shoppers, and accurate deadlines and stock claims remain allowed. Not legal advice.
measurement: Share of urgency messages backed by real stock or end dates; Count of timers that reset on reload; Complaints about misleading offers
method: Not applicable (regulatory guidance)
plain: In the UK it is now illegal to pretend an offer is about to end to rush people, such as a countdown that starts again. Real deadlines and true stock levels are still fine.
publisher: UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA207 guidance)
strengthWhy: A rule and its official guidance: says what's banned, not effects.
title: UK ban on fake countdowns and limited-time claims

application: On SaaS or subscription pricing pages, show plans in a side-by-side table with every feature visible, an inline explanation or link for each, and no truncated feature list.
do: Show every feature in the plan table with a short explanation on tap or hover.
dont: Cut the feature list short behind a 'See more features' link.
finding: All 20 benchmarked sites had a pricing page, and a side-by-side plan matrix was the most common format and the one testers found most effective for comparing plans. Matrices listed 40 features on average; most testers needed help with at least one feature, none of the sites consistently linked features to more detail, and hiding features behind a 'See more features' link made testers think products did less.
limitation: 2022 research on 20 large, well-known sites; no participant numbers or conversion data, and the full guideline set is in Baymard's paid tier (not used here).
measurement: Plan selection rate from pricing page; Use of feature tooltips or links; Sales or support questions about plan features
method: Expert benchmark of 20 SaaS and digital-subscription sites (10 B2B, 10 B2C) scored against 250+ research-based guidelines from Baymard's usability testing
plain: People choose a software plan by comparing a table of features side by side. They get stuck on unexplained feature names, and if features are hidden behind a link they assume the product can't do them.
sample: 20 sites, 4,750+ usability scores across 32 topics; usability-test participant numbers not stated
strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of 20 real sites plus testing, not a controlled test.
title: SaaS pricing pages: explain every feature in the plan table

application: Audit sign-up and sign-in forms for a single password field with a Show toggle, paste allowed, the right autocomplete value, no maxlength, and a generic error after a failed sign-in.
date: Date not shown (component added March 2024; last listed change March 2025)
do: Use one password field with a Show button and allow pasting from password managers.
dont: Make people retype a new password blind in a second 'confirm password' field.
finding: GOV.UK's password component hides the password by default and adds a Show button (announced to screen readers as 'Show password') so people can check what they typed, and the team says this makes a second confirm-password field unnecessary. It also advises allowing paste for password managers, avoiding maxlength, turning off spellcheck and autocapitalise, using new-password or current-password autocomplete, and clearing the field after a failed sign-in without saying which detail was wrong.
limitation: Design-system guidance with no research results on the page; the team says dropping the confirm field still needs real-world evidence, and browsers or password managers may add their own show/hide controls that can conflict with the button.
measurement: Sign-up completion rate; Password reset requests in the first week; Sign-in error rate
method: Not stated
plain: Instead of making people type a new password twice, give one field with a Show button so they can check it. Let password managers paste in, and never cut long passwords short.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Password fields with a Show button instead of a confirm field

application: On product pages, test a purchase-based 'customers also bought' module against no module (or a view-based one), and track whether sales concentrate further on bestsellers.
do: Test a 'customers also bought' module on product pages against a page without one.
dont: Assume recommendations help your whole range without checking whether they only push bestsellers.
finding: Purchase-based recommendations (items others also bought) raised purchases by 5% versus no recommendations, and view-based ones raised product views by 11%, with no significant change in the other measure. Both types concentrated views and sales on already-popular items, lowering aggregate sales diversity, even though niche items also gained slightly in absolute sales.
limitation: One retailer's Canadian site over two weeks with default algorithm settings; long-term effects, other recommender types and which specific items were shown were not studied, and individual-level results lacked statistical power.
measurement: Purchases per visitor; Product views per visitor; Share of sales from top 10% of products
method: Randomised field experiment on a top-five North American retailer's Canadian website: visitors assigned to no recommendations (control), view-based or purchase-based collaborative-filtering recommendations (10% of visitors each)
plain: In a live test with over a million shoppers, showing 'customers who bought this also bought' suggestions led to slightly more purchases. But the suggestions also pushed people towards products that were already popular.
publisher: Lee & Hosanagar (Carnegie Mellon / Wharton); published in Information Systems Research, 2019
sample: 1,138,238 unique users and 82,290 products in 16 categories, 8–22 August 2013

stat.text: more purchases with purchase-based recommendations than with none (randomised test, 1.1M users of one retailer, August 2013)

strengthWhy: Randomised field experiment, 1.1M users, but one retailer for two weeks.
title: Recommendations lift sales but narrow what sells

application: Use the 12% hard-to-use-website figure as an EU baseline when making the case for usability fixes, and add a post-purchase question asking buyers whether anything on the site was hard to use.
do: Ask buyers after purchase whether anything on the site was hard to use, and track the answers.
dont: Assume a completed order means the site worked well for that shopper.
finding: In 2025, 78% of EU internet users aged 16–74 had bought or ordered goods or services online in the previous 12 months, up from 62% in 2015. Of people who bought online in 2025, 63% reported no problems; the most common problems were delivery slower than expected (20%), a website that was difficult to use or worked unsatisfactorily (12%) and wrong or damaged goods (10%).
limitation: Self-reported problems across all shops over a year, so it doesn't show which sites or design issues caused them or how they affect sales; figures are EU averages and vary by country.
measurement: Share of buyers reporting the site was hard to use; Delivery-speed complaints per order; Post-purchase satisfaction score
method: Annual EU survey on ICT (information and communication technology) usage in households and by individuals; most countries collected data in the second quarter of 2025
plain: In an official EU survey, 12% of people who shopped online in 2025 said a website was hard to use or didn't work properly. Slow delivery was the most common complaint, at 20%.
publisher: Eurostat (European Commission), Statistics Explained: E-commerce statistics for individuals
sample: About 330,000 individuals aged 16–74 and 172,000 households in EU member states, reference year 2025

stat.text: of EU online shoppers in 2025 said a website was difficult to use or worked unsatisfactorily (Eurostat ICT survey, about 330,000 people)

strengthWhy: Official EU survey of about 330,000 people in 2025; self-reported.
title: 12% of EU online shoppers found a site hard to use

application: Before adding low-stock badges, test them against no badge and measure daily units sold per product and units per order, not only conversion rate.
do: Test any low-stock badge against no badge and compare units sold per day, not only clicks.
dont: Switch on 'only a few left' warnings as a default sales booster without testing or real stock data.
finding: Once the low-stock message appeared, the time between purchases of a product shortened by about 14.8% on average, mainly for slow-selling items, but average daily sales fell by about 17.6%, most for products usually bought in large quantities. Price cuts worked better: a 1% price reduction was linked to roughly 3% higher daily sales.
limitation: One retailer, one fixed threshold (5 units) and online-only durable goods; data were scraped irregularly and stockout days removed. It is observational, so it doesn't prove scarcity messages lower sales everywhere, and any message must reflect real stock.
measurement: Daily units sold per product; Units per order; Time between purchases per product
method: Regression discontinuity analysis of scraped price, inventory and sales data from before and after a retailer began showing a '5 or less left in stock' message once stock fell below six units; not a randomised test
plain: When one shop started showing 'only 5 left', people bought those items sooner, but overall daily sales of them fell, most for things people usually buy several of. Small price cuts did more to move stock.
publisher: Park, Rabinovich, Tang & Yin (SSRN working paper); published in Journal of Operations Management, 2020
sample: 199 online-only durable-goods products in 28 categories (apparel excluded) at one multi-channel retailer, August 2014 – January 2016

stat.text: lower average daily sales after a '5 or less left' message appeared (199 products at one retailer, 2014–2016, natural experiment)

strengthWhy: Natural experiment at one retailer; not randomised.
title: 'Only 5 left' messages: sooner sales, lower daily sales

application: Audit homepage and listing pages for key messages (delivery terms, offers, category links) shown in ad-like banners, right-hand columns or next to ads, and restyle them to match the page's normal content.
do: Style key messages like the page's normal content, inside the main column.
dont: Put important information in flashy banners, side columns or next to ads.
finding: People largely skipped ads and anything resembling them, including a promotion placed inside article text. In one desktop example, the right-hand column drew 1 of 132 fixations in the content area (about 0.8%). Content placed next to ads, or styled with animation, coloured boxes or text inside images, was often ignored too, and on mobile large images were sometimes mistaken for ads and scrolled past.
limitation: Observational eyetracking on a small sample doing information-seeking tasks in 2018; it shows where people looked, not effects on sales, and doesn't test specific ecommerce promotion designs.
measurement: Clicks on key promo or message; Fixations on promo area in eyetracking; First-click success for finding promoted content
method: Eyetracking study of people doing information-seeking tasks on desktop and mobile sites, analysed through gaze plots and gaze replays
plain: People learn to skip anything that looks like an advert. Useful messages placed in flashy banners, side columns or next to ads often go unseen.
sample: 26 participants for two of the desktop pages; mobile participant count not stated

stat.text: content-area fixations landed on a right-hand column in one desktop example (NN/g eyetracking study, 2018)

strengthWhy: Eyetracking of real tasks, not a controlled experiment.
title: Content styled like an ad gets ignored

application: Trigger a validation error on the payment step (for example a wrong expiry date) and check that every other field, including the card number, keeps its value and the message names the field to fix.
do: Keep every entered payment detail after an error and highlight only the field that needs fixing.
dont: Clear the card number and other fields when one detail fails a check.
finding: According to Baymard's benchmark, 34% of sites fail to keep entered data after a validation error on the payment step, and Baymard says clearing those fields directly caused abandonment in its testing. It recommends keeping entered card data, giving field-specific error messages and scrolling people to the field with the problem.
limitation: A short summary article: the 34% figure has no stated base or date, the site count differs across the page, and it doesn't measure how much abandonment cleared fields cause.
measurement: Payment-step abandonment after an error; Share of fields kept after a validation error; Payment resubmission success rate
method: Summary of Baymard's checkout usability testing and ecommerce UX benchmark; the article doesn't describe the method
plain: When someone mistypes one detail on the payment page, many shops wipe everything they typed. About a third of benchmarked sites do this, and Baymard saw it make shoppers give up.
sample: Benchmark described as 330+ leading ecommerce sites (the site footer says 344); the base for each figure is not stated

stat.text: of sites fail to keep entered data after a payment validation error (Baymard ecommerce UX benchmark; base not stated)

strengthWhy: Expert benchmark of real sites, not a controlled test.
title: Keep card details after a payment error

application: Review account and settings pages: replace any toggle inside a form that needs a Save button with a checkbox, and make every remaining toggle apply its change at once with a clearly visible on state.
do: Use toggles only for settings that apply the moment they are switched.
dont: Put toggles in a form whose changes only apply after pressing Save.
finding: Toggle switches suit on/off settings that take effect immediately, like a physical light switch; when a change needs Save or Submit, a checkbox or radio buttons fit better. Labels should be short, lead with the key word and describe what is on when the switch is on, and the on state should be obvious through knob movement and high-contrast colour.
limitation: Expert guidance built on examples, not a measured study; it doesn't quantify errors from misused toggles, and platform conventions may differ.
measurement: Task success changing a setting; Settings changes left unsaved; Support contacts about settings not applying
method: Not stated (expert guidance illustrated with examples from real apps)
plain: A toggle switch should work like a light switch: flip it and the change happens straight away. If people also have to press Save, use a tick box instead so they're not left guessing.
strengthWhy: Expert advice from real-app examples; no test data shown.
title: Toggle switches should act instantly

application: Check any AI feature (chat assistant, AI search, recommendations) for an upfront statement of what it can do and how reliable it is, an easy way to dismiss or correct it, and an explanation of why it gave each result.
do: Tell people upfront what the AI assistant can do and that it can make mistakes.
dont: Launch an AI feature with no way to dismiss, correct or question its answer.
finding: The paper sets out 18 guidelines across four moments: at first use (say what the AI can do and how often it may be wrong), during use, when it is wrong (easy to dismiss, correct or undo, and explain why it acted), and over time. In the evaluation, explaining why the system acted had one of the highest violation counts, and stating reliability and offering global controls were violated more often than applied.
limitation: Validated for relevance and clarity by practitioners mostly from one company in single sessions; it doesn't show that following the guidelines improves user outcomes, and it fits screen-based products better than voice-only ones.
measurement: Task success with the AI feature; Share of AI answers users correct or dismiss; Rate of users opening 'why this result'
method: Guidelines drawn from over 20 years of research, refined through a heuristic evaluation in which practitioners checked AI features of real products against each guideline, then an expert review of the wording
plain: Researchers wrote 18 rules for AI features, such as saying what the AI can and can't do and making its mistakes easy to fix. When experts checked 20 AI products, explanations of why the AI acted were often missing.
publisher: Microsoft Research (Amershi et al.), ACM CHI 2019
sample: 49 design practitioners evaluating 20 AI-powered products in 10 categories; 11 experts in the final wording review
strengthWhy: Peer-reviewed guidelines checked by experts; user outcomes not measured.
title: 18 checked guidelines for AI features

application: Walk through first launch and key flows, list every permission prompt, and move any that isn't essential to the moment its feature is first used, with a specific sentence explaining why.
do: Ask for location when someone taps 'Find a store near me', with a specific reason.
dont: Fire a stack of permission requests the first time the app opens.
finding: Apple advises requesting access to things like location, camera or contacts only when someone uses a feature that needs it, and not at launch unless the app can't work without it. The explanation in the system alert should be a short, specific, active sentence saying how the data is used; an optional screen before the alert should have one button such as Continue or Next, and tracking prompts preceded by incentives or imitation alerts are rejected in App Store review.
limitation: Apple platform guidance (App Store review rules apply to tracking prompts); it gives no data on acceptance rates and doesn't cover web browser permission prompts.
measurement: Permission grant rate per prompt; Share of prompts shown at launch; Feature use after permission request
method: Not stated (platform design guidance)
plain: Apps should ask to use your location, camera or contacts only when you start a feature that needs it, and say plainly why. Requests with no obvious reason make people suspicious.
strengthWhy: Platform guidance; no test data shown.
title: Ask for phone permissions at the moment of need

application: Before running a free-shipping promotion, forecast its effect on returns by product risk group, and consider excluding or separately handling high-return categories.
do: Track returns alongside sales whenever you test a free-shipping offer.
dont: Judge a free-shipping promotion on order count alone.
finding: In the randomised field experiment with 760,395 customers, those sent a free-shipping code bought slightly more often (purchase incidence .404 vs .397) and spent more on products with a high return risk, and their average return share rose (.337 vs .333). The retailer's panel data showed the same pattern: free shipping lifted orders mainly through riskier items, which come back more often.
limitation: One European retailer selling through catalogue and online; the per-customer effects are small, and the paper's profit estimates come from the authors' model rather than directly from the experiment.
measurement: Purchase incidence; Return share by product category; Net revenue after returns
method: Four studies: a panel-data model, a randomised field experiment (free-shipping promo code mailed with a catalogue vs. no code), a post-order survey with propensity score matching, and an online 2x2 experiment.
plain: Giving customers a free-shipping code made them buy a little more often, but they leaned toward items they were more likely to send back, so returns crept up too.
publisher: Journal of Marketing Research (Shehu, Papies & Neslin, 2020)
sample: Field experiment: 760,395 customers of a leading European online retailer (380,551 test, 379,844 control), Aug-Oct 2014; panel: 9,460 customers, 2010-2013; survey: 4,491; online experiment: 401.

stat.text: customers were randomly split into free-shipping-code and no-code groups in a European retailer's 2014 field experiment (Journal of Marketing Research).

strengthWhy: Randomised field experiment with 760,395 customers at one retailer.
title: Free-shipping codes: more orders, and more returns

application: Check that the site has HTTPS and a valid manifest (name, icons, start URL, display mode) before promising an add-to-home-screen experience, and don't rely on an install prompt in Safari.
do: Add a complete web app manifest if you want people to keep your site on their home screen.
dont: Assume every browser will offer to install your site; Safari shows no prompt.
finding: About 24.5% of crawled websites use either a service worker or a web app manifest, roughly 9% use a manifest, and only 3.3% on desktop and 3.5% on mobile use both. The chapter notes that Chrome and Edge no longer need a service worker to offer installation, while Safari shows no install prompt.
limitation: Counts technical features, not whether visitors install or use the site as an app; the chapter's service-worker shares differ between sections (about 19-20%), so treat feature percentages as approximate.
measurement: Manifest presence and validity; Installs from browser prompt; Repeat visits from installed users
method: Analysis of HTTP Archive crawl data for desktop and mobile, detecting service workers and web app manifests; queries published on GitHub.
plain: Very few websites are set up so people can install them on their phone like an app: only about 3.5% of mobile sites have both technical pieces that make it work well.

stat.text: of mobile sites have both a service worker and a web app manifest (Web Almanac 2025, 15.4M mobile sites, July 2025 crawl).

strengthWhy: Large real-world dataset with a stated size and period.
title: Few sites have both pieces needed to install as an app

application: If you offer pay-later, A/B test it with higher-value baskets first and measure conversion and order value, not only the share of orders paid that way.
do: Test pay-later on higher-value baskets and measure conversion and order value.
dont: Quote a vendor's best-case revenue figure as the result you will get.
finding: Stripe reports that over two-thirds of pay-later volume came from purchases it judged would not otherwise have happened, and that businesses saw revenue rise by up to 14% in sessions where pay-later was offered, through higher conversion and order value. The largest conversion gain was on orders of $500 to $1,500.
limitation: A payment provider's own blog about methods it sells; it reports a best case ('up to') rather than an average, with no conversion rates, confidence intervals or test dates, and no definition of how 'net-new' sales were identified.
measurement: Checkout conversion rate; Average order value; Share of pay-later orders replacing card orders
method: A/B test: in half of eligible checkout sessions a buy-now-pay-later option (Affirm, Afterpay or Klarna) appeared among the payment methods; in the other half it did not.
plain: When shoppers saw a pay-later option at checkout, Stripe says many of those orders were extra sales, especially for pricier baskets. It's the payment company's own data, with few details.
sample: More than 150,000 global checkout sessions across B2C businesses; period not stated
strengthWhy: Vendor A/B test; randomisation, period and average effect not stated.
title: Stripe's split test of pay-later at checkout

application: Browse the top tasks in a private window on a phone, count every overlay that appears, and remove or merge any that aren't required.
do: Count every overlay a first-time mobile visitor sees and cut it to the essentials.
dont: Stack a newsletter pop-up on top of the cookie banner on the first page.
finding: In NN/g's survey of 452 US adults, pop-ups ranked among the most disliked advertising techniques. In usability sessions, shoppers often met several overlays in one visit (privacy notices, marketing sign-ups, browser prompts), sometimes stacked on small screens or returning as floating widgets after being closed, which participants found exhausting.
limitation: The survey measures attitudes, not behaviour; the article gives no timing rules, no participant count for its observations, and no data on sign-up or sales effects.
measurement: Overlays shown per session; Overlay dismissal rate; Bounce rate on first visit
method: Survey of US adults rating advertising techniques, plus observations from NN/g ecommerce usability studies on live sites.
plain: People strongly dislike pop-ups, and when several appear in one visit, like a cookie notice followed by a sign-up offer, they find it exhausting.
sample: 452 US adult survey respondents; usability participant count not stated
strengthWhy: Survey plus usability observations; participant count not stated.
title: Stacked pop-ups wear visitors down

application: Where shoppers compare details closely, test a single-column list layout with key attributes against a dense tile grid on category pages.
do: Test a list layout with key details for products people compare closely.
dont: Assume a dense tile grid is always the fastest to scan.
finding: Finding a target product took longer and needed more eye fixations in the block format (a grid of tiles) than in the vertical or T-shaped list formats, which performed similarly. Participants also rated the vertical list slightly higher for browsing and for clarity of product information.
limitation: Small sample of young participants in one lab; the paper's degrees of freedom don't fully match its stated sample, it reports no pairwise tests, and it measures search speed, not purchases.
measurement: Time to find a target product; Product clicks from listings; Add-to-cart rate from listings
method: Within-subject eyetracking lab study: participants found target items on pages using three list formats (vertical, T-shaped, block) at two task difficulties; analysed with two-way ANOVA.
plain: In a small lab test, people found the product they were looking for faster in a simple vertical list than in a dense grid of tiles, and their eyes jumped around less.
sample: 28 participants aged 20-26 at Alibaba's user experience lab in China (3 excluded); card-sort pre-study with 25
strengthWhy: Small within-subject eyetracking lab study (28 participants), one platform.
title: Vertical product lists searched faster than block grids

application: On category pages, show roughly 10-30 products at first, lazy-load more as people scroll, switch to a 'Load more' button after 50-100 items, and check that Back returns people to the same spot.
do: Load a batch of products, then offer a clear 'Load more' button.
dont: Send people back to the top of the list when they press Back.
finding: With pagination, test participants browsed far fewer products and mostly used only Next and Previous. Infinite scrolling led people to view many more products but look at each less closely, and could make the footer unreachable; a 'Load more' button produced more browsing than pagination with closer reading than infinite scroll, yet only 8% of the top 50 US sites used one, and over 90% of those that did broke the Back button.
limitation: Published in 2016 and summarised by the researchers themselves; it gives no participant numbers or measured effect sizes, and the recommended product counts are expert judgement.
measurement: Products viewed per category visit; Back-button return-to-position success; Product page clicks from listings
method: Year-long large-scale usability testing of 50+ leading ecommerce sites on desktop and mobile, plus a benchmark of the top 50 US ecommerce sites.
plain: Splitting shop listings into numbered pages made people look at far fewer products. Endless scrolling showed more but got skimmed. A 'Load more' button gave the best mix.
sample: 50+ ecommerce sites tested; top 50 US sites benchmarked; participant count not stated

stat.text: of the top 50 US ecommerce sites used a 'Load more' button in Baymard's benchmark, reported in 2016.

strengthWhy: Usability testing and a site benchmark, not a controlled test.
title: 'Load more' beats pagination and endless scroll in shop lists

application: On grocery or repeat-purchase listings, keep an add button on each product tile and switch it to a quantity stepper with a typeable field after the first tap.
do: Switch a product's Add button to a minus-number-plus quantity control after the first tap.
dont: Leave the button unchanged with only a tiny 'in cart' label.
finding: In Baymard's grocery testing, shoppers adding dozens of items lost track of what was already in the cart and went back to check, which slowed them down and sometimes led to duplicate purchases; small 'in cart' labels were easy to miss, especially on mobile. Turning the Add to Cart button into a quantity control once an item is added confirmed the action and made changes quick.
limitation: Grocery-specific and qualitative, with no participant count or figures on the page; the full guideline set is behind Baymard Premium and was not used.
measurement: Items added from listing pages; Cart page visits per order; Duplicate-item removals in cart
method: Large-scale usability testing of grocery sites in which participants browsed food categories and added products, plus observations from Baymard's grocery site benchmark.
plain: When people fill a big grocery basket from product lists, they forget what's already in it. Changing the Add button into a quantity counter after the first tap shows what's added.
sample: Participant count not stated; benchmark of major US and UK grocery sites
strengthWhy: Seen in usability testing, not a controlled experiment.
title: Turn 'Add' into a quantity control in grocery lists

application: List every status message in a key flow and check that errors stay on screen until fixed, toasts carry nothing people must act on, and each actionable notice has a single short action.
do: Keep error messages in the page until the problem is fixed.
dont: Put a must-do action in a message that disappears after a few seconds.
finding: Carbon separates inline notifications (shown in the task flow and kept until dismissed or resolved), toasts (short, non-modal messages that can be set to disappear after five seconds and need a close button), actionable notifications (one action, kept until dismissed) and callouts (load with the page, can't be dismissed, for advice before a task). Messages should be one or two short sentences, and anything shown in a toast that disappears should be findable elsewhere.
limitation: One design system's guidance with no user data; the page is inconsistent about which variants it supports, and its timing rules are defaults rather than tested optimums.
measurement: Share of error messages that persist until resolved; Notifications with more than one action; Support contacts about missed messages
method: Not stated
plain: Messages that matter, like errors, should stay on screen until sorted. Short pop-up confirmations, called toasts, can fade away, so never put anything someone must act on in one.
strengthWhy: Platform or design-system guidance; no test data shown.
title: Choosing inline, toast or callout notifications
